ORDINARA; BRANCH.—For the Policies on single lives for the whole term with profits, which constitute the bulk of the risks, the average amount assured by each policy is nearly £137, the average Annual Premium £4 Bs. 6d., or at the rate of £3 4s. 9d. per cent. on the sum assured. From Mr. Hughes' report it will be observed that the num- ber of policies in force (exclusive of annuities) is 31,616, the Premium Income being £142,642. The business of this Branch alone is therefore of considerable magnitude and im- portance. The Valuation of the Liabilities has been made upon a basis the effect of which is to require a larger Reserve than most Life Assurance Companies retain or think necessary. INDUSTRIAL BRANCII.—In this Branch the average amount assured by each Policy is £9 45. 10d., the average weekly pre- mium almost exactly 2d., being• at the rate of £4 12s. id. per cent. per annum on the sum assured. The number of policies in force is £8,822,519, so that the lives assured comprise about one-eighth of the entire population of Great Britain and Ireland. The annual premium income is £2,051,024. Experience has shown that for business of this character two conditions are indispensable; the premiums must be payable weekly and agents must be employed tocall regularly for their collection. These two conditions occasion heavy expense, and as a necessary consequence the rates of premium are and must be higher than the Ordinary Branch. But offering as you do both systems of assunance to the public, you find that the majority are willing to pay the higher rates for the convenience of the weekly receipt and collection of the prethiums. Careful consideration has been given to the principles moon which these liabilities should be valued, comprehending risks from infancy to extreme old age. By the requirements of the Act of Parliament returns have to be made to the Board of Trade of the sums assured and premiums payable at every age of life, and calculations have been made of the present value of these quantities for all the policies in force. But of the recently effected policies, a large proportion are on the lives of children with whom the risk of death diminishes, instead of increasing as they become older; again, a large number of these recently effected policies are allowed to lapse after they have been a short time only in force. To such policies, therefore, it seems to me that the usual methods of Valuation are not properly ap- plicable. It was therefore decided, as explained in Mr. Dewey's report, that for Whole Life Policies exceeding £5O, all Endowment and Joint Life Assurances, and all other policies which had been five years in force, and where the lives assured were above ten years of age, a reserve should be made on the same principles as in the Ordinary Branch, except that the Tables of Mortality employed should be the English Life 'Tables. The other policies of which although the number is large the liability under the* is very small, have been regarded as short term risks. It is in the highest degree satisfactory to find that after sub- jecting the liabilities to the stringent tests that have been described your resources have been found to be so ample to meet all your engagements; and the general results of this searching investigation cannot but be most gratifying to all who are interested in the prosperity of the Company. EXTRACT FROM THE REPORT OF MR. W. HUGHES, ACTUARY OF THE ORDINARY BRANCH.

There were in force at the date of the Valuation 31,616 Life Assurance Policies, assuring with Bonita £4,242,949, and pro- ducing an Annual Premium Income of £142,642. The Imme- diate Annuities are 186 in number, and involve a charge of £4,202 per annum. The Table of Mortality employed for the valuation of the Lift' Assurance Policies is the Institute of Actuaries Hat Table, and for the Immediate Annuities Mr. Finlalson's Government Annuity Tables, being the same that were used at the last valuation. The rate of intere,t assumed in the calculations fcr both kinds of contract is 3 per cent. The whole of the loading, or difference between the premiums aetually receivabte and the pure premiums, has been reserved. This loading amounts to £31,377 per annum, and is available to meet future expenses and provide for future profits. EXTRACT FROM VIE REPORT OF MR. T. C. DEWEY, ACTUARY OF THE INDUSTRIAL BRANCH.
The policies in existence were 4,822,519 in number, assuring the sum of £44,558,814, and producing a weekly income from premiums. of £39,442 Ifs., and an Annual Premium Income of

.£2.051,024. The special tables for Endowment Assurance, issued after the last valuation, have been very successful, the amount of busi- ness now in existence producing an Annual Premium Income of £32,700. The facilities offered in this Branch for Assurances on the lives of the middle classes, have resulted in a large accession of incime. the Premium Income derived from Assurances of £5O and upwards being now £115,419 per annum,

During the Quinquennium the inortality of this Branch of the Company's business has been carefully recorded week by week. The results nearly correspond with Dr. Farr's English Life Table (No. 3), and, as directed by you, I have taken that Table as the basis of the valuation for every description of risk. As at previous investigations I have assumed that the interest realized will, for the future, be £3 per cent. per annum. Male and Female lives have been kept separate throughout the valuation, the number of each sex assured is in nearly similar proportion to that shown by the population of the country. Each year's business has been valued separately, and as the oldest policies have been 30 years in existence sixty separate valuations have consequently been necessary. A pure Premium Valuation has been made for all policies, upon lives exceeding ten years of age, which have been in existence five years, and for all policies issued under the Endow- ment Assurance. the Middle Class, and the Joint Life Tables, however short their duration. For Infantile Assurances and all other policies under £3O in 1 amount and of less than five years' duration, a method has been adopted which produces a liability oh every policy and reserves a sum sufficient to meet the permanent expenses of the Branch it folluws, therefore, that all negative values have been excluded.

LET OTHERS WEEP.
"Let others weep." s,le lightly cried. No tears sha.ll flow from me, I ween. My life is fair—its lucid tide Reflects a youthful summer's sheen. The stream is deep : Let others weep
‘. Let ottiers weep :" oh, let me feel o rombrous frown of care oppress,— I love the fashions nnnpareil, And all of life's exquisiteness That I can reap: Let others weep
" Let others weep :" from scented halls, Where good and noble faces shine, The voice of Pleasure sweetly calls, And I must go where, eyes like mine, Their lustre keep: Let others weep !
" Let others weep :" is life so long That I have time to think of tears ? Ah, no! for me the la,ighing, song! The ear is sad that sadness hears, And tears are cheap: Let others weep
Warrington, 6tli March, 1332.

I blow an arouse Through the world's wide house, To quicken the torpid earth: Grappling I fling ' Each feeble thing, But bring strong life to the birth. I wrestle and frown, And topple down; I wrench, I rend, I uprooot ; Yet the violet Is born where I set The sole of my flying foot. mends violets and anemones to February, who retires into the background.] And in my wake Frail wind-flowers quake And the catkins promise fruit. I drive ocean ashore With rush and roar, • And he cannot say me nay : Iy harpstrings all Are the forests tall, Making music when I play, And as others perforce, So I on my course Run and needs must run, With sap on the mount And buds past count And rivers and clouds and sun, With seasons and breath, And time and death, And all that has yet begun. [Becore March has done speaking a voice is heard approaching accompanied by a twittering of birds. April comes along singing, and stands outside and out of sight to tinish her song.]

APRIL (outside). Pretty little three Sparrows in a tree, Light upon the wing; Though you cannot sing, You can chirp of Spring Chirp of Spring to me, Sparrows, from your tree. —CHRISTINA ROSSETTI, froth "A Pageant and other Poems."

Count D'Orsay, in remarking on a beauty-speck on the cheek of Lady Southampton, compared it to a gem on a rose leaf. "The compliment is far-fetched." observed her Ladyship. "How can that be," rejoined the Count, " when it was made on the spot ?"

Never try to hurry Providence. It will come in due time—whatever it is—the something that is to fill your life and satisfy your heart. It may be something utterly dif- ferent from anything of which you dream. Don't take up with any less thing, and think it will do. It will never do. " Why, Mr. 8.," said a tall youth to a little personage who was in company with half a dozen huge men, "I pro- test you are so very small I did not see you before." "Very likely," replied the little gentleman' "I am like a sixpence among six copper pennies—not easily perceived, but worth the whole of them." A lecturer having been invited to deliver a lecture in a mountain town, wrote to the committee of invitation :—" I am informed that the roads leading up to your place are so steep and rocky that even a donkey couldn't climb them; therefore you most excuse me from making the attempt." Ha WAS unanimously excused. Charles Bannister, that inveterate punster, coming into a coffee-room one stormy night, said, "He never saw such a wind in his life." Saw a wind," replied a friend; "I never heard of such a thing as seeing a wind; pray, what was it like ?" "Like ?" answered Charles, "like to have blown my hat off."

A BIRD'S NEST IN A Buov.—Birds have been known to choose curious spots for building their homes, but perhaps the oddest place that could have been selected was a buoy in Long Island Sound (near New York), which was patronised for years by a pair of fish-hawks. The top of this buoy is shaped like a grocer's basket, to which the industrious hawks carried enough straw to build a nest. The same birds occu- pied the spot for a considerable period, and brought up their families apparently without difficulty. On the approach of a vessel the female used to fly round the buoy in circles. Daring the winter storms the nest suffers severe damage, , but the birds accept their fate with resignation, for they set I to repairing their dwelling as soon as spring-time arrives.— Little Falk' Magazine. Some years ago there was a number of army officers stopping at an hotel in Washington. Among them were a Captain Emerson and a Captain Jones. Emerson and Jones used to have a good deal of fun together at the dinner-table and elsewhere. One day at the dinner-table, when the dining-hall was well filled, Captain Jones finished his dinner first, got up, and walked almost to the dining-ball door, when Emerson called to him in a loud voice, " Hallo, Cap- tain! see here. I want to speak to you a minute." The captain turned and walked back to the table and bent over him, when Emerson whispered, "I wanted to ask you how far you would have gone if I had not spoken to you." The captain never changed a muscle, but straightened up and put his fingers into his vest pocket, and said, "Captain Emerson, I don't know of a man in the world I'd rather lend five dollars to than you, but the fact is I haven't a cent. with me to-day," and he turned on his heel and walked away. Emerson was the colour of a dozen rainbows, but he had to stand it. Os THE SLEEP OF INFANTS.—Dr. B. W. Richardson, writ- ing in House and Home on the care of the young, says : The infant should sleep in its own little bed or cot, should be allowed to sleep when it likes, and may pass three parts of its life in sleep. It should be put to bed at regular hours, and the bed should be so soft that the little body finds rest in every part. The infant should be kept warm while sleeping. The atmosphere of the room should be pure and comfort- ably warm, and the air should not be excluded. All arti- ficial methods of causing sleep are bad. Walking about with the child and rocking and jogging it are bad habits. Once taught these habits children fail to go to sleep with- oat them, and they create disturbed sleep, dreams, and starlings, which lead to feverish fretting the next day. Soothing syrups, laulanum, poppies, and all sleeping drugs are most injurious as a means of producing sleep, and should only he used under competent medical advice. They ought to be excluded from the houses of all psrsons who call themselves respectable, except, when prescribed, under medical direction. The sleep of the child should never be disturbed by noises and sudden surprises. It is most hurtful to take up an infant from its quiet repose to show it to strangers, or to amuse it in gaslight, candlelight, or lamp- light. The bedroom should be airy, light, and clean, and while the cot should be shaded, sunlight when present should be freely admitted. BRADFORD AND THE LEGEND OF THE BOAR.—Less than a hundred years since it was a quiet country town perched on a slope by the beck-side, amid the bare bleak uplands of Western Yorkshire; now its factories may be counted by hundreds—their hands by tens of thousands—the capital employed in them and passing annually through its banks perhaps even by hundreds of millions. The older part of the town lay near the head of an open valley in the uplands, down which a stream, or beck, descended towards a marly flat below. This the traveller was obliged to traverse; hence the name of the town, Brad,—or Broad—ford. The marsh has disappeared, having been drained towards the end of the last century, when the canal was made which brought the town into connection with Liverpool by uniting it to the main water-way from the latter place to Leeds. The town makes a little figure in ancient history. It has, indeed, its legend to account for the boar's head which fignres so prominently in the decorations of its municipal buildings. This is of the usual character, and tells how in olden times the forests around were infested by a wild boar of pesuliar ferocity, which had long defied all the efforts of the hunters, and had become a terror to the district. A reward was offered for its destruction, and a young man addressee himself to the task, and slew the tyrant of the woods. In proof of his success, he cut oat the tongue, and carried it off as a trophy, leaving the huge carcase where it fell. Presently comes by an ill-conditioned fellow, who, seeing the boar lying dead, thinks that he has a good chance of winning distinction cheaply, and hews off the animal's bead. With this he hastens to the authorities and claims the re-,vard. At this juncture, however, the real conqueror of the monster enters and indignantly puts forward his own claim. The pretender, however, is not to be baulked, and points triumphantly to the head as a surer proof of the deed than any words. 'But look for the tongue !" exclaims the other, and when this member is found to be missing he pro- duces it, to the confusion of the impostor. So a tongueless boar's head became the cognisance of Bradford.—Our Own Country. EPPS'S COCOA.—GRATEFUL AND COMFORTING. By a thorough knowledge of the natural laws which govern the oper- ations ol digestion and nutrition, and by a earekul applicatiou the tiitoprtenerties of well selected cocoa, Mr. Epps has prov:ded our break .ables wfth a delicately-flavoured beverage which may save us many heavy doctors' bills. It is by the judicious use of such articles of diet that a constitution may be gradually built up until strong enough to resist every tendency to disease. Hundreds of subtle maladies are floating around us ready to attack wherevek there is a weak point. We may escape many a fatal shaft by keeping ourselves well fortified w' th pure blood and a properly kourisheil frame."—Cm. div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

• The biography of Carlyle, by Mr. J. A. Fronde, which is looked for with much curiosity and expectation, will be issued by Messrs. Longmane during the present month. The Iron and Steel Inetitate, says the Atheneum, have arranged to hold their annual meeting this year in Vienna, commencing on the 20th of September. A visit will be paid to Gratz, the capital of Styria, and other places of metallur- gical interest. Swedish journals say that Baron Nordenskjold will under- take another Polar expedition as soon as the necessary pre- parations are made; but that will hardly be before 1834. A ship is to be built purposely for the voyage, and King Oscer will defray one-third of the expenses. The Taeglicher Rundschan says that the question of using the flow of rivers to provide the force necessary to generate electric light is rapidly coming Into prominence. Steps are being taken to utilise the Rhone at Geneva, the Furens at St. Etienne in France, and similar projects are afoot in Brazil. THE STORLGE OF POWER.—Professor Ayrton recently delivered a lecture at the London institution before a large aeclience on the storage of power. Among other experie ments, the lecture theatre was lighted, a circular saw driven, and a hoist used for raising boxes entirely by means of electricity, produced the day before at the other side of London, and transported to the institution in Faeare's accu- mulators. The total energy thus conveyed was about 30,000,C00 foot pounds, or about 25-horse power for one hour. AN ELECTRICAL TRA.MCAR.—On the morning of the 22nd ult. the first electric tramcar ever operated in this country, and, we believe, the first in the world, with the exception of some experiments made in France and Belgium last year with the same system, viz., Faure's accumulators was run in the aggregate 21 miles. The dead weight of the car was about 5-1 tons; the speed reached about seven miles an hour. Although the car was clumsily built, a bad fit on the rails, owing to the wheels having been constructed for a different pattern of tram-rail than where the run took place, the ex- periment was successful, stopping and starting the car being effected with great promptitude. The trial took place on the Leytonetone branch of the North Metropolitan Tram- ways, on the private line leading to their works. The work is in the hands of Mr. Radcliffe Ward.—Engineer. LIQUID FUEL FOR STEAM Botenns.—Experiments with liquid fuel in steam-boiler furnaces have been made at the works of the Co•operative Laundry, with the apparatus of Messrs. Crellin and Rolfe. The boiler is of 20-horse power, and has a large call for steam besides that required for the engine. The arrangement consists of a compound jet fixed through the sight hole of the furnace door. Steam is sent through one jet, which draws up and forces into the furnace, in the form of fine spray, a "special paraffin oil," while at the same time the air requisite for combustion is drawn in and highly heated in transit. No cold air enters at all; and even with dampen closed, the combustion is perfect and the temperature is much intensified. The patentees apply their system to all purposes for which a great and pure heat is required. SINGULAR FIND OF AN ANCIENT BOOK.-9 copy of the " Cronycle of Engelonde," printed at Westminster in 1497, by Wynkyn de Worde, has this week been bought by Mr. Robert Holt, bookseller, of Smithfield Market, for the sum of 205.! The book came from a Cheshire farm, with a quan- tity of other printed matter which the frugal housewife had used, in the country phrase, for " beating " the fire. Some of the earlier pages have accordingly been cremated, but the bulk of the copy is in a fairly good condition, and at the end is the colophon and the conspicuous device of William Caxton. Before passing into the hands of its present owner the book was vainly offered to more than one book- seller or collector, who failed to examine its with sufficient care. The copy sold at the Hastings sale fetched £6O, al- though it also was slightly imperfect. There is a long ac- count of the Althorp copy in Dibdin's " Bibliotheca Spen- ceriana." Lowndes only knew of the existence of four copies. MIGRATION OF SPECIES THROUGH THE SUEZ CANAL.— Dr. C. Keller is at present making observations in the Suez Canal and the seas at its two extremities, with reference to the interchange of species from the Red Sea and the Medi- terranean since the opening of the Canal. A communica- tion from him was read at the last meeting of the St. Gallen Commercial Geographical Society. The mixing of species is proceeding only slowly, the comparative smallness of the migratory movements being attributed to the influence of the Bitter Lakes, through which the Canal passes. The species in the Bitter Lakes themselves appear to have been the first to spread. One of the most interesting discoveries of Dr. Keller is a new species of sponge whose habitat is the Bitter Lakes, but which has now spread along the Canal in the direction of the Mediterranean. It has a rich violet colour, and has been named bg Dr. Keller Lessepsia violacea. Several large fish from the Mediterranean have migrated to Timsah Lake, and now constitute an important source of food supply to the inhabitants of Ismailia. Large specimens of Solea vulgaris are now taken there. Several species of fish have also penetrated to the same point from the Indian Ocean, and are regularly sold in Ismailia, including a large dark green mackerel. POURING OIL ON TROUBLED WATERS.—During a storm recently at Peterhead. Mr. John Shields, of Perth, made some successful experiments in pouring oil upon a rough sea. Five years ago Mr. Shields was making a mill pond in Perthshire, when he observed that the water, on which the wind was blowing, became suddenly smooth, and ascer- tained that this was owing to some oil having been acciden- tally spilt from machinery. This led Mr. Shields to consider '1 whether it would be possible by similar means to becalm the entrance to a harbour in a rough sea, and Peterhead, from its geographical position' was chosen as the most suit- able place for experiments. Iron and leaden piping was laid running from the beach into the sea, right in front of the entrance to the harbour. A force-pump was attached to the land end of the piping, and near it was placed a large barrel containing one hundred gallons of oil. Recently Mr. Shields was informed by the Meteorological Office that the sea was rough at Peterhead, and he went there from Perth, accomoanied by several seafaring gentlemen from Dundee and Aberdeen. When the white-crested waves were rising a height of ten to twenty feet at the harbour entrance the oil pump was put in motion causing the oil to spread in the bottom of the sea, and on its gradually rising to the surface the white foam entirely disappeared, and althoug the swell continued the surface of the sea was perfectly smooth, so that a ship or a small boat could have entered the dock without the slightest danger, which it would have been im- possible to do before the oil was distributed in the water. The experiments satisfied the shipmasters who witnessed them. Mr. Shields it is added, is willing to give any har- bour board the benefit of his invention, and render them assistance in carrying it out. CONVERTING SUGAR INTO CHARCOAL.—A given quantity of water will not dissolve an unlimited amount of sugar. If we still keep adding sugar to the liquid it will be found that a certain point is reached, beyond which the water can dissolve no more, and any farther additions of sneer will simply fall to the bottom of the vessel. The solution is then said to be saturated. Cold water dissolves three times

its own weight of sugar; hot water a little more. Tempera- ture, however, in this case influences more the rapidity of solution than the amount of substance dissolved. A cup of hot tea, it is well known' dissolves sugar much more rapidly than a cap of cold tea. Farther it is found that stirring the tea also hastens the solution of the sugar. The reason of this is, that, the liquid being still, that portion of it in the neighbourhood of the stationary dissolving lumps becomes fully saturated, and further solution is practically stayed. By stirring it, fresh portions of the tea are brought into contact with the undissolved mass, and solution is speedily effected. By such means, then, our lamp of sugar may be mechanically broken up, the process being so complete that the cohesion existing even between its ultimate particles is overcome, and its molecules of inconceivable minuteness are separated one from another. Is it possible to still further reduce our lamp of sugar? We shall see. Chemists tell us that each molecule of sugar is made up of the solid ele- ment carbon, or charcoal, and the compound substance water. Water, as we have already learned, composed of the two ele- mentary gases, oxygen and hydrogen, in the proportion of two of the latter to one of the latter. It is a substance for which oil of vitriol, or sulphuric acid, has a strong chemical affinity, as may be easily demonstrated by adding a few drops of the acid to half a wine-glassful of water. The ac- tion of combination is so intense and energetic that a consi- derable amount of heat is generated ; so much, indeed, that the glass becomes quite hot. This affinity of the acid for water may be taken advantage of in showing the chemical composition of sugar. Pulverise a lump or two, and place the powder in a large cup, or empty mustard-tin, then pour over it a few drops of sulphuric acid, and observe the rapid change. The water in the sugar dissociates itself from the carbon, and unites energetically with the acid, and at the end of a few seconds a black mass of amorphous carbon is all that remains of the sugar. The water may also be separated from the carbon in sugar by means of the force of heat. Pound up a few lumps as before, and empty the powder into a test-tube, flask, or other suitable vessel, and heat it gently over a lamp-flame. The crystals break up, and the powder readily melts into a yellowish-coloured liquid, and water, in the form of steam, is rapidly driven off. Continuing the heat, more water is expelled, the liquid gets denser, and the colour gradually changes to orange hue, with little dark specks occurring here and there. Eventu- ally, however, the volume of expelled steam decreases, the mass swells, becomes quite black, and in a few seconds more nothing remains in the tube but a quantity of rather spongy- looking charcoal.—Science for All.

CULTURE, &c. At Causeway Farm, Hereford, a ewe has given birth to four lambs, three of which are alive and doing well. The Earl of Dalhousie has granted a premium of £lOO in order to improve the breed of horses amongst his tenantry. In an article contributed to the Irish Farmers' Gazette by Professor Ferguson, on the soundness of horses as affected by what is termed roaring or whistling, the practice of striking or threatenem horses to make them grunt is con- demned as quite untrustworthy, together with that of pinch- ing the neck to induce a cough. Professor Ferguson con- siders that the only test is a severe gallop, which, by in- creasing and accelerating the respiration, will afford the evidence required. We are glad to see that Professor Ferguson lends his authority to discountenance the brutal practices alluded to above. HEREFORDS a. SHORTHORNS.—The following statement in reference to the respective merits of the Hereford and Shorthorn cattle as beef-producers is made by Mr. H. C. Burleigh, in a communication to the Kansas City Commers cial Indicator :—" When I commenced breeding cattle, something over thirty years ago, I was very much preju- diced in favour of shorthorns, perhaps as much so as some of their best friends of to-day, and I will say that I still admire a well-bred, fully-developed shorthorn as much as anyone. I was so prejudiced that I could see nothing de- sirable in any other breed, until about twenty years ago I put in some high-grade Herefords to fatten with high-grade shorthorn steers. In this first experiment I could hardly believe what my eyes assured me were facts, and it was not until I had tested the two breeds over and over again that I could fully realise the facts, that the same feed that would make 41b. of beef with shorthorns would make 51b. with Herefords, and when marketed the Herefords were worth, on an average, one halfpenny per lb. more money. At last, after buying the best Herefords in this vicinity that I could, I went and bought, in company with Mr. G. E Thores, the entire Hillhurst herd of Herefords, of the Hon. M. H. Coch- rane; this last-named purchase was in 1868, and the Here- ford cattle have been constantly gaining, not only in my estimation, but in public favour. They are destined to be the beef-producing cattle of this great nation." OBJECTORS TO AGRICULTURAL REFORM say that the men on the verge of ruin will not be saved by giving them security for their capital invested in improvements. Why not A considerable proportion of such tenants have in- vested capital in improvements, and would be entitled to compensation if they had to quit their holdings and to many others the reform referred to would give hope and new energy, as well as renewed credit. It is the utter hope- lessness of their position which is driving farmers to do anythinl to get out of it. Under existing circumstances the tenant farmer who should make a good tight to increase the production of his farm, and so pay his way, would have the probability of an increased rent before his eyes. To him the application of new discoveries in science and new inventions in mechanics may prove but a short-lived advantage, as all may be taken from him in rent. The re- cord of increased rental in twenty-four years is full of sig- nificance. It shows that rent is an Aaron's rod that swal- lows up all agricultural profits. Everything done by or for the tenant increases the competition against him; and until he is absolutely secured by law against the confiscation of , his improvements, either by taking them from him when I be quits his holding, or by renting him upon them if he stays in it, science and invention might almost as well die as to make progress, so far as he is concerned. AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION.—The muster of a class of DO less than six hundred students attending Professor Tanner's' new series of lectures on the Principles of Agriculture is in I itself a novelty, but it is one which is full of encourage- ment. Its influence will be all the greater as every one of these students is destined, in some sense, to be a focus' whence further instruction may be opened, for all are already teachers under the Education Department, or persons pre- , paring to introduce this particular subject either into our I Science Classes or into our Elementary Schools. There can I be no better proof of the interest awakened in the country I than the strong desire for this instruction aroused in the minds of teachers throughout England; and if the demand insures a corresponding supply, it will only be needful to see that the right sort of instruction is imparted. We need, however, greatly-increased facilities not only for assisting these teachers in qualifying for the posts they aspire to, but for meeting the requirements of the sons of tenant-farmers. The necessity for this help has been specially dealt with in the evidence recently taken by the Royal Commission on Agriculture. If we can have teachers.' classes numbering their 600, and if we can have between 5,000 and 6,000 can- didates entering for the annual examination on the princi- ples of agriculture, it now only needs a little good manage- , ment to make agricultural education progress OR a scale far ' more worthy of its national importance than anything we have yet seen attempted in this country, which, so far as I facilities for scientific instruction exist, is so lamentably behind both our continental and transatlantic neighbours.— The Farmer. INJURIOUS INSECTS.—THE TURNIP FLY.—For several years Miss Ormerod has done the State good service by publishing annual reports of observations of insects injurious, to farm crops. These have been very asceptable and useful to agriculturists, because they have contained descriptions of the most destructive insects, which have been given in plain, simple language, and illustrated with figures of various insects in their different stages, and have also been accompanied by all the known modes of prevention and cure as well as by suggestions, in some cases from the authoress, and those who have given her assistance, as to likely means of hindeting attacks. Miss Ormerod is doing an excellent work in encouraging farmers to observe more closely the conditions in which crops are more or less liable to insect attack, such as the influences of abnormal seasons and the methods of cultivation of certain crops, and by col- lating the results of their practical experience with the valuable addition of her scientific knowledge of entomology; and she is gradually collecting a mass of most valuable ma- terials which cannot fail to be of great advantage and in- terest, and of direct practical utility. Taking one of many insect pests mentioned, it will be seen from this report that fly attack in 1831 extended from Northumberland and Cum- berland, along the coast by Kent to Devon and Somerset, Including in this range some of the more inland counties, as Beds, Herts, Wilts, and the Isle of Wight. In the south- midland and western districts it occurred in localities in Oxfordshire, Gloucestershire, Monmouthshire, Hereford- shire, and Derbyshire. It was less prevalent in Stafford- shire and Cheshire; and, curiously, West Lancashire, for some reason or other, it is said, is never troubled with it. In Scotland, we find that the southern counties were exten- sively visited by this scourge, and the Border counties also. Many of Miss Ormerod'a correspondents speak of "hundreds of acres having been sown twice and ultimately failed," and in other places nearly everyone sowed twice, and then only obtained half a crop. "In Hants three sowings are men- tioned in various places, with an estimate of loss of £2 10s. per acre. In parts of Somersetshire there were four succes- sive sowings of rape and turnips." Taking the 22 counties of England and the eleven counties of Scotland where fly attack was noted, Miss Ormerod estimates the loss at £671,936, based upon the calculation that half their acre- age under swedes and turnips, given in the Agricultural Returns for 1881 as 1,343,873 acres, required re-sowing once. The loss represents merely the seed and the expenses, at the rate of £1 per acre, which must be admitted to be a moderate computation, and is only the direct amount of money loss. "Beyond this," as Miss Ormerod remarks, " there is still a heavy loss to be considered on lesser value of the white turnip than the swede crop, and also on the de- ficiency of late-sown crops, as well as in some cases the total less. Also the deficiency of crop affects other points of ag- ricultural supply, as want of cattle food and consequent lesser supply of manure, depreciation of price of stock, ex., so that it is almost impossible to say how far the loss ex- tends." As to the main methods of prevention or reducing the attack to a minimum, suggested by practical men and embodied In this report, it seems that the most important is to have a "stale furrow," and that land should be scuffled, or cultivated, or dragged, and should not be ploughed im- mediately before the seed is sown. Plenty of seed should be sown. Some of the correspondents state that they sow 5 and 61b. per acre. Forcing manures should be applied, in order to get the plants into "rough leaf" as fast as possible. , A good fine tilth or "season," plenty of seed, with liberal applications of guano or superphosphate of lime just under the plants is the best possible state. Steeps for se ed, such as par- affin, petroleum, turpentine, and other things have not proved of much avail. Many dressings have been tried to drive away the beetles from the plants. Gypsum and gas lime were found useful in some cases, and rolling has been useful occasionally if done in the very early morning. Professor Theckman'e plan of driving a frame of boards on which was freshly-tarred sacking fastened to the boards, close over the plants, has been of much service. Also flocks of sheep driven over the fields in the small hours of the morning greatly embarrass the enemy.

THE PITMAN'S WIFE.—If a brave man, struggling with adversity wins, as we are told he does, "applause from the gods," a brave woman surely is not less deserving of hearty commendation. The Northern pitman's wife affords an ex- cellent example of earnest and well-directed effort to make the very best of adverse circumstances. There exists in many of the colliery villages a wholesome rivalry among the women as to who shall have the best-furnished house and who shall keep it cleanest and tidiest. Unlike her sister of the Midland counties, where factory work is so commonly the lot of women, and more fortunate than the wives of the hardy fishermen on the coast, who have much of the rough drudgery of life thrown upcn them, the pittnan's wife devotes all her energies to household duties. Home is her domain, and there she remains supreme. But she is a working queen. She scrubs and washes, she knits and darns and sews, she cuts and contrives to make her narrow means go as far as pos- sible. She bakes and cooks, and excellent cooks many of the colliers' wives are, though they have not had the advantage —doubtless a great advantage it would be to them—of re- ceiving lessons in cookery at South Kensington. During the long and severe depre i ssion n the coal trade, her ability to make ends meat has been very strongly tested. Through shortness of work and reductions of wage, the actual money per workman received must have bean very little—often for long periods together not more than 12s. Or 15s. per week. i Yet on going into a colliery village n Northumberland or Durham at the worst time, you seld on! Saw—what is too com- mon a sight at all times in some districts—children running about dirty and ragged, and without shoes and stockings on their feet. The children were generally warmly if coarsely clad, they were neat and clean, and bore evidence of industry, care, and thrift on the part of their mothers. Entering these lowly dwellings you always got a cheerful welcome ; you heard no puling or whining; the stern, grim realities of life were met with courage, calmness, and self-possession, and a resolution was apparent to put the best face upon everything that it would bear.—Me. T. Burt, MP., in Cas- sell's Magazine.
No. XL—JOHN PHILPOT CURRAN. You re free to share his scanty meal, His plighted word he'll never vary; In vain they tried, with gold and steel, To shake the faith of Tipperary.—Tom Davis.

We are always ready to honor the men who have distin- guished themselves in battle. High up in the Temple of Fame we place those who have sealed their heriosm with their blood. But there is something which has tried the souls of men more than the muzzle of the gun ready to pour its contents into the unshielded breast of the soldier, and there have been heroes who have never bared their breast to the enemy's steel, or scaled the precipice under a heavy fire of shot and shell. To defend the truth when it is not popu- lar—to fight for justice like a second Abdiel, single handed and alone'—to withstand the sneer, the scorn, and the laugh of those by whom we are surrounded, may demand an amount of calm courage which is not needed amid the smoke, the din, and the confusion of a battle field. The world has had many such heroes. In all ages there have been those who have stood up courageously for the truth and the right when these seemed to have fallen in the street—who have sternly refused to compromise that which they believed to be right and just. In spite of flattery and frowns, blandishments, and browbeatings, pelf and pleasure, they have dared to champion the cause of truth." John Philpot Curran was one of these—a hero at the Bar. Per- sonally he was bold, intrepid, and uncompromising, always ready to assert svhat he thought right, and at any peril to defend what he asserted. Four times was he called forth to the field in defence of his principles;and four times did he risk his life. Marking his conduct during the State Trials of 1798, we find it difficult to decide whether his advocacy was the most powerful or his independence the most admi- rable. At every trial he defended the life and liberty of some death-devoted victim at the hazard of his own— willing to die if he could not live and speak a free man. When Erskine pleaded, he stood in the midst of a secure na- tion and pleaded like a priest of the Temple of Justice, with one hand on the altar of the Constitution, and all England below prepared to treasure every fantastic oracle that came from his lips. Not so did Curran plead. Not on the floor of a shrine, but on a scaffold did he plead, with no com- panions but the wretched and culpable men whose days V7Ol, numbered, and no hearers but the multitudes whose feelings were those of hostility to the advocate and his clients. But he blanched not in the face of danger. "I'll commit you, sir," exclaimed Judge Robinson, rising in his wrath. "I hope you will never commit a worse thing, my lord," was Carran's reply. During the trial of Bond a clash of arms was heard amongst the military men in the Court. "What is that ?" sternly enquired the dauntless advocate. Some of the soldiers who were nearest to him appeared from their looks and gestures about to offer him personal violence, upon which, fixing his eye sternly upon them, Curran ex- claimed—" You may assassinate but you shall not intimidate me." On one occaslon,when he was exerting himself in a cause with his characteristic firmness, the presiding Judge, having called to the Sheriff to be ready to take into custody anyone who should disturb the Court, Curran replied, "Do, Mr. Sheriff; go and get ready my dungeon; prepare a bed of straw for me, and upon that bed I shall to-night repose with more tranquillity than I should enjoy were I sitting upon that Bench with a consciousness that I had disgraced it." One more specimen of Cut ran's power and courage —one that must have been unpremeditated, for who could ever have supposed a Judge capable of sneering at a Barrister's poverty by telling him he suspected " his law library was rather con- tracted." Yet this was the brutal remark of Judge Robin- son, the author of many stupid, slavish, and scurrulous pamphlets, and by his demerits raised to the eminence which he thus disgraced. Read carefully the manly and scathing reply of our hero :—" It is very true, my lord, that I am poor, and the circumstance has certainly somewhat curtailed my library; my books are not numerous, but they are select, and I hope they have been perused with proper dispositions. I have prepared myself for this high profession rather by the study of a few good works than by the composition of a great many bad ones. I am not ashamed of my poverty, but I should be ashamed of my wealth could I have stooped to acquire it by servility and corruption. If I rise not to rank I shall at least be honest, and should I ever cease to be so, many an example shows me that an ill gained eleva- tion, by making me the more conspicuous, would only make me the more universally and the more notoriously corrupt." And thus in all these conflicts between the Bench and the Bar he proved that he was able to encounter and triumph over all the taunts and menaces of a hostile Judge. We have in former communications made our readers fa- miliar with some of the State Trials of 1793, but as it was during these that the rare ability and signal courage of this Illustrious Irishman gleamed forth in their most glowing colours, we propose to describe in the present article two more of them. One of the most memorable trials of this dark period of Erin's history was that of the two brothers—John and Henry Sheares. They were both members of the Irish Bar, and were both highly respected. One of them, the elder, had given many hostages to fortune. In the year 1793 they joined the Society of the United Irishmen. When the original members of the Irish Executive were committed to prison in the month of March, 1797, these two brothers were among those who were chosen to supply their places, and they took a very active part in arranging the plan of the approaching insurrection. Of all these proceedings the Go- vernment obtained accurate information through a Captain Armstrong, who had succeeded in insinuating himself into their confidence for the purpose of discovery. This gallant Captain wormed himself into their confidence with the design of betraying them. He pledged to them his friendship, gained their implicit confi- dence, persuaded them he would seduce his regiment, de- vised several secret meetings, and worked up sufficient guilt to sacrifice the lives of both. They were arrested on Mon- day, the 21st of May, and brought to the Bar, and arraigned on the 4th of July, 1798. Curran was the leading counsel. Having discovered that one of the Grand Jury who had found the bill of indictment was a naturalised Frenchman, Curran Pleaded that fact against its legality. After a long discussion it was ruled by the Court that the office of Grand Juror was not one of the offices of trust alluded to by the Legislature, and consequently that the person objected to was competent to fill it. The prisoners were, therefore, in the language of the law "awarded to answer over." Their trial was, upon their application, in consequence of the ab- sence of witnesses, postponed till the 12th of July, when it came on for final decision before Lord Carleton, Mr. Justice Crookshank, and Mr. Baron Smith. Mr. Curran's speech on this occasion, which was considered the most moving that he had ever pronounced, was rendered peculiarly affecting by the circumstances of its delivery. It was past midnight when the examination of the witnesses closed. The trial had already occupied fifteen hours, when Mr. Curran, ex- hausted with fatigue, applied to the Court at the close of the case for "a few hours interval of repose, or rather for recollection." The Attorney-General, the sanguinary Toler —the Lord Jeffries of Ireland—opposed the delay, and the trial proceeded at that unseasonable hour. It was between seven and eight o'clock on the morning of the 13th of July, when the Jury retired to consider their verdict. After a de- liberation of a few minutes they returned, finding the prisoners guilty. As soon as the verdicts were pronounced the unfortunate brothers clasped each other in their arms. They were brought up for judgment at three o'clock on the same day, upon wLich occasion they both addressed the Court. Both were sentenced to death, and at the prayer of the Attorney-General directed that it should be executed upon them on the succeeding day. At the hour appointed for execution they came hand in hand to the scaffold. Henry evinced a terror at his approaching death, and seemed appalled at the frightful spectacle before him. John main- tained his firmness to the end. His last words were "I for- give the world, as I expect to be forgiven." The brothers died as they had lived, "hand-in-hand." In life and death they were indeed "United brothers." Before we pass on, we cannot refrain from reminding our readers of the extraordinary difference in the administration and execution of the laws in the two countries supposed to enjoy the privileges of the same Constitution. Dr. Madden dilates upon this differenle with telling effect. Four years before this John Horne Tooke was placed upon his trial. It PM conducted with solemnity and decorum, and lasted seven days. The trial of the Sheares commenced on the 12th of July, 1798, at ten o'clock, and it terminated at eight o'clock the following morning. The Court then adjourned till three o'clock, when sentence was pronounced, and the next day, Saturday, the 14th of July, 1798, the prisoners were executed in front of the prison in Green-street. What

.. __ a striking contrast! But let us pass on. Day after day the trials and executions proceeded. WCann was tried and executed on the 19th of July. Wm. Michael Byrne was tried on the 20th of July, and executed on the 28th. Oliver Bond was arraigned on the 23rd of July. Mr. Curran was the leading counsel for them all, but his speeches in the two former cases haying been sup- pressed, we must confine ourselves to his defence of Oliver Bond. Before we do so, however, we must not fail to men- tion the affecting circumstances connected with the execu- tion of Byrne. "The 28th of July was the day appointed for his execution, and the negotiations between the State prisoners and the Government having been then entered into, there was very little doubt entertained by himself or his fellow prisoners, but that his life would be spared. On the morning of the 28th he was sitting at breakfast in Bond and Neilson's cell (the wives of the latter being present) when the jailer aPpeared and beckoned to Byrne to come to the door and speak with him. Byrne arose, a few words were whispered into his ear—he returned to the cell and apologised to the ladies for being obliged to leave them. Bond asked him if he would not return, and his reply was: , We will meet again.' He went forth without the slightest sign of perturbation or concern, and was led back for a few minutes to his cell, and then conducted to the scaffold. On passing the cell of Bond and Neilson which he had just left, he stooped that he might not be observed through the grated aperture in the upper part of the door in order that Mrs. Neilson and Mrs. Bond might be spared the shock of seeing him led to execution." (" Lives of the United Irish- men.") Oliver Bond, who was put on his trial on a charge of high 1 treason on the 23rd of July, 1798, was a wholesale woollen ' draper, who had acquired considerable wealth in his busi- ness. Arthur O'Conner speaks of him as "a beloved friend, whom he had himself brought into the undertaking," viz., into the Society of the United Irishmen. His amiable manners, extensive charities and generous dispositions had endeared him to his fellow•citizens of all parties. As the Sheares were consigned to the scaffold by the agency of Captain Armstrong, so Bond was convicted chiefly on the evidence of one Reynolds. If the turpitude of a man's character may be estimated by his own revelations that of Ithis infamous personage may -be fairly tested by his own ad- missions. On Bond's trial Mr. Reynolds gave a detailed account of the several oaths he had taken. He had sworn

to secresy on being made a member of the United Irishmen Society. He had taken an oath of fidelity to his captains on being appointed colonel. He had taken another before a county meeting that he had not betrayed his own asso- ciates at Bond's. He had likewise taken an oath of allegiance twice, and an oath before the Privy Council once, and thrice in the Courts of Justice, viz., on the trials of Bond, Byrne, M‘Cann. " Without disparaging the services of Mr. Reynolds," says Maxwell, in his "History of the Rebellion of 1798," it is impossible to look upon him except as a kind of man to whom the law resorts with abhorrence and from necessity, in order to set the criminal against the crime; and who is made use of by the lav';, for the same reasons that the most noxious poisons are resorted to in desperate dis- orders." • In his defence of Bond,Curran assailed this informer with all the vehemence and acerbity of invective. Of this man Curran had been heard to declare that his "heart was so indurated and gnarled that it was not in the arm of man to drive a wedge into it. It required the edge of the sword or the force of machinery to rive it asunder." "Are you then prepared," enquired Mr. Curran of the Jury, "in a case of life and death, of honour and of infamy, to credit a.vile in- former, the perjurer of a hundred oaths—a wretch whom I pride, honour, or religion could not bind? The forsaken prostitute of every vice calls upon you with one breath to blast the memory of the dead and to blight the character of the living. Do you think Reynolds to be a villain? It ,is true he dresses like a gentleman, and the confident expression of his countenance, and the tones of his voice savours strong of growing authority. He measures his value by the coffins of his victims, and in the fields of evidence appreciates his fame as the Indian warrior does in fight—by the number of scalps with which he can swell his triumphs. He calls upon you by the solemn league of eternal justice to accredit the purity of a conscience washed in his own atrocities." Yet on the evidence of this "loyal apostate" Mr. Bond was convicted and sentenced to die, but in consequence of a negotiation entered into be- tween the Government and the State prisoners, of which one of the articles proposed by the latter was that his life should be spared, he was respited. Shortly after he died in prison from an attack of apoplexy. We need not be surprised that Curran's conduct on these trials exposed his character to the foulest misrepresentation. Because he ventured to demand for the accused those legal privileges, and that fair hearing to which, by the Constitu- tion of the country they were entitled he was branded as

little less than a traitor.- Even in the House of Commons he had to meet that charge of having forfeited the character of a good subject 'by his efforts for his clients. "I am heavily censured," said he, in reply, "for having acted for them in the late prosecutions. I feel no shame at such a charge except in its having been made. I think every counsel is the property of his fellow subjects. If, indeed, because I wore His Majesty's gown, I had declined my duty or had done it weakly or treacherously—if I had made the gown a matter of hypocrisy, and had betrayed my client, or sacrificed him to any personal view, I might perhaps have been thought wiser by those who have blamed me, but I should have thought myself the basest villain upon earth." Are we not right in calling John Philpot Curran a "hero at the Bar ?" None but a hero could have uttered these words. None bat brave and earnest men could have done as he did, Such men create an " epidemic of nobleness." Men become better and greater from gazing at their ex- ample, more ready to do and dare, more willing to lift their eyes out of the mire of selfishness and the dust of anxiety and toil; more brave to try whether they too cannot "scale the toppling crags of duty," and hold converse with those their loftier brethren upon the
Shining tablelands To which our God Himself is moon and sun.
THE WIMBLEDON POISONING CASE.

The trial of Dr. G. H. Lamson, for the murder by poison- ing of his brother-in-law, Percy Malcolm John, at Wimbledon, a short time ago, was begun at the Central Criminal Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Hawkins, ' and it was concluded on Tuesday. The Solicitor-General (Sir F. Herschel') prosecuted; and the prisoner was defended by Mr. Montagu Williams. The crime, it will be remem- bered, was committed at Blenheim House School, owned by Mr. Bedbrook-, in which the deceased was a pupil; and it was while the prisoner was on a visit to the deceased that the poison was administered, it was alleged, in some sweets. Medical testimony was adduced showing that death had been caused by some irritant vegetable position, the symptoms being such as might be caused by aconitine; and the chief witness was Dr. Stevenson, who, under instructions from the Home Secretary, made an analysis of the contents of the stomach, and a minute examination of various portions of the intestines. He deposed that from the liver he had obtained an alkaloidal extract, which contained a trace of morphia, which placed on the tongue gave a faint sensation like that produced by aconitine. From an examination of the stomach he got the same result. The character of the sensation was a burning, tingling, peculiar numbness diffi- cult to define—a salivation—a sensation at the back of the throat as if it were swelling 'up. This was followed by a peculiar seared sensation as if a hot iron were being passed over it. An examination of the stomach gave like results. In reply to the Judge as to his acquaintance with aconitine, witness said he believed he had tasted most alkaloidal poisons known. He injected some of the extract obtained from the urine into the back of a mouse, and it died in thirty minutes. He obtained some of Morson's preparation of aconitine from Messrs. Allen and Hanbury, and injected a small portion into the back of a mouse, and it died ex- hibiting symptoms undistinguishable from the symptoms produced by the extract obtained from the urine. The evi- dence for the prosecution came to a close on Monday, when Mr. Montagu Williams addressed the jury for the defence, contending that, even assuming the deceased died from aconitine poison, the evidence as to its administration was most unsatisfactory. He further held that nothing contain- ing aconitine had been traced to the prisoner's possession. —The Solicitor-General, in reply, said there was no way of accounting for deceased's death from natural causes. Poison was found in the body, and everything went to prove that an aconite pill was given him.—The Judge summed up on Tuesday afternoon and reviewed at length the history of the deceased, his circumstances, and the relation of the prisoner towards him. He minutely recapitulated the evidence as to what occurred at the interview at the school when the alleged administration of poison took place, the subsequent symptoms and death of the deceased, and the important medical testimony adduced. He left entirely to the jury the question of the fact which must determine their verdict. The jury retired to consider their verdict at six o'clock, and, on re-entering the court thirty-live minutes later, they re- turned a verdict of guilty, and the prisoner was sentenced to death.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.
Martin Costello, a Kerry farmer, who was supposed to have paid his rent, was shot in the shoulder while he was sitting by the fireside on Monchy night. Four men have been arrested.

Lord Chief Justice Fitzgibbon, addressing the Grand Jury at Clonmel Assizes, on Tuesday, deplored the state of county Tipperary. There were 389 cases of outrage, compared with 181 for the corresponding period last year. On Monday afternoon, the Irish Parliamentary Party met at Charing-cross, London, and determined upon the formation of an Irish National Independence Association, Ireland's inalienable right to self-government being pro- claimed.

A largely-attended meeting of Lord Castletown's tenants was held in Rathdwny on Saturday for the purpose of effecting a settlement between his lordship and themselves as to the rents. It was resolved that the rent should be fixed by arbitration. The publishers of United Ireland claim £30,000 from the Government in respect of the suppression of that paper. An action has been commviced, and it is stated that Mr. Forster and the Commissioners of Police have entered ap- pearances to the writs.

Mr. Patrick Egan telegraphs from Paris that there is no foundation for the belief that Mr. Rourke, his partner, who has just been arrested under the Protection Act, had circu- lated the no rent manifesto, or had had anything to do with Land League matters like it was proclaimed. The United States Minister (Mr. Lowell) haying been asked to mediate on behalf of the imprisoned " suspects " who are naturalised citizens of his cottntry, has replied that "the Coercion Act" is the law of the land, and it is mani- festly futile to claim that such persons should be exempted from its operation. A Limerick correspondent telegraphs that on Saturday night a party of disguised men attacked the houses of two widows and broks into their dwellings. A police patrol was in the vicinity, and hearing a disturbance proceeded to the spot, when the attacking party decamped. The police, how- ever, state that they identified the assailants, and three arrests were made.

A correspondent of the Daily News in Ireland, writing from Killarney, on Saturday, describes the condition of the county Kerry. He has come to the conclusion that matters are rapidly mending, one of the best symptoms being that numbers of the tenants are now coming forward to claim the advantages of the Land Act. They were sceptical as to these advantages at first, and adopted the counsel of the Land League. The course of events has, however, convinced them of their true interest.

THE IRISH LAND COMMISSION.—A return has been issued of the proceedings of the Irish Land Commission up to February 24. Of fair rents, the total number of agree- ments and applications to the court was 74,588; and of these 841 were either dismissed or withdrawn, 2,365 rents were fixPcl, 3,206 fair rent cases were decided in court, and and 2,180 agreements to fix fair rents entered into. There were 1,424 applications to have leases declared void, of which 188 were dismissed, 219 were withdrawn or com- promised, and 33 leases declared void.

COWARDLY OUTRAGES. Another fearful outrage is reported, but on this occasion it is in Kerry-, near a place called Brosnan. The other night the house of a farmer named O'Connell was broken into by a gang of men, who were disguised. A light was struck, and O'Connell, who had hastily left his bed to ascertain what was the matter, was fired at, and fell apparently dead. The ruffians then rushed into the room where O'Connell's wife and daughter were in bed. Both were rudely dragged out of bed and maltreated. They were knocked down and struck with the butt end of a rifle. Mrs. O'Connell also re- ceived a gunshot wound in the le,. Two shots must have been fired at the farmer, for he °has a severe and lacerated gunshot wound in the right arm and a bullet wound in the left thigh. He is living, but in a very weak state from loss of blood. _ _

Several shots have been Bred into the house of a farmer named John Flynn, residing in the Cappagh district, county Waterford. He had a. narrow escape, two bullets having lodged in the post of the bed in which he was sleeping. Flynn had recently taken a farm on the property of Captain Wallace from which the previous occupants had been evicted. On Saturday evening he received a threatening letter stating that Captain Moonlight would not miss him. A young man named Callendar, who had been in competi- tioß with Flynn for the farm, has been arrested.

div.head: PASTORAL BY ARCHBISHOP 11PCABE.
div.p: PASTORAL BY ARCHBISHOP 11PCABE.

Archbishop M'Cabe has issued another pastoral, which was read on Sunday. In it he refers to the assassination of the informer Bailey as a disgrace to the city, and the work of a secret organisation of an illegal, anti-social, and irreligious character, originating in the publication of a certain manifesto subversive of the laws of property. It would be uncharitable, says his grace, to assume that the authors of that manifesto contemplated the results which flowed from it, and he is sure that if they could have fore- seen those results they would have refrained from putting their hands to such a document. He calls upon the clergy to desire their flocks to avoid all connection with secret societies. He denounced in strong terms the recent attempt on the life of the Queen, speaking of her as having strictly kept the constitution which she was sworn to defend, and as having in her private life given a beautiful example to her subjects, her reign affording a brilliant contrast to those of many of her predecessors.

div.head: PROPOSAL TO REMOVE MR. PARNELL.
div.p: PROPOSAL TO REMOVE MR. PARNELL.

There was a rumour current a few days ago that Mr. Parnell was about to be removed from Kilmainham, and that, in fact, the warrant for his transfer to another prison had been made out. The proposition to remove Mr. Parnell is not new, but has been entertained for some time by Messrs. Kaye, Anderson, and Burke, and the other [officials who constitute, apart from Mr. Forster, the executive of the Irish Government. It is also a fact that some apprehension has heretofore been entertained at the Castle that in the event of Mr. Parnell's transfer a rescue might be attempted, or in :some other way the principal detenu might escape from' custody. It is not positively known whetner there was any truth in the recent statement, positively made and as positively denied, that Mr. Parnell had been subjected to punishment for a breach of the prison rules; but the letters of complaint and other writings which have reached the press from within various prisons from time to time have shown plainly that the vigilance exercised at those prisons has not always been effective.

A tale is told of a certain bombastic colonel who was once riding in a stage coach with several.other passengers, when he accidentally dropped his hat out of the coach window, and exclaimed in a stentorian voice, "Charioteer, pause! I have lost my chapeau." The driver paid no heed to the demand. Again the bombastic fellow authoritatively spoke, "Charioteer, pause! I have lost my chapeau." No atten- tion being paid by the driver to this last command, a plain, blunt man, who had become disgusted with his fellow- traveller's silliness and pomposity, put his head out of the window, and said, "Driver, hold on; this fool has lost his hat." This was perfectly intelligible to the driver, and the hat was secured.

div.head: PRUDENTIAL ASSURA.NCE CO,,
div.p: THE PRUDENTIAL ASSURA.NCE CO,,
LIMITED.

In our advertisirg columns will be found to-day the thirty-third annual report of this company, and as it is the one company above all others popular among the working classes, we make no apology for drawing attention here to the extraordinary amount of business which it transacts. The extent of the company's operations, which increases year by year, seems to be almost illimitable; and the confi- dence which the putlic have in the society is amply testified by the amount of money entrusted to it yearly. The whole of the society's business is comprised in two branches—the "Industrial" and the "Ordinary." The greatest amount of business is done in the industrial branch, which is confined exclusively to the working classes; but as the figures sub- sequently quoted will show these in the ordinary branch as in the industrial are somewhat startling. The results on the whole atel conclusive enough to dispel much of the captions criticism which has been levelled at the society by some of its opponents. The premiums actually received in the industrial branch during the past year amount to no less a sum than £1,849,494 18s. 5d., as compared with £1,608,849 Bs. 7d. received during 1880. There was there- fore an increase in the premium receipts last year of £240,645 9s. 101, the largest, it is stated, which has taken place in this branch, and certainly it is highly satisfactory. The claims of the year in this branch amounted to £639,752 10s. id., and the total amount paid under this head was £3,786,112, and the assurance fund shows an increase of £402,945 12s. 4d. In the ordinary branch, we gather from the report, the new business completed during the year consisted of 6,949 policies, assuring the sum of £860,172, and producing a new annual premium income of £31,603 4s. Bd. The claims for the year amounted to £69,677 17s. ld., under 474 policies representing 432 deaths and 22 endowment assurances matured. The annual pre- mium income, at the end of the year in this branch showed an increase of £20,086 over the year 1880, and there was an increase in the assurance fund as well of £81,098 is. 2d. It is gratifying to note that in this, as well as in the other branch, the rate of expenses is less by one per cent than last year, and it is also deserving of special mention that the in- crease in the premium receipts of this branch are upwards of £21,000 more than in the previous year, and that it is the largest which has been obtained in the history of the com- pany. The quinquennial report is a most instructive and satis- factory one. The expenditure of the society in conducting its business has often been urged by its detractors against its efficiency and even solvency, and it is con- sequently a pleasure to know that the objections urged on that score are being steadily and surely overcome. The ratio of expenditure was somewhat reduced during the previons quinquennium, and during this quip quennium it has been reduced six per cent in the ordinary and seven per cent in the industrial branch. At the same time there is every reason to believe that the redaction in the latter branch will be continued. In the ordinary branch the quinquennial re- port shows the annual premium income has increased from £83,245 to £142,732, and the assmonce fund from £473,862 to £744,583: in the industrial branch the increase in the annual premium income has been from £980,575 to £2,051,024, and the assurance fund from £373,492 to £1,721,492. These results, too, it is well to bear in mind, have been secured after providing for every liability, after adding a considerable amount to the contingency fund, and carrying forward a large balance in each branch. On the whole, the figures given in the report disclose the fact that ' the society has now enrolled on its books more than one- eighth of the entire population of the United Kingdom,— men, women and children. The business done in the ordinary branch of the society is only exceeded by one other company which was started at the same time • as the Prudential (1844) and out of sixty companies which have been estall- fished a longer period than the Prudential the ineome of the latter exceeds 34 of them. As regards the industrial branch, according to the chairman of the company (Mr. E. Horne), it , costs the Prudential less to collect their pennies than it does I the General Post Office to deliver its penny letters. One, however, of the chief secrets of success of the society is the promptness with which it pays its claims this being done often before the claim is sent to the Board by the agents of the society, who are on the spot when any mining or other calamity occurs, and at once discharge the society's liability. The quinquennial valuation of the industrial busi- ness shows that there is a surplus of £273,413, of this £200,000 will be distributed as profit, £60,000 transferred to the contingency fund, and the remainder carried forward. In the ordinary business there is a surplus of £101,907, of which £90,000 will be divided, and the balance retained in hand. The premium income actually received last year is, we are told, almost exactly within a very small sum of two millions sterling. The total premiums of all the companies in this country is about thirteen millions, and therefore more than one-seventh is secured by the Prudential. As another evi- dence of the magrlitude of the company's operations it may be stated that no less than 600 persons were engaged for several weeks in making a valuation of the society's property for the five years ending 31st December last. This was done under the superintendence of Mr. A. H. Bailey, president of the Institute of Actuaries, who in concluding his report states it is in the highest degree satisfactory to find that after subjecting the liabilities to stringent tests the resources have been found to be ample to meet all engage- ments, and he adds that the general results of the searching investigation cannot but be most gratifying to all who are interested in the prosperity of the company. In an able article in The Review on the work of the society the writer says :—" By the skilful initiative invariably taken by district superintendents in all public calamities, the agent of the Prudential is now as regularly looked for as the arrival of the nearest medical man. Owing to the enormous number of policies issued by the society it is impossible that any ac- cident or public calamity should take place, in which the lives OA number of men are jeopardised, without finding that some at least of the unfortunates hold policies in the Pru- dential Assurance Company. By the promptitude of its agents it is always to the front with that assistance which is so valu- able because it is timely. . . . One of the most gratify- ing features of the report before us, is the fact, that with the growth of the business the percentage of expenses has dimi- nished both in the Industrial and Ordinary Branch. It is now a common item in the Prudential reports that the ex- penses of the year are less than those of the previous twelve months. Of course, it is obvious that there is a point be- yond which this reduction cannot go, and we think that point cannot be very far off."

KILLED BY A IlAtuFIN.—An inquest was held before the Manchester City Coroner, on Monday, on the body of a woman named Mary Ann Fisher, wife of John Fisher, of 18, Band-street, Pollard-street. Deceased's husband stated that on Saturday night last he and his wife went to bed, and that early on the following morning he was awakened by a scream from his wife, who was sitting,on the flopr. She said some- thing was the matter with her head. He raised an alarm, and when the landlady of the house came he went for a doctor. The landlady meanwhile had felt a hairpin in de- ceased's bead, and while someone held the woman she drew the hairpin out of the deceased's head. Death ensued almost immediately. The jury returned a verdict that " Death was due to an effusion of blood on the brain caused by a hairpin running deeply into her head."

HOUSE OF COWAONS.-THURSDAY.

TEE SALVATION ARMY.—The HOME SECRETARY explained the course he had taken in consequence of the rioting in various places in connection with the labours of the Salva- vation Army, and repeated a former statement that he had no power to give directions to magistrates to do ctrtaitt things; he had given such advice and assistance as he was able, and where his advice had been followed it had answertd the purpose. He added that if the magistrates did not pre- serve the peace they are liable to a criminal information for failing to do their duty. THE IRISH PRISONERS.—Sir Arthur Otway's appeal for a relaxation of the rules under which the suspects suffer solitary confinement was answered by the CHIEF SECRETARY, who announced that a modification of the rules was about to be made. Dealing with the allegations that the authorities at the Castle had been harsh in their judgments, the right hon. gentleman said he alone was responsible for the carry- ing out of the Act. Generally speaking, the state- ments respecting the treatment of the prisoners had been exaggerated. REPLIES TO QUESTIONS.—Sir CTARLES DUKE informed Mr. Maclvcr that it was not true that the Spanish Govern- ment had offered to England the most favoured nation terms in the return for the reduction of the duty on Spanish wines to is. per gallon, or that they were negotiating treaties with Spain, Portugal, and Italy •on terms of reciprocity which the Government had hitherto repudiated. Mr. FawcErr, in reply to Mr. Alderman Lawrence, said that, after careful consideration, he could not see his way to en- tertain the suggestion of the latter to establish a system of prepaid sixpenny reply telegrams containing ten words. THE FRENCH TREATY.—In answer to Sir Stafford North- cote, Sir CHARLES DILKE stated that no instructions had been given to Lord Lyons as to a resumption of the negotia- tions for a commercial treaty with France. Mason Boom.—Mr. CALLA called attention to the ap- pointment of Major Bond, late chief constable of Birming- ham, as a stipcndiary magistrate in Ireland.—Mr. FORSTER urged that wilful misrepresentation had never been imputed in the case, and said be did not feel justified in cancelling the appointment.—Upon a division, the motion censuring the Chief Secretary for making the appointment was rejected by 78 to 14.

THE VACANT SEATS.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply to Mr. Warton, said the Government had no intention at present of bringing in a bill in reference to the six vacant seats. Their intention would be duly announced, and due time given for members to take what course they deemed right. Mr. TREVELYAN afterwards explained the Navy Esti- mates.

div.head: DEPARTURE OF THE QUEEN.
div.p: THE DEPARTURE OF THE QUEEN.

The Queen, with Princess Beatrice and suite, left Wind- sor Castle on Tuesday morning and drove to the Great Western station. The royal train quitted Windsor at 10-n, vi tt Slough and Basingstoke, and arrived at Portsmouth at noon. The Windsor station was kept strictly private, but all who saw the Queen observed that Her Majesty was look- ing remarkably well. 'Unon her arrival at Portsmouth the Queen embarked on board the royal yacht and crossed the Channel en route for Mentone. The Queen travels in strict privacy as the Countess of Balmoral. Her stay at Mentone will probably extend over a month, at the end of which time her Majesty returns to Windsor, in order to attend the marriage of Prince Leopold and Princess Helen of Waldeck- Pyrmont.

div.head: QUEEN AT MENTONE.
div.p: THE QUEEN AT MENTONE.

A telegram from Paris on Thursday evening says :—The Queen arrived at Mentone this afternoon at 4-25, and met with an enthusiastic reception from the delighted crowds who had been awaiting the appearance of the train. Her Majesty bowed repeatedly in acknowledgment of the ap- plause which greeted her. A temporary platform had been erected in tfront of the Chilllet des Rosiers. As the Queen alighted she-seemea slightly fatigued. She was received by Mr. Henfrey and Canons Philpott and Anson. Mentone was gaily decorated, and filled with English visitors. The weather was magnificent.
