HOOD'S "OWN ". dr, " OUT OF THE HURLY-BURLY "(Messrs. Ward, Lock, and, Company.)—Slnce the publication of the "Voyage of the Sunbeam" at the low price of 6d.; there have been several other, well-known works, notably "The Ingoldsby Legends" issued at the same price, and the suc- cess which has attended these efforts has induced Messrs. Ward, Lock, and Co. to issue" Hood's Own" and "Out of the Hurley-Burly" at the low figure named. A copy of each has been sent us, and from every point of view they will bear favourable comparison with, if they do not actually surpass, the cheap editions of other works which has pre- ceded them. This firm has obtained an enviable notoriety for the publication of cheap literature, which for the most part is of an educational character, and the two sixpenny publications just produced, will, if anything, enhance the popularity of the company. It 'should be stated that the original engravings and illustrations are reproduced in the pages of the works. THE DAY OF 'REST (Messrs. Strahan and Co.)—This ex- cellent Sunday periodical is to hantl and it is ever welcome. It is the only magazine which gives coloured illustrations in its pages, and attractive as these are in themselves, they are not more so than the excellent literary contributions. "The Lord's Pursebearers" iicontinued by Hesba Stretton, and the interest is unabated; an article on "Stockwell Orphanage" is full of information, so also is" Summer Holi- days in Switzerland*" and the " Childrens pages" are such as will afford pleasure to the juvenile readers. "George Linton's Deliverance " is a pathetic story well told. A copy of FARM AND HOME, a new weekly illustrated jcurnal of agriculture in all its branches, has been sent us. We are informed that "Farm and Ifozne, is projected as a purely practical paper, dealing with every branch of its subject, and written by farmers for farmers. It is not poli- tical, and has all its space devoted to suli:7ects of vital interest ' to the farmer and his wife, a large portion of its columns being set apart for housekeeping, domestic economy' and the other departments of which women take charge." Judging from the first issue the paper is likely to be a success, and we have pleasure in commending it to the notice of the agricultural community especially. WELDON'S LADIES' JOURNAL AND WELDON'S ILLUSTRATED DRESSMAKER ,(Messrs. Weldon and Co., Northampton- street, Strand)jand Swags HOME JOURNAL, Messrs. Ward, Lock and Co.)—These periodicals compete for favour chiefly among the ladies, by whom they are much appreciated. The March parts contain all the particulars that can be !i'leaned as to the latest fashions not only at home but in Paris and elsewhere, and the illustrations and instructions given as to cutting-out, S:c., must be very useful. We have received from Messrs. Ward, Lock, and Co. the usual pace! of their monthly publications, not no of which • should be absent from any good library. Without enumerating all the productions we may state tlat to those engaged in writing" Hadyn's 'Dictionary of Dates" is indis- pensable ; readers of history will derive pleasure in perusing "Epochs and Episodes of History ;" and literateurs will welcome " Hallam's Literature of Europe." Biblical -students will find "Dr. Adam Clarke's Commentary on the Bible" very useful; to the piously disposed we commend -" Holy thoughts on holy things ;." the lovers of poetry will be re- freshed after consulting the "Great Book of Poetry;" and "Thrift Book "will give hints to all on economical anti other questions.

div.head: ADULTERATED COTTON.
div.p: ADULTERATED COTTON.

There 'were exhibited on Tuesday in the portico of the Manchester Royal Exchange several -samples of adulterated cotton, consigned from America to a ferin in Oldham. The samples purported to be good ordinary American, and, in. order to mark the contrast, a specimen of the unadulterated article was placed side by side with them. Fully two- thirds of a bale, which when delivered weighed over 400ib., consisted simply of the sweepings of the packing-house, and was so filthy that had the Manchester ship Canal been an accomplished fact one might have supposed the cotten was salvage from some vessel wrecked in the Irwell. This i sample would not fetch more in the market than the drop- pings from under a carding engine; better cotton, in fact, is said to be swept up every day from under the mules in any Oldham spinning-room. Another sample on view of good cotton contained a large proportion of sand. As much as a shovelful had been thrown into the bale in one place, but the sand had permeated the cotton and damaged the fibre. A bale that arrived in Oldham the °thee day weighed scwt. lqr. 51b., of which one-fifth was simply sand. On a repre- sentation being made to the broker, he, without viewing the cotton, made an allowance of 1001 b. That these are not ' solitary examples of the adulteration practised by the planters is proved by the conversation and remaiks of numerous spinners who inspected the samples. many of them asserting that they had received cotton almost, if not equally, I as bed. ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION OF THE QUEEN. LETTER FROM HER MAJESTY.

A supplement to the London Gazette, published on Mon- day night, is as follows : Home Office, Whitehall, March 13. The following letter from the Queen has this day been received by Secretary Sir William Vernon Harcourt : "Windsor Castle, March 12, 1882. "The Queen wishes, before she leaves England for a short while for some comparative rest and quiet, to express from her heart how very deeply touched she is by the outburst of enthusiastic loyalty, affection, and devotion which the pain- ful event of the 2nd inst. has called forth from all classes, and from all parts of her vast empire, as well as by the universal sympathy evinced by the Sovereigns and people of other nations. The Queen cannot sufficiently express how deeply gratified she is by these demonstrations, and would wish to convey to all, from the highest to the hum- blest, her warmest and most heartfelt thanks. It has ever been her greatest object to do all she can for her subjects, and to uphold the honour and glory of her dear country, as well as to promote the presperity and happiness of those over whom she has reigned so long, and these efforts will be continued unceasingly to the last hour of her life. The Queen thanks God that He has spared her beloved child, who is her constant and devoted companion, and those who were with her in the moment of danger, as well as herself, and she prays that He will continue to protect her for her people's sake, as He has hitherto so visibly done."

MISCELLANEOUS.
The prospects of all the crops are exceedingly favourable for the time of year.

At the Hi...;h Court of Justiciary. Edinburgh, on Monday, James Munn, innkeeper, was acquitted on a charge of mur- dering his wife by stabbing her. At Plymouth, on Monday, a coloured seaman, named William Brown, was sentenced to three weeks' imprisonment for mutinous behaviour on board the Liverpool ship Prince Rupert The Prince of Wales presided on Monday at a meeting of the governors of the city guilds of London Institute, when a most satisfactory report was made of the progress of the cause of technical education.

On Monday morning, the dead body of a woman named Bennett, wife of a labourer, and one of her children were found in a field near South Stockton. It is supposed that she killed the child and then committed suicide while insane. _ _

A fatal gun accident occurred on Monday at Linley Wood, Staffordshire. Mr. Chisman, butler to the Misses Marsh, was cleaning a breechloader, not knowing it was charged, when the piece went off, and the contents lodged in his wife's chest, causing instant death. The arrangements for a military shooting match with the United States have been completed, but, instead of an American team coming to Wimbledon in the summer, an English team will go to Creedmoor in September, and the return match is to take place at Wimbledon in 1883. A discussion on the Westminster Confession of Faith took place at the monthly meeting of the Liverpool Presbytery of the Church of England, on 'Monday. Mr. Bell moved an overtere in favour of giving a general instead of a particular adherence to the confession. The question was finally Adjourned till the next meeting. The inquest on the body ef the woman who was killed through an explosion in a sewer at Bradford terminated on Monday in a verdict of accidental death. Scientific opinions were given to the effect that all danger of the escape of bisulphide of carbon into the sewers might be prevented by placing a settling tank between the grease extractors and the sewers. Earl Cairns, speaking at Bournemouth, on Monday even- ing, on temperance, said it was the astounding and almost incredible fact that there was spent in this country every year in the purchase of intoxicating liquors £150,000,00.0 Werling, nearly twice the national revenue. What waswanted was greater legislative control over the houses as to number, and other matters. Countess Cowper narrowly escaped a serious carriage accident en Monday evening. Whilst driving a pair of ponies in a pbseton, up Cork Hill into Dublin Castle, one of the ponies stumbled and fell, and its struggles caused the other pony to fall also. They were rescued before any damage could occur. FATAL STABBING AFFRAY.—William Ewing, aged 26, residing in Centre-street, Glasgow, died in the Glasgow Royal Infirmary, on Monday morning, from four stabs which be received on Saturday at midnight, from a man still un- known to the police. The stranger wanted to fight when Ewing was giving him friendly counsel, and the stranger attacked him. In the struggle the fatal injuries were received. Ewing's dying deposition was taken. The Marine Hotel, North Berwick, -one of the most fashionable resorts in the north-east of Scotland, was gutted by fire on Monday. The flames broke out in the upper story, and there being no fire engine in the place, it burnt ;hrough three flats, causing damage to the amount of £15,000, fully covered by insurance. A large stock of valuable wines and a considerable portion of furniture were des- troyed. THE VICTORIA Cnoss.—The Queen has signified her intention to confer the decoration of the Victoria Cross upon the undermentioned officer and men for conspicuous bravery during the recent operations in South Africa :—Lieutenant Alan Richard Hill, 2nd battalion Northamptonshire Regi- ment, for gallant conduct at the action of Laing's Nek, on January 28th, 1881. Private John Doogan, late Ist Dragoon Guards, for gallant conduct at Laing's Nek, on the above date- Lance Corporal James Murray, late 2nd battalion Connaught Rangers; and trooper John Danoher, of Nourse's Horse, for their gallant conduct during the engagement with the Boers at Glandsfontein, on January 16, 1881; and Private James Osborne, 2nd battalion Northamptoeshire Regiment, for gallant conduct at Wesselstroom, on Febi iry 22nd, 1881. THE NORDON CASE AGAIN.—In the Queen's Bet b Division of the High Court of Justice, Westminster, n Monday, before Mr. Justice Mathew and Mr. Justice eave, tne case of Nordon v. Defries was heard and judgment given by their lordships. The parties interested live at Liverpool. It was an appeal plaintiff against an order made by a judge in chambe s giving defendants right of inspection of some shorthanu notes whidh plaintiff alleged he had taken to assist him in his case, which was a charge of conspiracy against members of his wife's family respecting a certain marriage settlement. This defendants denied, and main- tained that they were perfectly entitled to see the documents. , Their lordships held that the documents had been brought into existence in order to assist plaintiff in his case, and that therefore the shorthand notes must be protected from inspec- tion as being privileged; and the appeal he allowed. NEW hum CARDINAL.—The Tablet announces that news has been received from Rome that Dr. 111'Cabe, the Arch- bishop of Dublin, is about to be created a cardinal. By Sunday's post the" biglietto' " or official letter of the Cardi- nal Secretary of State, which conveys to his grace the inti- mation of his approaching elevation, was despatched from Rome, so that there is no longer any secret about the matter. The Irish Times says that the announcement "will cause general and wide-spread satisfaction among the many friends and admirers of the distinguished prelate, whose promotion in the Church has net 'been more marked than deserved. The official appointment, it is said, will be made at the Con- sistory to be held in Rome immediately after Easter, when a number of other cardinals will be named. Dr. M`Cabe rose en pure merit from rank to rank from a humble curate in a suburban parish to be one of the princes of the Church. During the administration he has shown splendid courage in the face of a strong and angry antagonism, loyalty to duty, and to the great trusts reposed in him." THROWING OIL ON TROUBLED WATERS.—A SUCCESS- Fur. EXPERIMENT.—The Calcutta liner Airlie arrived at Dundee on Tuesday morning after a-etormy passage, lasting over 131 days. Captain Foreman reports that on the 28th February a storm of hurricane force prevailed. The storm lasted four days, and when it was at its height Captain Foreman determined tc try the effect of allaying the sea with oil. For this purpose a large number of bags were filled with oil, and, having been perforated so -as to allow the oil to escape gradually, they were towed in the sea on the weather side of the vessel. This was continued for 48 hours, and was entirely successful. The waves which had been breaking constantly over the ship, gradually ceased, and soon moderated so much that the crew were able to work with safety on the deck, and the sea in the immediate vicinity of the vessel became comparatively smooth. Cap- 'thin Foreman is of opinion that had it not been for the use of the oil the ship, if she had not foundered, would have had her decks swept and would have sustained considerable damage. ALARMING COLLIERY ACCIDENT : MANY MINLRS IM- rßlSONED.—Considerable consternation was caused in the neighbourhood of Lumley.Colliery, Fence Houses, Durham, on Tuesday, when it was reported that the shaft of the col- liery had fallen bodily hi, imprisoning and imperilling the lives of the miners in the pit-variously stated as numtering 150 or 250. Thousands of ,persons rushed to the pit mouth as the news spread to ascertain the truth of the report. It was then ascertained that the shaft of the winding engine had broken whilst winding up .coal, completely blocking up the shaft. One hundred and twenty-two men and boys were in the pit, and for some time considerable alarm pre- vailed. Mr. Robson, the viewer, was soon on the spot, and immediately sent a message down the pit by a crab rope, end an answer came back to the eflect that the men and boys were all right. Another-communication followed, resulting in the imprisoned miners making their way to the Peele Flat Shaft, where they were drawn up safely, the last batch being landed at the pit's mouth at half-past three. The broken shaft of the engine became a fixture, otherwise damage would have been considerable. No person wac injured. A " DISGUSTING " BREACH or PRO3IISE CASE. The case of Adams v. Bull has been before the Queen's Bench Division. This was an action brought by Annie Adams, a girl of 18, who resides at Dunstable, against the defendant, who is an innkeeper in a small way of business at the same place, and who is 35 years of age, for breach of promise of marriage. The plaintiff, who had been ono-aged in straw- plaiting work, entered the defendant's employment as bar- maid within a few weeks after his wife's death, when inti- mate relations sprang up between the master and servant, and shortly afterwards, she having in the meantime, as alleged, gone to London at his request, in order to be married, be married another woman. The defendant was called, and in the most positive terms denied that he had ever peomised to marry the plaintiff. In the course of the examination of one of the witnesses, there was loud laugh- ter from the body of the court, on which his lordship said —lf, in the course of this disgusting case, any one displays levity in this court, he shall sleep this night in prison. After m short discussion, the jury found a verdict for the plaintiff for 40s.—Mr. Justice Stevens: I will give judg- ment for that amount, and will deprive the plaintiff of the costs. All, therefore, that she will get out of the most dis- gusting case I ever tried in my life will be her 405., which will go into the pocket of her solicitor. (Laughter.) ELECTION EXPENSES.—Twenty pounds is the utmost that the Attorney-General's Corrupt Practices Bill allows a can- didate for Parliament to spend himself as personal expenses at an election. Anything further is to be paid by his elec- tion agent. The maximum scale that is allowed for print- ing, advertising, stationery, postage, and telegrams is £lOO. where the number of electors on the register does net exceed 2,000, and for all other expenses (except personal ones and returning officer's charges) £250. For every additional 1,000 electors, £lO and £2O may be added to these sums respectively. The only expenses that according to the bill are to be legal are: (1) The returning officer's charges; (2) the candidate's personal expenses; (3) those of printing and advertising in newspapers; (4) of stationery, postage, and telegrams; (5) of holding public meetings; (6) of committee rooms, not exceeding one for each polling district in a county and one for every 500 electors in a borough; (7) of miscel- laneous matters, not exceeding £lO for every 1,000 electors, or in the whole £lOO. With regard to the persons who may be legally employed kr payment, they are—(l) one election agent only, who must not vote, though be is not precluded from being an elector; (2) one polling agent in each polling station under a similar disability; and (3) a number of non- electors to act as clerks and messengers for conducting busi- ness in the committee rooms, one clerk and one messenger being allowed for each polling district in a county and for every 500 electors in a borough.

The University crews had their last practice on the Isis and the Cam on -Saturday. The race takes place on ,Satar- day, the Ist of April, about half-past twelve o'clock. The recent Exhibition of Fine Arts at Bolton turns out to have been a financial failure, there being a deficiency of £lB3, which will have to be made good by the guarantors. The sculling match for .ZlOO between James Rix, of Rich- mond, and George Thomas, of Stroud-on-the-Green, took place on the Thames in a dense fog on Saturday. Rix won.

It is stated that the Queen has Tdictated a telegraphic message of thanks to the new Irish Cardinal for the grace- ful and touching reference to Her Majesty in his pastoral read in Dublin on Sunday. Mr. Chamberlain, writing to a Bolton gentleman, sans he is fully aware of the scandals in the present system of bills of sale, and he hopes that something will be done during the session to render them impossible. The council of the West of Scotland Rifle Association have resolved to adopt the National Rifle Association rules as to position in shooting, and have fixed the week ending Saturday, July 10th for the meeting this year. A jury in the Court of Session have awarded damages to the amount of £2,500 to John M`Gregor, a wine and spirit merchant, Greenock against the Caledonian Railway Com- pany, for injuries suffered by M‘Gregor in the Pennilee rail- way accident. Messrs. W. and R. Chambers have just issued a new edition of their "Etymological Dictionary of the English Language," which has been in preparation for some years under the eelitorship of Dr. Findlater. The dictionary has been entirely rewritten, with special attention to etymology, and is practically a new work. The Rev. W. Robertson Smith—who, by the way, has just been elected by the Senatus of Aberdeen University to receive the honorary degree of LL.D.—will issue in a few weeks a volume on "The Prophets, their Work and Times." The substance of the work has been delivered in the North in the form of lectures.

A return was issued on Saturday showing the gross amount received and expended in respect ef the telegraph service from the date of the transfer of the tele- graphs to the state (February, 1870) to March 31, 1881. It states that the total received was £13,226,047 13s. Old., and and the total expenditure £11,229,051 Bs. lop., a balance thus resulting of £1,996,996 4s. 2d. On Sunday morning there was found in the Preston and Lancaster Canal, near Preston, the body of Mr. John Collin- son, weaving overlooker, who so mysteriously disappeared over a fortnight ago. Deceased left home as usual, and was last seen in Lancaster-road, Preston. He had been low- spirited for some time. There were no marks of violence on the body. A remarkable instance of the overcrowding prevalent in labourers' dwellings in some part of the country has been afforded at Atherstone. The nuisance inspector stated that at Witherley he found thirteen persons sleeping in one bed- room—viz., a man, his wife, four daughters (whose ages ranged from eleven to twenty-three years), six sons (from five to seventeen years of age), and a child of one of the daughters. On Saturday, Mr. Prentice, Q.C., the commissioner ap- pointed to try the petition againt the return of Councillor Frank Wright (son of the late J. S. Wright, M.P., president of the Birmingham Liberal Association), gave his decision. He declared the respondent duly elected, and ordered the petitioner, Mr. Lewis Spoke Richards, to pay the costs of the respondent which had been incurred with respect to that part of the petition which charged him personally with being guilty of corrupt practices, and also that part of the petition which alleged undue influence and personation. At Oldham Police Court, on Monday, John Gallagher was charged with inflicting grevious bodily harm on a boy named Samuel Howard. The evidence showed that on the 6th of February Howard was running along Ashton-road, when prisoner seized him by the chest and threw him down, the noise made by the complainant's head on the pavement being heard some distance away. Complainant became insensible, and concussion of the brain followed. His life was despaired of for some days, and Dr. Robertson thinks his hearing permanently injured. The prisoner was sentenced to four months' hard labour. ALARMING RAILWAY COLLISION NEAR MILES PLATTING —On Tuesday forenoon an alarming collision occurred at Thorpe's Bridge, between Newton Heath and Miles Platting An engine was on the side line at Thorpe's Bridge, and it appears to have gone too far down, the consequence being that it came into collision with the passenger train for Old- ham, which left Manchester shortly after ten o'clock. The engines did not run full tilt into each other, only one buffer struck; but as the Oldham train was going at a fair speed both engines were damaged. The passengers were severely shaken, but no complaints were made to the officials at New- ton Heath as to injuries. The train was delayed three- quarters of an hour. A large picture by Paul Veronese has just been sent to England for sale, and is now in the hands of Messrs. Ander- son, Fenchurch Avenue. The subject—" Christ at the Pool of Bethesda "—is treated in a manner ve.y characteristic of Paul Veronese, with large, well grouped figures, some cleverly foreshortened, in the foreground; and an architec- tural background formed by the long range of a classical colonnade. The picture is, on the whole, well preserved, and is a good specimen of Veronese's more finished manner; but, unluckily, two of the heads have been repainted by a very unskilful hand. No doubt this wretched daubing might be cleaned off. The death is announced of Colonel Sir James Bourne, C. 13., head of the firm of Messrs. Bourne and Robinson, of Liverpool, and for fifteen years member of Parliament for Evesham. The deceased baronet was in town on Monday in apparently good health. He died at his residence at Wayertree yesterday morning after a few hour's illness. Sir James Bourne was born in 1812, and came of an old Lanca- shire family, which particularly prides itself on having held land in the county since the time of King John. Sir Henry Brougham Loch, K.C.8., Lieutenant-Governor of the Isle of Man, intimated on Tuesday to the Tynwald Court, that in a few days his resignation of the office would be forwarded to the Home Secretary for submission to her Majesty. He has served as lieutenant-governor during a period of 19 years. Some observations were made on the subject by the Attorney-General and the Speaker, who both bore testimony to Sir H. Loch's unwearied exertions, and the sorrow of the people at his departure. SCENE IN A CHURCIL—Durina the service at the Thurnby Parish Church on Sunday, the organist, owing to the recent attempt on the life of the Queen, played the National Anthem. When in the middle of it the vicar, the Rev. Mr. Redhead, shouted from the reading desk, "Stop it ! " The organist failed to hear him, and the vicar walked up to him, exclaiming, so that all the congregation could bear, "Stop it, I tell you!" He then walked to the organ blower, stop- ped the supply of wind, and suddenly brought the anthem to an ignominious end. The vicar next shouted to the organist, "I discharge you from ever playing at this organ again." The service was then proceeded with, but the pain- ful occurrence caused great ecitement among the congre- gation. It is stated that the National Anthem was played at the special request of the lady who presented the organ to the church, and who herself defrays the organist's ex- penses.

A RACING DREAMER.—This anecdote about the late Lord Wilton is sure to be much quoted. The late earl had a colt entered for the Chesterfield Cup at the Goodwood meeting some years ago—" The colt had previously always run as by Cotherstone from Duchess of Lorraine, and Lord Wilton had not troUblea himself about giving him a name. Shortly before the race, however, he receired a letter from Lora Chesterfield, enclosing him one which he himself had got from a gentleman,stating that he had dreamed most dis- tinctly a horse named Pumicestone had won the Chester- field Cup at Goodwood, and as he could not see one of that name in the entry he concluded it must be Lord Wilton's animal that had not been named. The colt being got by Cotherstone, he did not consider Pumicestone altogether in- appropriate, and, willing to humour the fancy of the dreamer, adopted the name. The vision was realised, for, without being quoted in the market, he beat Vanderdecken and a larze field very cleverly."—lllustrated Sporting and Dramatic _Yews.

THE MURDER IN FINCHLEY WOODS.—The following official statement has been issued from the Criminal Inves- tigation Department, Scotland-yard :—" Up to the present time it has not been possible to establish the identity of the burglar who was murdered in Finchley Woods on the 4th instant by his companion. Until this is done no legal result is possible. and the body has been seen in vain by police warders, keepers of common lodging-houses, gipsies, &c. The Government has offered a reward of £lOO and a free pardon to any accomplice for information on the subject at any police station which may lead to the conviction of the actual murderer. Among the proceeds of the burglary not recovered were a midshipman's telescope, by J. H. Steward, 366, Strand, covered with black morocco; naval signal flags painted on the sides, and having one German silver slide; a family volume of 'Shakespeare,' in brown binding, and a silver fruit knife, with a mother-of-pearl handle ; also a cocoa-nut-wood flute, four joints, silver keys and mouth- piece, maker, Bambridge. The utmost vigilance is enjoined upon all pawnbrokers and second-hand dealers in the event of the same being offered in pledge for sale." The arrangements for the review to be held at Ports- mouth, on Easter Monday, are well in progress. Of course the number of volunteers who are likely to be present is not yet known. It is expected to be a large force, chiefly from the Southerarcounties, though there will, no doubt, be a con- siderable contingent from the northern districts. The field day promises to be an interesting one. The programme is being arranged by Prince Edward of Saxe-Weimar and staff at Portsmouth, and by the headquarter staff at the War Office. The arrangements for the marching column are being made out by General Higginson and Colonel Methuen. The Mayor of Portsmouth has had an official communica- tion, announcing that the Prince of Wales will be present at the review, and the Duke of Connaught and other mem- bers of the Royal family have promised to attend. DEMONSTRATION OF SOCIAL DEMOCRATS.— A public meeting, convened by the Social Democratic Club, was held on Monday night in London, to commemorate the execution of Rornanoff. About 150 persons, composed of Russians, Germans, Frenchmen. Poles, and Englishmen attended. The chairman, a German, said they had met to commemorate a glorious deed performed a year ago, and to thank those instrumental in its accomplishment, and who afterwards suffered for it. People had to do horrible things to revenge great hardships. Had M'Laan not been half starved he would not have attempted the life of the Queen. The whole system of society was rotten, and the time had arrived when the English democracy should unite with the demo- cratic associations in other countries in aiding Russia to throw over the incubus despotism and Czardom. Resolu- tions were unanimously passed sympathising with those in Siberia, approving the assassination of the Czar, and urging the working classes to recognise that material force alone could achieve their emancipation.

Sir Charles Wyville Thomson died suddenly at his resi- dence, near Linlithgow, on Tuesday. The people of Plymouth have finally resolved to transfer Smeaton's lighthouse at Eddystone to the Hoe on the terms laid down by the Board of Trade. The proceedings in connection with the branch of the Salvation Armyat Exeter culminated on Sunday in a street scene, which resulted in the arrest of the captain. Elijah Richardson,!a fisherman, who was in custody at Hull on a charge of murdering John Smith, a constable belonging to the Hull police force, on the 19th Sept., 1880, has been 9et at liberty. Colonel Shaw, American consul at Manchester, has pro- mised to report to his Government on the adulteration of cotton sent to England, and, therefore, wishes for special in- formation.

The Royal Agricultural Commission have now concluded taking evidence—at least it is not expected that any further witnesses will be called—and at the next meeting the com- mittee will probably begin the preparation of their report. The police have apprehended three men on snspicion of being concerned in the death of William Ewing, who died in Glasgow Inffirmary en Monday from injuries recieved in a quarrel on Saturday night. The hat manufactory of Mr. John Ashworth, Dukinfield, has been destroyed by fire, which broke out at a late hour on Thursday night. The loss of property is estimated at £lO,OOO, and 300 persons are thrown of work. A Ballina correspondent telegraphs that Mr. Geo. Carter, a magistrate for county Mayo, while driving through the gateway of his house, near Belmullet, on Wednesday night, was shot at and seriously injured in the right leg by some upkown person. It was stated that the body of .the man recently fdund murdered in Finchley Wood, under mysterious circum- stances, has been fully identified. Some important infor- mation in reference to the matter has also transpired, and a description been given to the police of two men supposed to be-implicated in the murder. In the division upen Mr. Mitchell-Henry's motion to ad- journ the debate upon Mr. Findlater's bill to amend the Land Act 15 Home Rulers voted in the majority for the motion, and eight in the minority. Mr. Gladstone, Lord Harting- ton, and Mr. Foraer voted with Mr. Mitchell-Henry; and Mr. W. H. Smith and James Lowther against. A married woman named Jane Close, who has been deserted by her husband, and who lives at Middlesborough, administered some rat poison to her child and afterwards took some herself. Both were removed to the infirmary. where they died shortly after admission. The borough magistrates of Shrewsbury have remanded a woman named Annie Wycherley for deserting her boy, aged two years, in October last, and leaving him chargeable to the Atcham Union. The child was found left in a waiting- room with its arm broken and its shoulder dislocated. The unnatural motker avoided detection unil now.

It is officially announced that Vanderstein and Fulton, arrested at Brussels snspected of the Hatton-garden robbery, will first be tried for offences committed in Paris, the French authorities haying applied for extradition. It will there- fore be a considerable time before they undergo trial in this country, as evidence against them in Paris is so clear that they will undoubtedly be sentenced. It is believed that had the French police moved earlier the whole gang would have been captured. ' At Manchester, on Thursday, William Edwards, a burglar, was committed for trial for burglary and wounding the police. The other night prisoner and another man broke into a tea shop, the back of which opens upon the canal bank. They were discovered by a policeman, and, jumping on the canal bank, one held him while the other beat his head with a jemmy, rendering him insensible. Other policemen came up, when the men ran across the lock gate. One escaped, but prisoner was caught. PRESCoT WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT S6CIETY.— The fifth and last lecture during the present session of the above society was given on Tuesday evening in the Chapel, Eccleston-street, by the IL v. J. M. Warnsley, his subject being "Peeps at society." I chair was occupied by Mr. Jas. Pratt, and there was a moik te attendance. As a re- port of the lecture has already apps. ,c 1 in these columns it is unnecessary to republish it; suffice it to say that it was of a masterly character, and was heartily enjoyed by all present. At the close a collection was made in aid of the funds of the society. CLAIMS ARISING OUT OF A COLLIERY EXPLOSION.— Claims under the Employers' Liability Act were made at Tunstall County Court, the other day, on behalf of the relatives of the 19 men killed by the explosion of gas at Whitfield Colliery, the property of the Chatterley .Colliery Company, in February last year. The total amount of claims is between £3.000 and £4,000. It was stated that de- fendants had applied in the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice to remove the action by writ of certiorari, but the application had failed. It was ultimately agreed to take the case at special sittings of the county court in April next, when it was stated they would occupy three days, there being 15 plaints in all. On Thursday morning, at the West Riding Police Court, Bradford, a middle-aged man named John Keelin. was charged with being in possession of a battery mould, and other appliances, and with making counterfeit coins. The pr.:seller, who has undergone penal servitude for coining, has lived in Queen's-road, Salttire, and for some time past has been suspected, owing to the counterfeit number of florins and shillings which have been in circulation in and around Bradford. On Thursday the police made a raid on his house, and found him in the act of silvering some coins by means of the battery. Two unusually perfect moulds were also seized, and numerous florins and shillings. Receipts were found for large quantities of spoons purchased at Birming- ham, and which furnished the metal for coining. The ring and appearance of the coins were excellent ; but the defect was in the milling, or the finishing of the edges. When the. Mint authorities have completed their arrangements the pri- soner will be again brought up. THE WORKINGTON MURDER.—On Saturday Maynard James Harrison, aged 19 yea?* ironworker, was brought up in custody at Workington Police Court charged with the wilful murder of Lucy Sands, at North Side, Workington, on or about the Ist of December last. It will be remem- bered that the body was found under a stone heap a fort- night ago.—Superintendent Bird asked that the prisoner should be remanded for a week, remarking that the charge was,one of such magnitude as to require a great amount of inquiry. By next Saturday he hoped to lay before the court evidence in connection with the charge against the prisoner.—Mr. Paisley, solicitor, Workington, appeared for the prisoner, and asked if he might be permitted an inter- view with prisoner after the close of the court.—The magis- trates refused the application. The police have been digging up Mr. Harrison's garden. The inquest on the body of the girl Lucy Sands was concluded at Workington on Tuesday, when the jury returned a verdict against some person or persons unknown. RUSSIA AND PERSIA—FOREIGN OFFICE PAPERS.—A parliamentary paper was issued on Tuesday, containing a copy of correspondence that has passed between the English Foreign Office and its representatives at Teheran, on the affairs of Central Asia, with paratcular reference to the negotiations with the Persian Government for the demarca- tion of the Russo-Persian ;boundary in Khorassan, and the construction of the Trans-Caspian Railway from Kras- novolsk to Rizil Arvat. The correspondence includes the text of the treaty signed between Russia and Persia at Teheran in December last, whereby power is given to Russia to-extend the Trans-Caspian Railway a distance of 146 miles in the direction of Askhabad and Sarakhs, bringing the new Russo-Persian frontier, according to the Gobs, only sixteen versts short of Sarakhs. Mr. Thomson, English consul at Teheran, alleges this statement to ,be without foundation, and says that, according to the trea‘y forwarded to him by the Persian Government, the new Russian frontier will be nearly 150 miles short of Sarakhs ; and the Persian Minister for Foreign Affairs had most positively stated that this treaty contained the only agreement come to with Russia in regard to frontier. Denial was also given to the assertion that the question of the Atek region was included in the negotiations. "JUMBO "AND HIS CAGE—At last " Jumbo " has been "caged." The ingenious and laborious efforts of his pro- prietors, old and new, were on Saturday crowned with suc- cess. Another great and concerted attempt to indute the elephant to go through the huge wooden cage prepared for his reception was brought to a practical test on Saturday forenoon; and when he was led out of his house and shown the superstructure which he has hitherto shown such an in- superable suspicion of, the officials present were surprised to see how quietly and unsuspiciously he walked into it. Of course, the surprise was an agreeable one to Mr. Barnum's i agent, who was present, and who looked upon t as a great triumph. " Jumbo " was not instantly confided in his new cell. He was merely led through it; and the docility with which he acceded to the wishes of his captors was regarded as removing the only difficulty standing in the way of his shipment for exportation. It is believed that there will now not be the slightest difficulty in inducing him to enter again whenever it is necessary for him to be secured for removal. It will ba remembered that the last effort was made to cage Jumbo in order that he might sail by the Egyptian Monarce I which left Gravesend on Thursday last; but all efforts to secure him in the beginning of the week being unsuccessful, it was then resolved to delay his shipment till the departure of the Assyrian Monarch, which is advertised to sail on the 22nd inst. from London. The Press Association has authority for saying that there is good reason to believe that if a sum of £15,000 can be raised or duly guaranteed by this day (Saturday) for the release of the elephant Jumbo, Mr. Davis, the agent for Mr. Barnum in this country, would be willing to telegraph to that gentleman for his sanction to an arrangement by which this valuable animal might remain in England, and would probably not dissuade Mr. Barnum from acceding to these terms. An appeal will forthwith be made in the course of' a day or two to members of the Zoological Society, and ladies and gentlemen of position throughout the United Kingdom, to open subscription lists, notifying their intention to the leading" daily papers. The Lord Mayor will also be appealed to to open a fund for the purpose. div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

A. Bitt restricting Chinese emigration into the lUnited States has been passed by the Senate. The second centenary of Murillo is about to be celebrated at Serille, his birthplace, by, among other things a collection of his pictures. A Vienna journal states that 800 individuals not fur- nished with passports have been expelled from Moscow within the last few days. From Sophia we learn that, upon the proposal of the mayor of that city, it has been resolved to expend £B,OOO towards the erection of a new chapel in memory of the late Emperor of Russia. Various rumours have been afloat as to an intended journey of the Shah of Persia. The Ahter of Constanti- nople says that His Majesty's journey will be confined to a visit to the Sultan. According to intelligence which has reached Vienna from St. Petersburgh, the reception of General Scobeleff by the Emperor at Gatschina was anything but gracious, and he has had to listen to earnest reproaches about having alie- nated Germany and isolated Russia. The movement against the Monaco gaming tables is evi- dently gaining ground in France. The Committee on Petitions will shortly report on it to the Senate, and a dis- cussion will doubtless be devoted to it. Meanwhile, papers of different shades are denouncing the scandal. A Times Kurrachee telegram of Sunday says :—The western frontier of Afghanistan has resumed its normal con- dition, but in Candahar men of position continue deli- berately to discuss the probability of the Ameer playing a double game, and retain their disbelief of the Shah of Persia having compelled Sirdar Ayoub Khan to retire to Teheran. The advance of Russia is still the prevailing topic among; Afghan chiefs and merchants from Candahar through Quetta and Shikarpoor to Kurachee. Yet the public is no doubt impressed by our indifference, knowing us to be as interested as themselves, but they speak of Russia as fearless and reckless.

The passage through the Bosphorus a few days ago of a Russian transport, with some 1,600 men on board, ex route for a Siberian port, has, it appears, given rise to an exchange of notes between the Porte and the Russian Government,the latter having, it is affirmed, neglected to obtain the custom- ary permission of Turkey. The Russian Embassey con- tended that asthe vessel was a merchant ship and the troops, who embarked as passengers, were unarmed, it was unneces- sary to ask permission. The Porte does not admit the validity of this argument, and though it allowed the vessel to proceed, entered a formal protest so that the incident may not be used as a precedent in future.

div.head: AFFAIRS IN TUNIS.
div.p: AFFAIRS IN TUNIS.

The Tunis correspondent of the Times reports that the Italian Consul-General there has received information which unfortunately leaves no doubt that two distinct massacres have taken place in the vicinity of Keiriva, in One of which alone five Italians have lost their lives. The sole survivor has been brought to Tunis mortally wounded, and his dying deposition has been taken. The details of the second out- rage are still wanting, but an Italian carter telegraphs to his employers here that his nine companions were all killed in his presence. These fresh disasters have much excited the Italian colonists, and the Italian representative will pro- bably issue a notice informing Italian subjects that if they continue to accept service with the French commissariat convoys or go.into the interior they do so at their own risk and peril. The French detachment at the outpost of Sidi el Ham has attacked the Arabs engaged in the recent razzias, and a sergeant of artillery has been killed. The Governor of Sias reports officially to the Tunisian Government that the insurgents now appear to be well armed, and that the Arabs shot in the recent razzias were wounded by bullets of European manufacture. The military authorities in Tunis do not attempt to conceal the gravity of the situation in Southern Tunis, and the probability of another campaign becoming necessary. It appears that the insurgents who committed the recent razzias passed northward by way of Nefta,amovement which was .wholly unexpected. Rein- forcements are to be sent into the disaffected districts, and it is even said that the line of the Tripolitan frontier will be occupied. The various estates granted by the Bey to the Mussalis are'being sold prior to their departure. One ot these properties was purchased lately by a British subject for 260,000 piastres. THE 'INSURRECTION IN THE HERZEGOVINA.

At a Council of Austrian and Hungarian Ministers held in Vienna on Sunday, the Minister for War announced that Crivoscie had been completely occupied by the Austrians, and that the speedy pacification of the Herzegovina was mpected. Nevertheless the withdrawal of the forces would not be possible at an early date, and additional frontier fortifications would be needed. The sum required for this purpose wa51,500,000 florins, which, with the additional cost of maintaining the troops on a war footing, renders a further grant necessary.

According to accounts received through Sclaconic sources, the engagement between the Austrian troops and Crivoscian insurgents at Jankow Urb, on the 11th inst., was very obsti- nately contested. The Austrians are stated to have lost about 200 men killed and wounded, while the insurgents' loss was only 10 men killed and 20 wounded. It is added that an engagement was proceeding at the same time at Markovdo, which resulted in the retreat of the Austrians, who left two guns on the field, which were captured by the insurgents, together with a quantity of war material,

THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION. The Egyptian Controllers presented their annual report to the 'Khedive on Sunday. It shows a surplus of revenue over expenditure in 1880-1881 of £800,1300, which surplus is divided between public works and the redemption of the debt. It is stated, however, that the Budget for 1882 im- perils the liquidation scheme by exceeding the allowances fixed by the Commissioner of Liquidatioß, and by increas- ing the military estimates by nearly half. A Cairo telegram states that M. de Blignieres sent in his resignation on the 6th February, but it was declined, and he was requested to remain at his post. On Sunday evening, however, the Comptroller received a telegram from M. de Freycinet accepting his resignation. The step taken by the French Government is interpreted in diplomatic circles at Cairo as ,sn abandonment by France of the policy of action which was strongly advocated by the French Comptroller General.
SERIOUS EARTHQUAKE IN SOUTH AMERICA. FOUR TOWNS DESTROYED AND GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.

A telegram from Panama announces that an earthquake has occurred in Costa Rica, by which no less than four towns have been destroyed—viz., Alajuela, San Ramon, Grecia, and Heredia. Several small villages have also suffered, the loss of life reaching a total of many thousands. The survivors have been rendered homeless, and very great distress prevails.

Within the last twenty or five and twenty years there have been many serious earthquakes in Central and. South America, but they have been most frequent during the last ten years. The town of San Salvador seems to be specially subject to visitations of this kind. It was destroyed on 16th April, 1854, by an earthquake.; on .Bth December, 1859, it was again severely shaken, and many buildings wrecked; and on 19th March, 1873, it was nearly destroyed, and about fifty people were killed, the nunir,•er being thus small be- cause of the timely warning given. In 1859, at. Quito, 5,000 persons perished, and much property was destroyed by an earthquake.; in 'lB6l two-thirds of the town of Mendoza I were destroyed, and 7,000 people killed; in 1862, in Guatamala, fourteen churches and 0.50 buildings were des- troyed. Then there was a rather long interval of rest; but in 18/08 a terrible eattliquake wrecked Areguipa, Iquique, Tacna, and Chencha, and many other towns in Peru and Ecuador, killing 25,000 people and rendering 30,000 home- less. On this occasion a relief fund of £ll,OOO was col- lected in London. After an interval of a few years, dis- turbances again began and in 1872 several small towns were destroyed in California, and thirty people killed; in 1874, Antigua and other places in Guatarnala were destroyed, with great loss of life • in 1875, San JcsO de Cercata and the other towns near Santander were destroyed, and 14,000 tlives lost; in 1877, an earthquake, accompanied by a great tidal wave, near Callao, went southward, doing much 1 damage and injuring many towns; and in 1878 the town of Cua in Venezuela, was nearly destroyed, 300 people being killed and property wrecked to the value of L 30,000.

What may be the extent of the present disaster is as yet uncertain. Costa Rica is supp3sed to have a total popula- tion of about 185,000, and the town of Alajuela—the largest of the places destroyed—is believed to have contained about 12,500. _ _ _

A New York telegram says :—News received here from Panama states that the report of the earthquake at Costa Rica was taken from an official dospatch, but proves to be grossly exaggerated. Advices which have reached Panama by mail do not bear out the statements relative to the great destruction of life and property contained in the official telegram.

div.head: ANGLO-FRENCH TREATY.
div.p: THE ANGLO-FRENCH TREATY.

A Paris telegram says a conference was field there on Wednesday morning, at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, between M. de Freycinet, President of the Council ; M. Tirard, Minister of Commerce; and Lord Lyons, British Ambassador, on the subject of a resumption of the Anglo- French Treaty negotiations, which is regarded as certain, although no date has yet been fixed.

RUNCORN TRUE BLUES V. WARRINGTON- ST. JOHN'S.— This match was played on the ground of the former, and resulted ma win for the home team by two goals, four tries, and five minor points to nil. The game was not so one- sided as the score would lead one to suppose, on the con- trary, it was a bard-fought and pleasant one. Andrews was the best on the side of the winners, and obtained two tries. Worthington (a forward) by following hard on the ball gained two more, and Dutton and Hankinson got one each. Besides those mentioned, Gatley, Hughes, and Speakman rendered good service for the Blues. On the side of the losers, J. Powhall (sub.) was the best, his kicking saving his side many a time, and Proctor and Boardman ran well for Warrington and tried hard to avert defeat. Sides:— True Blues: Full back, J. Jones; three quarter backs, Skel- horn, Speakman, and Johns,: I; half-backs, Hughes and. Andrews; forwards, W. C'e s, A. Barnes, T. Barnes, Wright, and Spencer. ENGLAND v. SCOTLAND.—This great event in the annals of Association football took place on Saturday, on the Queen'n Park Ground, Glasgow, in the presence of 12,000 spectators, and ended in favour of Scotland by five goals to one, al- though two of the score were considered by many to have been offside. The weather was good, and the ground in fair playing order. Scotland won the toss, and played with a strong wind during the first round. The Englishmen made a grand run after the kick-off, and the Scotch goal-keeper had to throw away the ball. The game, in fact, notwith- standing the strong wind against them, was very much in favour of England for the first 20 minutes, and they had several shies at the Scotch goal by Mosfroth, Vaughton, and Parry. The Scots after this played better together, and a good run by Ker, Fraser, and Harrower ended in the latter scoring a goal for Scotland. The English umpire appealed for offside, but was not sustained. After the next kick-off, the Englisnmen made it hot for the Scotch by Cursham and. Brown. The Scots had three corner kicks, which were grandly saved by Greenwood and Bailie, and a magnificent run by Brown and Mosfroth against the wind, ended in Vaughton making a fine goal for England against wind. This was received with tremendous cheering. A few minutes before half time the home team attacked the English goal, and Ker made a beautiful hard shot under. It was thought that England now, with the wind in their favour, would completely lick Scotland, but, in one minute from ends being changed, Ker, Fraser, and Kay made a grand run and middled to APPherson, who scored a third goal for the Scotch ;an appeal to off side dismissed. After the start, the English came away finely, and a shot by Bam- bridge just shaved the bar. A corner-kick to them followed, and the Scotch keeper 1-tad to throw out. Do what they could, the Scotch backs could not shake off the English forwards, and four shies at goal occured within seven minutes. The game was now standing at three goals to one and the Scotch made a desperate effort, and a beautiful goal come from the foot of Ker, and a fifth followed by Kay. The last was a clear case of off side, but the referee con- sidered it a fair goal. Just as time was called, the English- men had a corner-kick, and from the scrimmage the ball hit the post and rebounded into play, and eventually passed the posts. The play was the fastest ever seen in Scotland, and the result does not show the real nature of the game. Sides—England: H. A. Swepstone (Pilgrims), goal; H. D. Greenwood (Blackburn Rovers) and A. Jones (Walsall Swifts), backs; N. C. Bailey (Clapham Revers), captain, and J. Hunter (Sheffield), half backs ; E. C. Bambridge (Swifts) and W. H. Mosfroth (Sheffield), left wing; H. A. Vaughton and A. Brown (Aston Villa), centres; H. A. Car- shame (Notts County) and E. H. Parry (Old Carthusians)„ right wind. Scotland : G. Gillispie (Rangers), goal ;A. Watson (Queen's Park) and A. MSlntvre (Vale of Leven), backs; C. Campbell (Queen's Park) and P. Miller (Dunbar- ton), half-backs; E. Fraser and W. Anderson (Queen's Park), right ; G. Ker and W. Parrower (Queen's Park), centres: J._ L. Kay (Queen's Park) and R. M`Pherson (Arthurlie), left. Referee; Mr. J. Wallace, vice-president S.F.A. Umpires : Mr. T. Anderson (Renfrew) and Mr. S. R. Bastard (Upton Park). ENGLAND V. WALES.—This intertnational match, under Association rules, was played at Wrexham yesterday after- noon in glorious weather. Wales won the toss, and Eng- land kicked off at seven minutes past three. The Welsh- men at once commenced a siege on the Engligh citadel, and were more than once within an ace of scoring. The English- men made a splendid run, and the attempt to score was splendidly got away by Adams. Wales cotinued to play splendidly, Price, Morgan, and Hughes being the most pro- minent. Mosfroth made a grand run on the left wing, and scored the first goal for England. A second run was made by I Brown, the ball just grazing the bar. Mosfroth made a grand , run, passed to the centre, and Parr scored a second goal. for England at 3-44. A difficult shot by Vaughan was well got away by Swepstone. A corner fell to Wales, and Owen scored for his side at 3-50. The game was well contested up to half time, England only playing ten men, Bambridge having his shoulder put out. Ends were now changed. England at once scored a third goal at four o'clock. Owen made a splendid shot, but Swepstone proved equal to the emergency. A good run on the right wing was made by Owen and scored by Roberts at 4-20 for Wales. A deter- mined attempt by Wales was rewarded by scoring a third- goal, thus balancing matters. At 4-47 Wales scored another goal, and Vaughan scored a fifth goal directly afterwards, the game thus ending in favonr of Wales by five goals to three. Teams : Welsh: Goal, Adams (Berwyn Rangers); backs, Morgan (Derby School) and Powell (Druids) ; half backs, Williams (Druids), Edwards (Wrexham), and Hughes (Northwich); right wing, Owen (Ruthin) and Roberts (Ruthin) ; left wing. Vaughan (Druids) ; and Roberts (Cot- wen) ; centre, Price (Wrexham) ; umpire, Mr. Kendrick. English : Goal, Swepstone (Pilgrims) ; backs, Hunter (Sheffield) and Jones (Walsall Swifts) half backs, Brown (Aston Villa) and Bailey, captain (Clapham Rovers) ; right wing, Cursham (Nottingham) and Parry (Swifts) ; left wing, Mosfroth (Sheffield) and Vaughton (Aston Villa) ; centres, Bambridge (Swifts) and Parr (Oxford). Umpire, Mr Bastard. Referee, Mr. Roberts. HIGH LIFE BELOW STAIRS.

Andrew Heinrich Hermann, a German upper footman in the service of Mrs. Aimes, of 37, Eaton-square, Belgravia, appeared to a summons before Mr. D'Eyncourt, at the West- minster Police Court, on Saturday, charging him with assaulting Mildred Kate Smith, the upper housemaid in the same establishment, bv throwing a jug of boiling water in her face. Mr. Alfred I`. Bristow defended. The complainant, a good-looking girl, bad her face bound up with a surgical bandage. and she deposed that at half-past ten on the morn- ing of Wednesday, the 22nd ultimo, she was having break- fast in the servants' hall, when she bad a few words with the defendant, who thereupon threw a cup of hot tea upon her, and then took a jug of boiling water and dashed it in her face. She was badly scalded, and had to go to the hospital. For two or three days the scalds were very pain ! ful. Mr. D'Eyncourt asked what they had a dispute about. The complainant said the defendant wanted to make out that he was more "than a footman "—in fact, he would like to make out that he was a butler. (Laughter.) In cross- examination the girl admitted that she said " I wish I was a favourite," and that the other housemaid said there ought Itobe no favourites. They were not jealous of the defendant having hot suppers, but they did not think that ha was entitled to the privilege of having his meals in the house- keeper's room. Defendant was a foreinger, and they might have chaffed him. Mr. Bristow: When you said, "It was well for some people to be favourites," what did you mean ? Witness: I -meant that the housekeeper encourages him in her roomwhen it is Rot his place there. I told him he was "only a footman," and thee he threw the boiling water over me.—Mr. Bristow : Well, did it hurt you much? (Loud laughter.) The complainant said it caused her considerable pain, and she was afraid that she would lase some of her hair. The next day the defendant apologised to her, and she agreed to forgive him; but as he afterwards laughed at her, she, acting on the advice of her aunt and father, took out this summons. Mr. Bristow said the young man bore a very good character, and lie was instructed by his employer, Mrs, Aimes, to defend him. Undoubtedly, on this occasion, de- fendant had acted improperly, but, becoming aggravated, he had list his temper. Being allowed to take his meals in the housekeeper's room, gave mortal offence to the other servants, and they were continually annoying him by saying "that he was only a footman." Mr. D'Eyncourt said he had no business to throw boiling water over the girl. It was a cruel thing and might have blinded her. But for the fact that she had once forgiven him, he should have imposed a very heavy penalty, but as it was, he would have to pay 20s. ! and 325. costs, the latter to be allowed to the complainant !as compensation. The money was immediately paid.

BOTELER GRAMMAR SCHOOL, WARRINGTON. FOUNDED A.D. 1526. Head Master: The Rev. E. J. WILLCOORS, M.A. Late Scholar of St. Catharine's College, Cambridge. Second Master: The Rev. H. G. SMITH, M.A., Scholar of St. John's College, Cambridge; And five Assistant Masters. The School contains two divisions. The work of the Lower Division comprises a regular course of instruction in English, French, the rudiments of Latin, elementary Mathematics and Science, with Reading, Writing, Arithmetic, Drawing, Drill, and Vocal Music, and all other elements of a sound modern education. In the Upper Division, the choice is offered of a thorough mercantile or high classical course ; German and Greek being optional subjects. , Eight Free Scholarships. Two Exhibitions to Oxford and Cambridge. The year is divided into three Terms. Capitation fees, everything included, £.l and £3 per term in the Upper and Lower Divisions respectively. Entrance Fee, £l. next term commences Thurday, April 27th. For further particulars apply to the Head Master.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, MARCH 18, 1882.

ONE of the three great watchwords of the Liberal party is "Retrenchment," and the present Adminis- tration, following the example of every other Liberal Administration which has preceded it, would appear to keep that steadily in view in their dealings with the finances of the country. It will be remembered that the last Liberal Government, when they sur- rendered the seals of office, left a surplus of several millions to their successors, but a 'very different state of things existed when the Beaconsfield Administra- tion was dismissed. Thea the coffers of the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer were empty, the money of the nation having been recklessly expended in a spirited foreign policy, and the finances of the country were a chaotic mass. Now, however, thanks to the financial ,genius of the Premier, something like order has been restored, and by a steady policy of retrenchment being pursued there is every Probability that the coming Buget will be one of the most satisfactory which Mr. Gladstone has yet unfolded. The estimates for the year 1882.3 of the three great spending departments of the country have now been published, andideserve consideration. Both the navy and army estimates show a considerable reduction as compared with pre- vious years; though it is true the estimates for the civil servisce are exceptionally high. This is chiefly owing to the fact—much to be regretted—that the maintenance of law and order in Ireland is, and has been for some time, a heavy charge upon the Ex- chequer. The estimates for the navy, which were issued on Saturday, are the lowest that have been sub- mitted, it is gratifying to know, for the past three years. The total sum to be voted is £10,483,901, as against £10,945,919 last year. The net apparent decrease is therefore £462,019, but the net actual decrease is much less, being stated at £221,130. On the transport of troops alone there is.a reduction of no less than £323,650, which is caused mainly by the heavy expenses in 1881-2 consequent upon the Transvaal rebellion, an item which is not likely to appear in the estimates again; but against this saving there are increases in other depart- ments of the service. On the whole, • however, the figures are such as to show that, judicious economy, consistent with efficiency, is exercised. The army estimates are equally satisfactory. They are this year for £15,458,100, against £15,589,500 for 1881-2, end- ing with the present month. The net apparent de- crease here is £1,131,400, but the net real decrease is £563,000. The principal decrease in the army as in the navy estimates is in respect of the special expendi- ture for the war in South Africa, the restoration of tranquility there being a saving to the tune of £1,065,500; and there is a further decrease of £568,000 in what is designated "extra receipts taken in aid of the rates," 'which sum had it been returned to the Exchequer would have increased the estimates by that amount. Against this apparent saving there must be placed an additional expenditure of £247,000 in providing for naval guns and projectiles, an item which under a new arrangement enters into the army estimates, and this outlay is consequent upon the gradual re-armament of the navy, a movement initiated by the late Government. For that outlay, therefore, we receive an equivalent. While that is the chief item of any account in which there is an in- crease in the army estimates, there is one other item of increase which it would have been well had it not been necessary to provide for, that is one of X rB,OOO for additional troops in Ireland. This, it is hoped, may not be necessary on a future occasion. Comparing the army estimates for the coming year with those for 1879, when a Tory Government was in power, the result is most striking. The amount voted in the latter year was £17,900,000, no lass than X t,900,000 in excess of the current year's estimate, and £2,400,000 in excess of the amount asked for the year 1882-3. This is one of the advantages which accrues from a peace- ful as opposed to a bellicose policy being pursued; and it is one which the taxpayer can appreciate. The combined army and naval expenditure at the present time, Mr. Childers pointed out the other night, is £25,940,000, equal to 145. Bd, a head on the present population ; in 1858-9, which was the year of the least expenditure between the Crimean war and the increase of charges, it was £21,300,000-155. a head on the then population; and in 1865-6, when the expenditure for army and navy purposes reached the smallest point after the higher expenditure a few years before, it amounted to 422,700,000, or at the rate of rss. 2d. a head on the population. If, again, the War Secretary showed, a comparison were made between the expenditure for the army and navy and what would be produced by the income tax, the result would be that while in the early years of that tax the combined army and navy expenditure was equal to rs. 6d. in the X, it has gradually fallen till it amounts in the estin3ates of the present year to 4d. in the L less—ls. 21. The comparisons, it will be noticed, are all in favour of the present expenditure; at the same time it is much too large, and if any means can be devist?d for the reduction of the permanent charges 0 much the better. The civil service estimates are tea most unsatisfactory of all that have been published. They are for £25,292,818, while last year the sum voted was £24,616,950, showing an increase of £675,868. It is on these that the cost of our troubles in Ireland are felt. The estimated charge of the Irish constabulary
