div.head: EXAMINEE, SATURDAY, "MARCH 18, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINEE, SATURDAY, "MARCH 18, 1882.

is for the coming year £1,332,146, whilst in the cur- rent year it was £1,192,975, an increase under this head alone of £139,171.* The bailiffs and sheriffs' officers charges are set down at .4;11,508 more than last year, and the expenses of the Land Commission are estimated at £92,552. These three items combined, and they are purely Irish, absorb £243,231 of the ex- penditure this year. There are other items of extraor- dinary expenditure in these estimates which may be easily accounted for, but the increase of £29,450 in stationery and printing seems to require explanation. The education estimates are this year much higher than they have yet been. The estimated cost of education for England and Wales is £2,749,863, more by £65 903 than in 1881- 2 ; in Scotland the estimate is £468,512; and in Ireland, £729,868. This, how- , ever, is an expenditure for which the nation will be recouped at some future time, if not in hard cash, in the increased enlightenment of the people, and the corresponding decrease of the expenditure necessary in the maintenance of paupers and in the cure and Punishment of crime which may be expected to follow the development of the education scheme. As we have pointed out, while there is a decrease in the army and navy estimates there is an increase in those for the civil service. The combined army and navy decrease is £784,130, and if the increase in the civil service votes of £675,868 be deducted from that amount there is still, however, left a margin on the right aide of £108,262. If the same economy which is manifest here is practised in other departments of the State—and there is no reason to doubt that it is not —its effect will be welcomed by the taxpayer, whose burdens will be made the easier to bear in consequence.

RUNCORN AND THE STARR-BOWEETT SOCIETY.—NearIy £40,000 shares have been issued by the Runcorn and district Starr-Bowkett Society, which appears to be making good headway under the secretaryship of Mr. William Handley, who is emphatically the right man in the right place. The second appropriation will take place on Wednesday evening next, at Bethesda schoolroom.

FAILURE AT RUNCORN.-A meeting of the creditors of William Lyon, of Runcorn, soda, &c., manufacturer, has been held at the Law Association-rooms, Cook-street, Liver- pool. The statement of affairs showed liabilities (partly secured), £2,988; estimated value of securities, £2,674; assets, £365. It was resolved that the estate be wound up in liquidation. Mr. E. B. RoOse, chartered accountant, 26, North John-street (receiver), was appointed trustee, with a committee of inspection. The debtor had ;the sympathy of the meeting, and his discharge was granted.

WIDNES RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION AND THE COMING LOCAL ELECTION.-A very well attended meeting of the members of the Widnes Ratepayers' Association took place on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr. David Wright, at Simm's Cross Hotel, for the purpose of reconsider- ingthe decision arrived at with regard to the number of can- didates to be brought forward at the forthcoming Local Board election. The Chairman remarked that the meeting had been convened owing to the fact that the Owners' and Occupiers' Association appeared to be of opinion that the society, in connection with which they assembled that night was really of no account, and entirely nninfluential. This was proved by the fact that the association he referred to had taken upon themselves to nominate candidates for all the vacant seats upon the Board. Their own organisation would have been quite willing to accept a compromise, but the offer they made had been refused, and they had, therefore, come to the conclusion to lay before the members a recom- mendation in favour of contesting all the vacant seats. The committee suggested that the candidates to be placed before the public should be Mr. David Wright, Mr. E. Martley, Mr. Midwood, Mr. Webster, and Mr. J. E. Johnson. Mr. Johnson was really the nominee of the Rev. Father Finegan, on behalf of the Catholics, Mr. Hayes having declined to steed again. It was ultimately decided that the gentlemen suggested by the committee should be adopted as the can- didates of the association. As to the Guardians' election, the Chairman said the gentlemen who retired this year were, in fact, the nominees of the Ratepayers' Association, but they had been taken up by the Owners' and Occupiers' Organisation. The Ratepayers' Association would nominate them as well. He also observed that on a former occasion they had brought forward the Rev. Father Finegan. He thought it was time the ratepayers, as a body, began to look more closely after their own interests. They had now the prospect of a 3s. poor rate to cover a 'period of eight months, and they had been told that there was a further prospect of another 3s. rate for general district pnrposes, so that they would soon, in all conscience, be sufficiently taxed. The other business was of a conversational character.

CONCERT AT ST. BED', APPLETON.—The fifth con- cert of the season was given at St. Bede's Catholic Church school room, on Monday evening, to a crowded audience. The opening chorus was the "Gloria," from Haydn's First Mass. Miss Kate Nono, a soprano with a voice of great range, and who is better known in the neighbouring town of Runcorn than at Widnes, gave Handel's charming piece "Angels ever bright and fair" with much effect, and was awarded with a round of applause. Bennet's quartet "God is a spirit "was sung with mueh expression by Mrs. Mahon, Miss Brown, Mr. Morrison, and Mr. Lawton. Miss Brown next sang "But the Lord is mindful of His own." Mr. Lawton was put . down in the programme for Mozart's " Redempto Mundt Deus," but sang instead "Honour and arms," from Samson's oratorio, with much power and 'felicity of expression. He was encored, and replied to the request by singing another piece in an equally effective manner. In Curschmann's "Ti Prego," which was rendered by Miss Norio, Miss Brown, and Mr. Morrison, the powerful voice of the first-named lady was heard to much advantage, and, we need scarcely say, that Mr. Morrison sang with great force anti expression. The audience loudly demanded an encore, but it was not granted. Cherubini's "Ave Maria" was sung by Miss Smith in a manner which won her very i hearty applause, and, n response, she repeated the last verse. The first part of the concert terminated with the "Gloria," from Mozart's Twelfth Mass. The second part was entirely devoted pieces of a secular character. It was commenced with Richard's glee " Up, quit thy bower," followed by the song" Some day," by Miss iNono, which won her an encore. The lady replied with "A letter from over the sea," which was rendered with much natvetO, and thoroughly pleased the audience. Bishop's "My pretty page" was sung by Miss Brown and Miss Wright, and they were encored. A similar mark of approval was given to Miss Smith in Sullivan's pretty song" Looking back." Mr. Mahon and Mrs. Mahon next gave " The fisherman's de- parture," in a manner which was thoroughly appreciated. Miss Nono followed with "Tit-for-tat,", and: was very warmly received, on which she replied with " Coinin' throughthe rye," which she sang with a vivacity truly charming. Balfe's piece" The sailor sighs," was taken by Miss Nono and Mr. Morrison, and proved a rich treat. The concert proved a most successful one, and concluded with the singing of the song "Auntie," by Miss Smith. FRIARS' GREEN CHAPEL, WARRINGTON.—Mr. W. Bellamy, of Leigh, preached two sermons in this chapel on Sunday last to good congregations, and the collections in aid of the chapel fund realised £9..

GIFT TO THE WARRINGTON INFIRMARY. Yesterday afternoon the funds of the Warrington Infirmary were in- creased by the sum.of £5, which was presented by Mr. Jas. Naylor, of Stockton Qaay. FIRE AT WaunnraroN.—About a quarter past three o'clock on Tuesday afternoon, a fire Vroke out in a wooden erection belonging to Mr. William Stringer, 22, Victoria-st. and situate at the rear of the premises. The fire brigad was summoned by the ringing of the fire-bell, and a reel- cart was immediately despatched, but the fire was ex- tinguished on its arrival. WARRINGTON PETTY SESSIONS.—At these sessions on Wednesday, before Mr. Geo. Artingstall (chairman) and Mr. P. Stubs, John Perrin, Rixton ; and John Peak, Croft, were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness.—Richard Young, Winwick, summoned for an offence under the Educa- tion Act, waS dismissed.—Wm. Mason, Haydock, a young man, for assaulting an elderly lady named Emma Hughes, of the same place, was fined 10s. and costs, with the alterna- tive of a month's imprisonment. WESLEY HALL CRICKET Cnun.—The annual tea meeting in connection with the above club was held in the school- room, Silver-street. on Saturday last, when over 80 members and friends were present. % After tea an entertainment was given, consisting of songs, readings, and glees, which were rendered by Miss Turley, Miss Daniels, Miss Waterfield; and Messrs. J. Mercer, J. Lewis, D. Jackman. S. Catterall, and J. Young. The chair was taken by Mr. Miles. WABRINGTori INFIRMARY AND DlSPENSABY.—House- surgeon's report for the week ending Thursday, March 17. Patients admitted and discharged—Home Patients, 10; out patients, 28; accidents, 6; total, 44. Cured, 0 ; dead, 1; discharged, 0 ; total, 1. Present number of home patients 36. In-patients: Admitted, 4. discharged, 0; remaining in hospital, 13. Hon. Treasurer, J. R. Buckton, Esq. ; Hon. Secretary, Jos. Davies, Esq. ; House Surgeon, Mr. C. E. Rich- mond. The House Surgeon will feel obliged for contributions of old 'linen, drc. Medical officer for the ensuing week Dr. Gornall.

Docrons' DIFFERING.—This is an old adage of which we have had a practical proof in that the medical man at Liverpool refused to pass recruits who would be, and it is said were, passed by the doctor at Warrington. As recruit- ing sergeants obtain no "bringing money" for men who are rejected, it is said that the sergeants found it profitable to pay the railway fare of recruits from Liverpool to Warring- ton, there being a much greater chance of their being passed at the latter place. It appears that in connection with this anomaly a sergeant-major and colour-sergeant have been placed under arrest, and the whole of the militia staff warned that they are not to be bringers of army recruits until further orders. The medical men can hardly both be right; one is either apparently too strict or the other too lenient,—Liver- pea Courier. SILVER-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL CRICKET CLUB.—Last Saturday the members and friends of the above club held their annual meeting at Silver-street schools, when between seventy and eighty sat down to tea, which was of a very substantial character. After tea the meeting was presided over by Mr. Miles in the absence of Mr. Loudon. The secretary, Mr. Cottrall, read the report, which was a fair one, and cordially invited members to join the club and the Young Mens' Bible Class on a Sunday afternoon. Several interesting pieces were sung by the Misses Firley, Daniels, drc. Readings were given by Messrs. Lewis, Hickman, Mercer, and Young. Very amusing were the readings and recitations given by Mr. Lewis, "The Parson's Predica- ment" and "The Virginia Leather Tanner." The meeting, which on the whole was a most enjoyable one, was brought to a close—after a slight refreshment in the shape of desert, a vote of thanks to the ladies, the chairman, and the com- mittee for their self-denial—by the singing of the National Anthem. Mr. Charles Tanner presided at the harmonium. ST MARY'S CHURCH, BUTTERMARKET-STREET, WARRING- TON.—On Sunday morning last there was a grand service held in this church to celebrate the opening of the new altar rails, which had been erected during the preceding week. The rails, which will cost about £9O, are composed of white marble, beautifully carved, present a splendid ap- pearance, and are a capital addition to the ornamentation of the church. They are from the design of the late Mr. Pugin, architect, of London, from whose plans the church itself was built; and have been put up by Messrs. Williams and Clay, of this town. The choir which had been augmented for this occasion by members from St. Alban's choir, rendered Haydn's No. 6 mass with orchestral accompaniments under the leadership of Herr Praeger, with Mr. R. Eccles, acting as conductor. The principal soloists were Miss Burrows, and Miss Hind; Mr. P. Mather, and Mr. Jos. Dolan. Before the offertory the Rev. F. Pozzi preached an eloquent ser- mon, in the course of which he made an earnest appeal to , the congregation for their support, that the debt incurred by the erecting of the altar rails, might be cleared off as early as possible.
Mr. Win. Leach, of Runcorn, delivered a lecture on Friday night, to the members of the Camden Mutual Im- provement Class, his subject being "Local GeeOgy."

WIDNES HASTE TO THE RESeuS 1.0.G.T. LODGE.— At the weekly meeting of this lodge on Tuesday evening, Bro. Bradshaw, W.C.T., occupied the chair, and an entertain- ment took place. Readings were given by Bros. Williamson and Johnson, recitations by Bros. E. Johnson and A Parkin- son, and Sister Bola and Sister Routledge sang songs.

LECTURE ON THE Muss TRAFFIC AT WnaxEs.—On- Thursday evening Mr. Joseph Matthews, of Runcorn, delivered a lecture in connection with the Star of Widnes Lodge (1.0.G.T.), the subject being "The tree of intem— perance, and the instrumentality for pulling it down!' Mr. W. Hunt presided, and there was a good audience. At the close, a collection was made to defray expenses.

RUNCORN NELSON STREET SCHOOL CHAPEL TIESSION. —On Wednesday evening, about 60 people were provided with tea, it being the anniversary of the foundation of this branch of evangelistic work, which has proved itself of great use in the neighbourhood. The tea was given by Mr. Peter Pendlebury, and during the evening that gentleman was presented with a portrait of himself, and a work entitled "The Class Leader's Assistant." Addresses were also delivered by several friends.

MR. ROBINSON WATSON AT RUNCORN.—During the week Mr. Watson has continued his series of special ser- vices at St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, to large audiences. Mr. Watson shows much originality in his mode of procedure, and he has a winning manner which has won him golden opinions on all hands. On Thursday, there were numerous enquiries as to whether the gentleman would close his course on that evening, and the public will no doubt be pleased to hear that Mr. Watson has consented to remain several nights longer. IMPORTANT SALE OF Wonic AT WIDNES.—The friends in connection 'is ith the Milton Congregational Church, Simm's Cross, of which the Rev. T. Peters is pastor, have lately incurred considerable expense by erecting a neat wall round the sacred edifice. In order to raise funds for the dis- charge of this, and another small debt, a sale of work will be held on Wednesday afternoon, at the church. The sale will be opened at three o'clock, and tea will be provided at six. A public meeting will afterwards take place, at which Mr. R. Webster will preside. Several ministers and friends will deliver addresse., and a Farnworth musical party will contribute to the evening's proceedings.

INTERESTING TO RUNCORN THEATRE - GOERS. The lovers of the drama in Runcorn and the immediate neigh- bourhood, have a rich treat in store for them on the 27th inst., and two following nights, when the well known plays, "Caste," "Ours," and "School," will be performed at the Public Hall, by one of Mr. T. W. Robertson's London com- panies, under the management of Mr. F. Fayre. The theatrical press have all spoken in high terms of the manner in which these most interesting and popular plays have been placed upon the stage in other towns by this particular company, and we have not the slightest hesitation in strongly recommending them to the notice of the Runcorn public. LANCASHIRE PETITIONS. —ln the House of Commons on Monday, petitions were presented for the removal of the electoral disabilities of women duly qualified by law by Mr. Whitley from citizens of Liverpool, Mr. David Maclver from Rock Ferry, Mr. Thomasson from Bolton, Mr. Jacob Bright from Manchester, Mr. E. L. Stanley from Oldham, and Sir R. Cunliffie from Wrexham. In' favonr of Sunday closing by Mr. Whitley from the Richmond Chapel, Everton ; and in favour of opening museums, ttc., on Sunday by Mr. Jacob Bright from the National Sunday League. TREAT TO VOLUNTEERS' WIVES AND CHILDREN AT WARRINGTON.--ID accordance with the annual custom, some 500 of the wives and children of the married members of the 9th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers were entertained at tea on Monday afternoon in the Drill Hall, Bath-street. The arrangements for the tea were ably carried out by the following committee :—Sergoant Major O'Brien, Instructor Blease, Colour Sergeants Plinston and Daniels, Sergeants Hewitt, Massey, Baines and Long- shaw, Corporal Jolley, and Sergeant Bramhall (secretary); and they were assisted by Sergeants Jones and Cliffe, Cor- porals Buckley, Ford, and Baines. In the evening the usual ball was held, and dancing was kept up until twelve o'clock, the music being supplied by the band of the corps. GRANTS BY THE LANCASHIRE CONGREGATIONAL UNION. —At the annual business meeting of this Union at Burnley grants were made to churches in the county as follow :—ln the Blackburn district to 14 churches, in the Manchester dis- trict to 27 churches, in the Preston district to six churches, and to seven stations known as the Fylde initerancy ; and in the Liverpool district to 17 churches, making a total of 64 churches. The total of the grants to the churches was £2,601, and a further sum of £9OO was voted to other ob- jects, the principal one being an increased grant of £3OO to the General Church Aid Society of England and Wales. Strong appeals were made to the delegates to press upon their churches the desirability of rendering increased aid to this fund, as in other counties there is urgent need of help. An invitation was received from the Southport churches that the Union should bold next year's meeting in that town, and it was unanimously accepted. CaananinGE EXAMINATIONS. The University of Cam- bridge has established an additional Local Examination, to be held in September. This examination is undertaken at the request of the General Medical Council, to meet the con- venience of these who desire to register as medical students in October, for whom it will serve as the preliminary ex- amination which all such students are required to pass. Those who intend to enter into articles of clerkship with attorneys and solicitors can avail themselves of this means of satisfying the preliminary requirements of the Incor- porated Law Society. It will be convenient also for those who intend to enter the University in October and desire exemption from the previous examination ("litt:o go "). For these three classes of candidates there is no limit of age. The examination will commence on Monday, Sept. 4, and will be held in the same subjects as those for the ex- amination for Seniors in the December following, and the usual senior certificate can be obtained by students under the age of 18 on September 1. . The centres of examination already announced are Cambridge and London for which centres applications for entry must be made to London, Rev. G. F. Browne, St. Catherine's College, Cambridge, and R. St J. Corbet, Esq., 10, Portman-street, London, W. The Examina- tion may be held at other centres if there appears to be sufficient demand.

Lexcesinan Barnalurrs, &c.—(From last Friday night's Gazette.)—Bankrupts : W. Bartley, late of Rainhill, Lancashire, now of 90, Wordsworth-street, Liverpool, corn:' mercial traveller; and W. Hughes, 67, Tithebarn-street, and 1,3, and 5, Higbfield-street, Liverpool, trading as W. Hughes and Co., engineer, gasfitter, plumber, brassworker, and metal merchant, and residing at 10, Palmerston-street, Rock Ferry, Cheshire.—Liquidations by Arrangement: W. E. Sabin and H. S. Jennings, Everton-road, Chorlton-upen-Medlock, inn- keepers; J. Hirst, Henry-street, Oldham-road, Manchester, builder; C. Walker, Kremlin-drive, Stoneycroft, Liverpool, dealer in india-rubber manufactures; C. Sayer, Han ington- street, Liverpool, quarry proprietor; J. Pye, Ormskirk-road, Rainford, grocer; W. Hilditch, Wavertree-road, Liverpool, provision dealer; D. Robertson, Boundary-lane, Liverpool, shipwright; W. Gamble, Bold-street, Liverpool, bootmaker ; J. W. Baker, Dale-street, Liverpool, dining-room keeper; J. Haward], Gauxholme, near Todmorden, farmer; J. Ellison, New Springs, Aspall, joiner; G. C. Hunt, New Kinknell Farm, Culcheth, near Warrington, farmer; J. Ashcroft, Friargate, Preston, hotel keeper; I. Walton, Well-bank, Haslingden, yarn agent; E. Mackie, Oxford-street, Warring- ton, draper; and D. Murray, Rawlinson-street, Barrow-in- Furness, ale dealer.—(From Tuesday night's Gazette.)— Liquidations by arrangement: J. Ashmore, Minshull-street, Manchester, and Sloane-street, Moss Side, joiner; E. A. Groves, St. Ann's Place, Manchester, and of Blackpool, smalhvare and fancy goods dealer; S. Gembitzki, John Dalton-street, Manchester, tobacconist; W. C. Lowe, Hyde Road, Manchester, greengrocer; C. E. Kenworthy, Rochdale, dyer: S. Hall, Oldham, grocer ; M. Sellers, Preston, skip manufacturer; J. W. Rigby, Preston, weavers' overlooker ; A. Hampson' Fairfield, near Manchester cloth finisher, out of business; J. Houghton, Lower Ince, Wigan, engine-driver; C. Mottram, brewer, El ulme. FOUND DEAD IN THE RIVEII AT WARRINGTON.—An inquest was held at the Ship Inn, Bank Quay, yesterday, by Mr. T. W. Barker, deputy coroner, on the body of Rose Ann Dutton, married woman, who left her heme on the evening of the 22nd December last, and whose body was found in the Mersey at Bank Quay. on Wednesday evening. —Thomas Dutton, labourer, residing at Twelve Houses, Howley, said the deceased was his wife, and was 54 years of age. On the 22nd December last, between five and six in the evening, she left home to go for milk. She would have to go along the river side. It was a very foggy night. De- ceased got the milk at Messrs. Fairclough and' Sons, for whom he worked. She knew her way perfectly, having traversed the road for 11 years. Deceased should have re- turned about six o'clock, but as she did not return he went to the house to enquire about her, and found she had not been for the milk. He then went down the bank in which there was a fresh. He searched during the night and part of the next day without success, and he got a number of copies of a handbill printed announcing that his wife was missing. He had no doubt the body he had seen was that of his wife. He could not recognise the features, but he identified her by the clothing. Before she left home his wife was in good health and spirits. There was a lock close to the house which she would have to pass, and he thought deceased had fallen into the water there as the path was very narrow.--James Whitfield, 12 years of age, said about half-past six on Wednesday evening he was walking on the sands along the river side with a boy named Walter Warburton. They saw two boot heels sticking out of the sand, but as they could not get them out witness fetched his brother, and also a peliceman.—P.C. Shaw said at seven o'clock, on Wednesday evening, he received in- formation of the find of the body, which was completely buried,with the exception of the boot heels. He assisted to get the body out, and had it removed to the Ship Inn. The body was found opposite Crosfield's soapery.—A verdict of "Found dead" ssas returned.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

Your readers will be gratified to hear that a successful effort has been made to form a volunteer band at Widnes. On Thursday evening a meeting of ratepayers is to be held at Runcorn, which promises to be of a lively character, Dr. McDougall having given the overseers notice of a very important resolution affecting the Free Library question. Mr. C. B. Wood, of Runcorn, who is a practical electrician of many years' experience, has patented an invention by which the exact position of a poacher, or an attempt to enter a house by a burglar, may be instantaneously ascer- tained.

Mr. Robert Davies, solicitor, of Warrington, has forwarded to Dr. MeDougall, of Runcorn, a complete edition of the works of William Makepeace Thackeray, the king of Eng- lish satirists, for presentation to the Free Library which has just been formed in that town. Other well-wishers to the institution will no doubt follow this good example. One of Mr. T. M. Robertson's London companies will visit Runcorn within the next few days, and perform "Caste," "School," and "Ours," at the Public Hall. There is every probability of a contest in connection with the forthcoming election of members of the Local Board at Widnes, as seven candidates have been brought forward for the five vacant seats. Nominations are to be sent in to Mr. Kershaw, tbe returning officer, before the 23rd ult. The voting papers will be distributed on the 31st; on the 4th prox. they will be collected; and on the following day the work of casting up the figures will commence. During the week Runcorn St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel has been crowded with audiences who have 1 istened with rapt attention to the appeals of Mr. Watson, a gentleman who has devoted himself to evangelistic work, in which he has proved remarkably successful. There is probably no denomi- nation of Christians which has solved the problem of utilising the rich mine of the lay help in so splendid a manner as the Wesleyan Methodists. Every Sunday from John-o-Groat's to Land's End, their vast army of local preachers fulfil their appointments, and enable the denomi- nation to occupy ground which otherwise would be exclu- sively in the possession of the vicars of the various parishes. The Congregationalists have never succeeded in exerting the influence to which they are entitled in many of our vil- lages. The monetary difficulty has met them at every step, , and the nut of how a pastor could be maintained in many of the out-of-the-way places in the United Kingdom has proved too hard for the "union "to crack. The consequence has been that whilst they were able to sustain their position fairly well in the towns, their influence in the villages is comparatively very small indeed, and but for my Wesleyan friends the clergy of the church by law established would have matters entirely their own way in rural England. The employment of men of means like Mr. Watson is another step taken in the right direction by the Wesleyan Conference, and the success which has attended that gentleman's efforts in Runcorn proves that it was a wise thing of the stationed ministers to vacate their pulpit and allow a stranger to test the power of an original style of appeal. There is no doubt that the brethren connected with what is known as "the regular ministry," are apt to fall into a routine style of carrying on their work, and they may obtain many a hint by carefully watching the methods adopted by a gentleman like Mr. Watson. It is more than probable that many people will feel a strong ob- jection to some of the proceedings of this evangelist, who rather astonished the congregations on Sunday by asking those who were opposed to theatres and balls to stand up. Such requests as these will probably prove offensive to people of refined taste, for when men like the Bishop of Manches- ter express themselves rather in favour than otherwise of theatres when wisely conducted, Mr. Watson may rest as- sured there are many in his congregations who cannot bring themselves to believe they are going straight to the place paved with good intentions, because they occasionally enter the doors of a building devoted to dramatic entertainment, so that they may witness the acting of some genius like Irving. Colleges are provided by the various religions denominations for the training of young men for the ministry, and they are kept up at a very heavy expense, but notwithstanding this there is grumbling on all hands at the inability of many ministers to interest an audience. They have a theme of transeendant interest; they have very often extensive libraries; and if they have not they have easy access to very large ones; and yet with this mass of material many of their discourses are worthy of a Dryasdust. I was amused to hear that immediately previous to Mr. Watson making the above appeal, several young ladies- of a good family who had been invited to a ball which takes place within a very short time, left the chapel. If they had been present when the request was made they must necessarily , have been placed in a rather uncomfortable position, and I their cheeks would probably have assumed a roseate hue. FLACCUS.

THE CASE AGAINST THE GROSVENOR HOTEL, WIDNES. —Mr. Sankey, the landlord of the Grosvenor Hotel, has decided not to appeal against the fine of £lO and costs imposed upon him a few weeks ago. .WIDNES ALDEUT-ROSD WESLEYAN BIND OF HOPE. —A tea meeting and entertainment were held on Tuesday evening, in conneetion with this society. Mr. J. Williamson presided at the meeting, and delivered an address, after which a miscellaneous programme was gone through, in which J. Harscott, Gertrude Davies, Walter Kirkham, John Fairhurst, J. Bates, Charles Bate, W. Davies, M. A. Holmes, Louisa Corkhill, L. Glover, T. Glover, A. Manning, and J. Johnson took part.

INQUEST AT WIDNES.—On Thursday afternoon an inquest was held at the Derby Arms Hotel, Simm's Cross, before Mr. C. E. Driffield, county coroner, touching the death of James Hardman. aged 59 years, of Lugsdale-lane, Widnes, which took place on Tuesday. The evidence showed that deceased was tolerably healthy, but occasionally had fits of an alarming character. On Tuesday night, whilst deceased was sitting with his son and another man in the kitchen, he rose suddenly and went out by the back door. Shortly after the son's attention was attracted by the sound of his father's returning footsteps, and on turning round, he found that the poor fellow had fallen upon the kitchen floor, and was speechless. A neighbour came in, and they lifted him on to the sofa, but he never spoke again. Dr. Brown was sent for, and he pronounced life extinct. A verdict of "Death from natural causes" was returned.

SACRED CONCERT AT WIDNES.-011 Tuesday evening, the ninth of the series of fortnightly entertainments which, dur- ing the present winter, have been given in connection with the Widnes Parish Church, in aid of the class-room funds, took place at the Waterloo-road schoolroom. In place of the customary miscellaneous entertainment, a programme of select sacred music was gone through. The chair was taken by the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar of Widnes. The pro- gramme comprised several pieces by a string band, in which Messrs. A. Thorp, E. Morlow, H. Rowe, W. Simkin, J. Rideyard, and F. Johnson were the instrumentalists; and performed the various selections with ability and taste. Mrs. H. Lea (Miss Davies), the favourite Widnes contralto, was heard at her best in "He was dispised," but she ap- parently most favourably impressed the audience in Tenny- son's duet "Too late, to late," which she sang in conjunc- tion with Mrs. J. W. Davies. Mrs. J. W. Davies gave "Remember now thy Creator," ,:with taste and effect, and this was followed by a solo and quartette, in which Messrs. Fairley and Broad, and Messrs. Walker and J. B. Imison sang in a manner which won them well deserved applaus& The glee class gave the anthems "0, how amiable are Thy dwellings," "I will lift up mine eyes," and "In Jewry is God known," all of which were sung with spirit and com- mendable correctness. Mr. Imison wielded the baton. The other pieces were the air "He shall feed His flock," by Mrs. Henry Lea and Mrs. J. W. Davies, and "Angels ever bright land fair," by the last lady. The National Anthem brought the proceedings to a close.

div.head: FALL OF A °TENNEY AT WARRINGTON. A MAN KIL.LED.
div.p: FALL OF A °TENNEY AT WARRINGTON. A MAN KIL.LED.

An accident of an extraordinary char,,'cter, and, unfortu- nately, attended with fatal results, occurred at Warrington on Monday last. It appears that Messrs. J. Collin and Son, builders, had received instructions from Messr..l. J. and J. Tinsley, tanners, Mersey-street, to repair their chin:ney. At nine o'clock Messrs. Collin sent several workmen to pi'epare the base of the chimney for the inspection of Mr. R. W. Collin, and shortly after twelve o'clock, while the workrneh were engaged excavating, the chimney fell without warn-' ing. The chimney adjoined the premises of Messrs. Roberts, Dale and Co., chemical manufacturers, and fell in a south- westerly direction into their works, where much damage was done. A decomposing room and crystalising room in the works of this firm were totally wrecked by the debris, which also demolished part of the boundary wall near the entrance off 'Wharfe-street. On the premises of Messrs. Tinsley a hide shed, about 90 feet long, was cempletely de- stroyed, and thousands of hides were buried beneath the bricks. The chimney was about NO feet high, and is be- lieved to have been one of the, if not the, tallest in Warring- ton. It was formerly considerably higher, but a few years ago it was found necessary to lower it. Shortly after the accident a labourer named Patrick Foy, in the employ of Messrs. Collin and Son, was reported to be missing, and search was at once made for him. The bricks near the base of the chimney were removed as quickly as possible, and about half-past two the body of the poor fellow was found, the head being shockingly crushed. The body was removed to the deceased's residence in Vernon's-yard, Fennell-street. A number of men were working near the chimney, and had it fallen in the opposite direction the probability is that many of them would have been killed.
"ASTRONOMY, OR THE TELESCOPE

div.head: AND ITS REVELATIONS."
div.p: AND ITS REVELATIONS."
LECTURE AT WARRINGTON.

By means of the Educational Fund of the Warrington Co-operative Society, an opportunity of hearing a lecture on "Astronomy, or the telescope and its revelations," was afforded to a large number of persons who assembled in the Co-operative Hall on Monday evening. The lecturer was the Rev. J. Freeston, of Staleyhridge. Mr. T. G. Rylands. F.R.S., &c., occupied the chair; and amongst those present were the Rev. R. Filcher, 8.A., Messrs. E. Bolton, Thomas Birchall, Joseph Knowles, W. Jeffreys, N. Greening, G. ' Wallington. G. Molyneux, J. Peers, ktc. The CHAIRMAN congratulated the Co-operative Society on the possession of the room in which they were assembled. (Applause.) He had never been in it before, and he did not hesitate to say that he was delighted with the appearance of the room. He must add that it was a possession, and all possessions necessarily begat responsibilities; and he could therefore go on and say they must allow him also to com- mend them—and it was commendation in which he was sure they would everyone join—for the use they were making of that room, He could not imagine a better use to make of such a room as that, than such use as was being made of it that night, and such use as he understood the society purposed making of it in the future. He said that not without strong feelings. Those of them who had read ' anything of history would have noticed that great empires had gradually risen, and reached what might be called their summit, and had then more or less rapidly decayed and dis- appeared. He believed it would be found in the history of lempires, they went on in certain conditions and got certain powers, until the period came when there was a struggle for life, which depended upon the capacity the people of that empire had to assimilate themselves to the conditions in which they found themselves. If they were unable to assi- milate themselves they were necessarily under a disadvan- tage, and with their disadvantage the empire suffered and disappeared. He did not hesitate to say that during the last 50 years influences had been at work in this country which were naturally most likely to produce such a crisis as he fled been speaking of, and it behoved them—it was most important to the health and life of this country that the people of the country should be put in a position to stand abreast of the requirements of the age in which they lived. (Applause.) In conclusion, he pointed out that we wanted to widen the basis of our thought ; and it was for such a purpose that he esteemed such lectures as that they were about to listen to, and it was on that ground he wished to congratulate and commend the society. (Applause.) The LECTURER, who was received with applause, said whenever he gave the first lecture on astronomy to an insti- tution, he always made it his objeet to give a simple, popu- lar lecture, to try and interest a considerable number and persuade them to commence this most interesting and sublime study; and then on a future occasion he took up some particular. part of the science and went more deeply into it. The telescope, as they all knew, was an instrument for enabling distant objects to be seen more distinctly, just as a microscope was an instrument to make very minute objects appear much larger. As in a very many other instances there was a little uncertainty as to the invention of the first telescope, and who should have the credit for the invention. The lecturer described the accidental discovery, by the son of an optician, that two lenses placed in a proper position had the power of making a distant object appear much nearer, and the important results this led to in the hands of Gallileo. The moon was 240,000 miles distant from the earth, a distance which was nothing compared with the sun which was 92,000,000 miles away, and this long dis- tance was comparatively insignificant when compared with the immense space which separated the earth from the stars. Gallileo made the first astronomical telescope and having explained the manner in which light was affected by the lenses and the object made to appear enlarged, Mr. Freeston ' said looked at through these early telescopes, objects were always encircled with a coloured border, and the difficulty of correctly observing the heavenly bodie,s in consequence, caused Sir Isaac Newton to invent the reflecting telescope. In this instrument the lens was replaced by a speculum or mirror placed at the bottom of a tube. A representation of the enormous reflecting telescope of the late Lord Bosse, Parponstown, Ireland, in which the speculum measured six or seven feet aerogs, was shown, and the lecturer asked what was the first revelation of the telescope, giving an interesting account of Gallileo's discovery of the volcanic mountains on the moon, which unlike the mountains on the earth, were isolated and not in ranges. The moon was the nearest to the earth of any heavenly body, and, it had been decided, had no life upon it; or at least if it had, it could not be life like ours, because so far as astronomers could tell, there was no atmosphere, no moisture, no rain, no snow, and no clouds. By a very curious coincidence the moon happened to spin on its own axis just in the same time that it went round the earth, and the result was that we had seen only one side of the moon. If there were people on the moon they would be on the other side, and to them, if they were able to see it, the earth would appear a great glorious body, giving out much more light than the moon did. Gallileo next turned his attention to the sun, which he had much diffi- culty in viewing, in consequence of its brightness, and in his attempts he blinded one of his eyes. But he persevered, and at last, by smoking the eyepiece of his telescope, he succeeded, and there were revealed to his astonished gaze the spots on the sun. These spots had been objects of great interest since that time, and many theories had been pro- pounded respecting them. Through them, Gallileo discov- ered that the sun revolved on its own axis, in the same manner as the earth, every 25 or 26 days. Astronomers had thought they had detected some relation between the spots on the sun and the kind of weather we had, and one went the whole length, a few years ago, of tracing bad trade to the spots on the sun. (Laughter). So distant was the sun from the earth that a train travelling at the rate they did from Liverpool to Manchester, would be 250 year in making the journey. Mr. Freeston advised the audience to use their own eyes, and some bright evening in about a fortnight, if they would look towards the west just when the sun had set, they would see a bright planet—that was Venus, just now becoming the evening star. To the left of that were Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and tbe constellation of Taurus. He urged them to obtain a knowledge of the planets, and de- termine to watch them,and he could assure them they would be sources of interest to them as long as they lived. Having related the discovery of Jupiter and its moons by Gallileo, Mr. Freeston said the moons were of great practical value, as by them longtitude was calculated, and it was by means of the eclipses of these moons that the speed at which light travels was calculated. He referred to the conflicting theories of Copernicus and Gallileo with regard to the phases of Venus, and related several incidents in the life of William Herschel, and his discovery of Uranus. He stated the dis- covery of Neptune in 1846 to be the grandest ever made, the honour of which was equally divided between an English- man named Adams, and a Frenchman named De Avery. Speaking of comets, he said it was a very singular thing that though a comet never had done any injury, the mention of the appearanceof one made a great many people frightened. A short time ago the Bishop of Manchester endeavoured to frighten people into goodness—(laughter and applause;-- by telling them that Mr. Proctor, the great astronomer, had been writing a book specially about comets, and had ex- pressed the opinion that a comet would appear and fall into the sun in 15 years, and that if it did, it would add so much to the heat of the sue that the earth would be scorched up. He (Mr. Freeston) did not know how he got that information. He bad seen a letter from Mr. Proctor, who said that he could quite as readily believe that the earth would go on rolling for fifteen millions of years, as that it would be destroyed in fifteen. (Hear, hear.) Don't be frightened at comets, because, as Sir John Herschel said, most of them, if they had any solid matter about them, could not weigh above a few pounds, and were one to fall in the sun could not do much mischief. Were a fly to dash against an express train it would not be much felt—(laughter)—and it would be much the same with a comet. Stars were suns, and shone by their own light, and were an immense distance from the earth. It had been calculated that light, which travelled at the rate of 186,000 miles per second, would be three and a half years in traversing the distance between the nearest star and the earth. Logic, analogy, and every- thing, pointed out that the stars were centres of systems, that they had planets revolving round them, as the earth revolved round the sun. Soma 3,000 stars could be seen with the naked eye, but when looked at through a telescope, the number was increased to millions and millions. They could see a firmament with the naked eye, but with the aid of a telescope they could see other firmaments. He advised them to study the stars,/ and they would agree with hien that astronomy was the grandest and most sublime of sciences, and concluded 'Thy heavens on which 'tis bliss to look Shall be my pure and shining book, Where I may write in words of flame • The glories of Thy wondrous name."

Mr. T. BIRCHALL proposed a vote of thanks to Mr Freeston for the elequent address they had received. He thought they would uaite with him most cordially in giving a hearty vote of thanks to that gentleman for the admirable lecture he had deliverea that evening. (Applause.) The Rev. R. PILCITER said it gave him great pleasure to second the vote of thanks. • By attending the lecture be knew hi s ould get a great deal of instruction as well as a great Cul ,f amusement, and he thi,ught they would bear him out that that had been the case. (Hear, hear.) lhe CHAIRMAN supported the resolution most earnestly- ! and willingly; and he hoped they would carry from that ' meeting as profitable and affectionate remembrance of Mr. Freeston as be carried of some scientific connections be had with Mr. Freeston's brother many years ago, to whom he was indebted for information which he should never forget. The proposition was heartily carried, and a similar com- pliment having been paid the Chairman, the meeting ter- minated.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
A cab-hiring establishment at Aberdeen was destroyed by fire yesterday morning, and an old man, the proprietor's father, was burned to death.

Yesterday a telegram from Constantinople says that Nazif Effendi, Director of the Public Debt Department, has been appointed Imperial Commissioner to the Bondholders' Council. The election of an Ottoman delegate to the coun- cil is expected shortly. The Irish Times of yesterday says :—The Home Rule League, established in 1870, is about to be diEEC-ed. A meeting has been convened for to-day in Dublin for the purpose of considering a resolution suspending all further proceedings of the bogy and closing the offices. At Hanley, yesterday morning, William Hawkin's fore- man marl worker, was ordered to enter into a surety of £25 himself and to find two sureties in the same amount, for riotous conduct at a Salvation Army meeting at Hanley. The bench spoke very strongly on the matter. About £3,000 damage has been caused by a fire at Britan- nia Mills, Middleton. Beginning in the third storey the fire had obtained a good hold on that and the room above before the fire engines were got to work. The workpeople were safely got out of the mill. It took two hours to extinguish the flames. The damage is covered by insurance.

div.head: PERILOUS ADVENTURE.
div.p: A PERILOUS ADVENTURE.

At Cheadle, North Staffordshire, yesterday, the magis- trates, ors behalf of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to animals, presented the certificate of the society and a sum of money to a collier named Herbert Weston, who had saved a dog's life under singular circumstances. The animal had been heard howling at the bottom of an unused pit shaft 160 yards deep for three days, and on the third day Weston allowed himself to be lowered at the end of a rope, and, after a perilous adventure, brought up the animal alive.

div.head: REMARKABLE SUICIDE.
div.p: REMARKABLE SUICIDE.

Yesterday night the body of a man, supposed b be Robert Cawley, Tranmere, Birkenhead, was found suspended from the bough of a tree in Duddon Fox Cover, on Delamere Forrest, Cheshire. The deceased entered the Headless Woman public-house last Friday, at Duddon, and repre- sented himself as impecuniaus. He was treated to refresh- ment, and he then appears to have wandered into the wood, where he slung one end of a rope over the bough of a tree, put two coils of it round his neck, and, holding the other end, threw himself down, and so hanged himself.

div.head: AN EXTRAORDLNARY MURDER.
div.p: AN EXTRAORDLNARY MURDER.

An extraordinary crime has been committed by an old man 75 years of age, at Bec Mulluin, in the Seine Inferieure, France. One Cordier had living with him, as •' dame de compagnie," an aged female of 82. A few days ago, he found out that she had made her will, bequeathing all she possessed to one of her neighbours. Furious at being set aside, Cordier resolved on a terrible revenge. He murdered the old woman in a most brutal manner, and, dragging her corpse to a remote corner of his house, deliberately set ire to the place. Notwithstanding this precaution, his crime was discovered, and he has been arrested.

div.head: FRENCH TREATY NEGOTIATIONS.
div.p: THE FRENCH TREATY NEGOTIATIONS.

The report that Lord Lyons has had an interview with M. Tirard and M. de Freycinet with the view of re-opening negotiations for a commercial treaty with England is incor, rect. The establishment of commercial relations with Canada was the topic discussed at the interview which Lord Lyons had with the two Ministers. The Paris press is becoming more vehement in its tone against the Government in refe- rence to the negotiations with England. It is felt that communications must shortly Ite re-opened, but if a good treaty is to be obtained the first move must come from France.

div.head: 11.IEETING OF THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY YESTERDAY.
div.p: 11.IEETING OF THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY YESTERDAY.

A meeting of the members of the Conservative Party was held at the Carlton Club at noon, yesterday, to confer as to the attitude of the party as to several questions now before Parliament. Sir S. Northcote and Lord Salisbury arrived together, and by 12.20 quite 200 members of the party had assembled. The proceedings were marked by a unanimity of views as to the future policy of the party. Sir S. North- cote, who opened the preceedings, and delivered a speech of a temperate character, said that in view of the existing situation of affairs there was every necessity for the exer- cise of the utmost caution so as not to give the Government the opportunity of charging them with obstruction of any kind when the new rules of procedure came on for discus- sion. With respect to Ireland he condemned the course of , the administration in that country, claiming it had entirely failed in its attempts either to pacify or ameliorate the con- dition of the people. Referring to the question of the cloture he spoke strongly against the introduction of that measure into Parliament, maintaining that there were other ways and means by which the Government, had it earnestly desired to do so, could have hastened the transaction of public business and other matters engaging the attention of the House. He thought that with respect to the cloture the best course to adopt would be to support in the first instance the amendment of Mr. Marriott, the Liberal member for Brighton, and press the question to a division, giving Mr. Marriott the support of the entire Conservative vote. If his views met their acceptance they might be able to divide on Mr. Marriott's amendment by next Thursday week. They could afterwards also oppose the proposed changes in the rules of the House by supporting Sir Drummond Codliffe's amendment and the various other proposed amendments, of ' which notice had been given by various members of the party. Lord Salisbury, who followed, concurred fully in all that hal been said by Sir S. Northcote. He was followed by by the Right Hon. Beresford Hope, Sir Walter Bartelot, the Hon. Cecil Raikes, Mr. Sclater Booth, Sir Jno. Hay, Mr. Thos. Collins, and Lord Folkestone. Expression was given to the opinion that whilst it was unwise to obstruct the Administration, at the same time the party should insist upon a full divisior. of the chief questions at issue. It was likewise urged that it was undesirable for mettbers of the party either to go out of the way to praise Mr. Forster or the Irish Government or to fall into the other extreme of sympathising with the suspects or their friends. Sir Walter Bartelot characterised the cloture as un-English and un- necessary. Mr. Raikes spoke on the new rules of procedure. No formal resolution was proposed or adopted, but it was agreed to support the line of policy laid down by Sir S. Northcote.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

Lord REDESDALE gave notice that the second reading of the Parliamentary Declaration Bill would be moved on the 23rd inst. Lord BnanourarE moved an address to the Crown to refuse assent to the Charity Commissioners' scheme for the management of Bodingfield Charity in Kent.—Lord CLIN- TON supported the scheme.—Earl SPENCER justified the action of the Commissioners.—The Marquis of SALISBURY saw nothing objectionbble to the scheme.—The:motion was withdrawn, and the House adjourned.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

THE MEETING OF DEMOCRLTS.—Sir W. HARCOURT, replying to Mr. Bellingham, said he had no information at all relative to the meeting of Social Democrats and Nihilists in Soho, where murder was glorified and assassination en- couraged. THE SUSPECTS--Mr. FonsrEn said he had given in- structions that an investigation be made into the charges made by Mr. Sexton as to the treatment of suspects in prisons. THE PROCEDURE RULES.—The SPEAKER, replying to Sir Stafford Northcote, said that in the event of the amendment moved to the first rule relating to the business of the House by the member for Brighton being negatived, it would be open to other on. members to move an amendment to the rule.

THE No= BORNEO CO.—On the motion for going into committee of supply, Mr. GORST called attention to the charter recently granted by Her Majesty to the British North Borneo Co., and expressed disapproval of soveign rights being given to the company, which was n)t commercial, but political. He thought the Government censurable for re- commending the grant of the charter. He concluded by moving an address to the Crown praying Her Majesty to revoke or alter so much of the charter as gave an implied sanction to the maintenance of slavery under the protection of the British flag.

PRINCOT LOCAL BOARD AND GUARDIAN ELECTIONS . Great interest is being taken in the coming election of mem- bers for Prescot Local Board and Board of Guardians. The committee of the Prescot Ratepayers' Association met on Wednesday night, and after some discussion the secretary was instructed to submit certain test questions to the candi- dates bearing upon economy and other business connected with the respective Boarqs, in order that they might decide as to whiCh candidate the association should support.
