div.p: Utero to the tlitor.

" CHATTER " IN THE TOWN COUNCIL. Sir,—Can nothing be done to relieve poor mortals who are members of the Town Council from the almost unbearakle and unceasing " chatter " of the" Seraphic" Doctor? Many of us who know him of old were moderately well prepared to expect an unceasing flood of oratory i from the individual in question, but we certainly did not think t would be one- half as bad as it. Why, Mr. Editor, last Tuesday night it was nearlv as bad as being in the House of Commons. One of my fellow members who, sitting next to me, was keeping count—l had in my suffering lost count altogether—told me that Councillor Mackie had spoken during the evening either seven or eight times. Why should we be punished like this? Are we greater sinners than the rest of the Galileans? And then, you know, it wouldn't be half so bad as it is if Mr. 141ackie's voice wasn't so unpleasant to listen to. Ido hope our worthy Mayor will apply the "cloture," or some- thing even more stringent still, in cases of "emergency " like this. If something isn't done before long some of as must resign our seats, or our days will be numbered, for the present state of things is more than mortal man can bear.— Yours, A TOWN COUNCILLOR.

THE PAYMENT OF THE MAYOR'S AUDITOR. Sir,—Notwithstanding the opinion recently quoted by the Deputy Town Clerk, I still believe that the Mayor's auditor has no right to receive any payment for his services in this capacity. The lawyer to whom this matter has been referred admits that " the question is by no means free from diffi- culty," and therefore in the interests of good government, and also because it is most essential that there should be no suspicion even of wrong doing on the party of any members of our municipality, it is very desirable that steps should be at once taken either by the Corporation themselves or some other body—say the Ratepayers' Association—to have the true position of things ascertained onc?for all. Previous to the passing of the Municipal Corporations Act, 1835, a state of things obtained in municipal government which was in large numbers of instances a scandal and disgrace to all con- cerned. Jobbery of all kinds was openly connived at. Members of the then local governing bodies secured to them- selves remunerative contracts, or in other ways plundered the public purse for the sake of their own aggrandisement and that of those with whom they were in collusion. This disgraceful and ruinous state of things led to the enactment of the measure previously referred to, and in order that for the future such abominations might be rendered impossible, several clauses were inserted which were then, and have al- ways been since, recognised and adopted as essential and vital in regard to local government. One of these clauses states most distinctly that "no person shall be qualified to be elected or to be a councillor during such time as he shall hold any office or place of profit other than that of mayor, or during such time as he shall have directly or indirectly any share or interest in any contract or employment with, by, or on behalf of such Council." Another clause provides for the imposition of a fine of £5O for every case where a member of the Council acts in contravention of the first- named clause. It is quite true that a subsequent Act—the Public Health Act, 1875,—by which a Town Council is con- stituted an Urban Sanitary Authority—states that the ac- counts appertaining to its functions in the capacity named shall be audited by "the auditors of the borough ;" and fur- ther, that "each of such auditors shall in respect of each audit be paid such reasonable remuneration, not being less than two guineas a day." The question therefore arises, does this clause in a subsequent and minor Act set aside clauses which were inserted in the original Act for the pur- pose of protecting the interests of the public, and of elevat- ing the character and tone of municipal government beyond the possibility of jobbery or collusion of any kind? I sub- mit, sir, that it is absnrd to suppose for one moment that what has all along been considered a general principle, and binding upon all subsequent municipal legislation, should be considered nullified because of the vague composition of a clause in the Public Health Act. I therefore venture to hope that the Town Council will take such steps as are necessary to put this vexed question for ever at rest, and, pending their action, I am, MAX.
THE CULTIVATION OF SACRED MUSIC OF A HIGH

CLASS. Sir,—l was much interested in perusiug• perhaps the only remaining copy of a small pamphlet, the title of which is— 'A selection of sacred music, to be performed at St. Helen's Church, on Easter Tuesday, April 13th, 1819. Printed by J. and J. Haddock, Warrington." When I came to St. Helens the dearth of musical taste and power was such as to make the performance of such a programme as is subjoined impossible. Not so now. St. Helens can hold its own in musical taste and skill with most places similarly circum- stanced. It is therefore highly desirable that the highest style of music, which is sacred music should have its proper place. With that view, as well as with the view of connect- ing the present with the past of St. Helens, it has been decided to repert "the selection" in the same church and lin the same month jfl which it was "performed Chlirch,"ju3t 63 years ago, and it is hoped that The repetition of this oratorio may lead to the establishment of a Sacred Music Choral Society in St. Helens. Programme: let part. • From "The Messiah ;" recitatives, choruses, Pas- toral Symphony, and Hallelujah Chorus. 2nd part. Over- ture, by Handel; hymn, "Great God, what do I see and hear ?" anthem, "Hear my prayer ;" recitative, Haydn; hymn, "The splendour bright is rising now ." chorus, "The Heavens are telling air, by Handel, "Return, 0 God of Hosts ;" hymn for three voices; recitative; trio, from "The Creation," "On Thee all living souls depend." There are some, though few, remaining who will be glad to welcome a reminiscence carrying them back to the days of the Rev. Thomas Pigot (venerabile nomen); and many others, it is hoped, who will value the oratorio for its own merits, and for the future benefit which may accrue from it. It is pro- posed that the oratorio shall be given on the 27th of April. —Yours truly, EDWARD CARR. rielens Vicarage, March Bth, 1882.

div.head: WARRINGTON 'TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: WARRINGTON 'TOWN COUNCIL

SPECIAL MEETING. His worship the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) presided at the adjeurned special meeting of the Council, held on Tues- day evening, for the purpose of considering the expediency of , opposing the electric lighting bills now in Parliament, and if thought necessary, to pass a resolution or resolutions authorising the Council to oppose such bills, and to charge the costs Sze., upon the borough fund or other fund or rate applicable thereto. The other members present were Alder- men Davies, Webster, Kean, Holmes, Chandley, Harrison, Thewlis, and Burgess; and Councillors Monks, Broadbent, Collin, Jeans, Mackie. Caldwell, Pierpoint, Barker, Dixon, Woolfall, Taylor, Brown, Fairclough, Francomb, Milner, Platt, Greening, Bdro•'ess, Litton, Sutton, Ridgway, Whittle; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. S. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), J. H. Gornall (medical officer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), J. Pater- son (gas manager). A number of ratepayers were also pre- sent.

THE COUNCIL AND THE ELECTRIC LIGHTING COMPANIES. The MAYOR moved the following resolution :—"That the Council do oppose in Parliament. in the present session thereof, the following bills :—A bill to facilitate the carry- ing into effect the objects of the Anglo-American Brush Electric Light Corporation (Limited) ; a bill to facilitate the carrying into effect the objects of the British Electric Light Company (Limited); a bill for conferring certain powers on !ocal authorities and companies in England who may be entitled to use Edison's system of electric lighting, beating, or motive power, and for other purposes; a bill to facilitate the carrying into effect the objects of the Electric Light and Power Generator Company (Limited) ; a bill to facilitate the carrying into effect the objects of the Siemens Brothers and Co. (Limited); and that the costs, charges, and expenses incurred and to be incurred in opposing the said bills be charged upon the borough fund, borough rate, or other fund or rate, or ac- count of said Council applicable thereto." The Mayor said the object of the Corporation was not to oppose electric lighting in any sense, but to oppose these bills, for if one were carried they would have a monopoly, and could go into a town and do just as they liked with the streets and other property. It was consequently thought inadvisable to allow any single company to have a monopoly of the electric light in this borough. They were opposing all the bills, but it must not be supposed that they were op- posing electric lighting. What that might be in the future no one could tell. As far as he had seen of the light, it did not answer the purposes which it was expected to do. He was not aware that there would be any more expense con- nected with the opposition to the bills further than had already been incurred. If there were any more expense to be incurred the Council would be informed of what was in- tended to be done. The DEPUTY-MAYOR seconded the resolution. Alderman HARRISON said he thought the opposition in- tended to be taken to the bills ought to be more clearly defined. The Council, according to thi3 resolution, seemed to be opposing the bills "hip and thigh "as it were, whereas from what His Worship had been pleased to say, their op- position would only be limited. Did not the Mayor think it !could be as well that that should be stated to the Council hi order that they might better understand what they were doing? If they pasbed that resolution they should be op- posing altogether the introduction of the electric light in the town.

The MAYOR: By these companies. Alderman HARRISOX: Exactly. The MAYOR said the intention of the resolution was simply that the Corporation could get the best company introduced into the town, and it was impossible to say what there might be in the future. Alderman HARRISON : But we are opposing the whole of them. The MAYort: On principle. Alderman IVE.BrEt-t said it was one of the formalities the Council was obliged to take to put themselves in a right position. Councillor PIERPOINT wished to know what amount of costs had been already incurred, for as the Mayor had said the Council would have very little more to pay, be inferred they had already paid something. He thought it would be information fo themselves as well as the ratepayers

generally. The MAYOR said the Town Clerk informed him £5O had been expended. Councillor PIERPOINT : Would not exceed £5O? The MAYOR : It is impossible to say the amount. Councillor PIERPOINT.: It is very small sum. It Is not often we get such cheap law. Alderman HARRISON: It is tecoming cheaper now. Councillor JEANS observed that he thought the Mayor VIM under a misapprehension as to the companies being able

to do as they pleased with the streets. He had read through 1 the bills, and there were clauses in them that they should not have power to enter into any town and pull up the streets without the consent of the local authority, and therefore there was no ground for opposition on that head. With regard to the costs of the opposition not exceeding £5O, that seemed a very small amount for opposing five bills. The TOWN.CLERK : Pardon me. Mr. Pierpoint said up to the present time. Councillor PIERPOINT : And I understood you, Mr. Mayor, to say that would be all. The MAYOR: No, no. There will be more expense if they allowed it to go on; but the Corporation would be informed what that expense would probably be. Mr. JEANS: Of course you cannot oppose bills in Parlia- ment without cost, and I do not think we can oppose five bills for £5O; it will be nearer £5OO. Councillor PIERPOINT: Or another cypher. Councillor JEANS: Yes; or another cypher. Councillor MONKS explained that the Council, by their resolution, wished to put itself in a position to be able to adopt the electric light on its own account. (Hear, hear.) They objected to any monopoly growing upon the town which would have to be purchased some day at an enormous price. He thought it was better that they should spend even -£5OO now than spend £5,000 or £6,000 some 10 years hence. No one who had seen the development of the electric light within the last 18 months, could hesitate for one moment that it was the light of the future. Alderman HARRISON: Oh dear! That is new to me. Councillor Mono (continuing) said he thought the Government would take this matter up, and it .was not unlikely that towns might have power granted to them to adopt the electric light themselves. And as far as the companies not being able to take up streets without the consent of the Corporation, they all knew what that meant. ' They might be unable to pull up the streets without the consent of the Corporation, but do what they would they could not .get the companies to put the streets back in the same state as they found them. (Hear, hear). It was quite clear that they should have all matters relating to the electric light in their own hands, and deal with it in the most satis- factory way. Councillor MACKIE said he had not the slightest objection to the Council putting themselves in a proper position to meet any applications which might,be made for the admission of the electric light into Warrington, if they had the as- surance of the Mayor that the expenditure should not ex- ceed £5O. It was a remarkably small sum, and it had put to flight the amazing amount of gossip which has been going on during the week about a "barrel load" of their chief men havinc, gone to London, and going through all kinds of wonderful experiments and enterprises. (Alderman Harrison : And gymnastics.) No, I did not use any offen- sive word. But suppose they had the assurance, they could not suppose that the Committee which was moving in this matter, or any other Committee, would for one moment tie its hands when it thought it could do a good stroke of business in the interest of the town—(hear, hear),—and if they passed that resolution authorising the costs to be charged on the borough fund, they certainly put it in the power of the Committee to work wonders which might sur- prise them. Alderman HOLMES observed that the Committee could not take any further action without the consent of the Council. The MAYOR said the Committee would propose certain action and it was for the Council to say whether they were agreeable to pass it. Councillor MacKIE remarked that Committees were by no means so willing to submit their doings to the Town Council and in fact they took some very high steps—(a voice: They do.)—without the sanction of the Council. It was not very long since that he called attention to the Rivers Conservancy Committee which had the cool assurance to assume the name of the Mayor, the Town Clerk and the borough seal, and to send a petition to Mr. Gladstone, assuring him that the burgesses of Warrington were in favour of a bill which was introduced in connection with rivers. If there was any attempt to keep out the electric light companies because the Council held the gasworks, he would say, as he said -last week, rather perish the gasworks and the large sum of money they had cost them. He be- lieved in gas, he believed it would be a growing necessity, and the returns of the London Gasworks showed that the demand for gas was growinc, in a rapid manner. After some further remarks, Mr. Mackie suggested that a petition be sent to Parliament asking it in its wisdom to see that such general laws were laid down for the governing of all electric lighting companies as would not interfere with the spread of science. Alderman HOLMES said no further expense whatever could be incurred in opposing the electric lighting companies with- out the Parliamentary Committee or General Purposes Com- mittee, from whom he supposed these proceedings emanated, first obtaining the sanction of the Council to any step they might desire to take; and therefore he thought Mr. Mackiefs apprehensions rather without foundation. He thought he need not be af, all afraid on that score, and the course adopted of xecommending Parliament to oppose those bills was to enable the Council, if necessary, to take any further steps. Other Corporations were proceeding on the same lines. Alderman HARRISON: But if we pass this resolution to oppose the introduction of these companies, what further powers does the General Purposes Committee require, or what further authority does the Town Clerk require? (Hear, hear.) Alderman HOLMES believed he stated correctly that they could take no further proceedings in this matter without obtaining the sanction of the Council. , The Towli CLERIC said none of the committee's proceed- ings were taken without being subject to the confirmation of the Council. Alderman HARRISON remarked that he was quite satisfiei the committee would be at liberty, without coming before the Council again, to take such steps as they felt desirable, Alderman WEBSTER thought it was quite right that the Companies should be opposed. The Corporation considered the powers sought by the companies ought to be invested in themselves.

Councillor PirnPotryr : So do I. Alderman WEBSTER (Continuing) said in the Corpora- tion's original Improvement Bill there were clauses inserted for the introduction of the electric light into Warrington. These were objected to by Lord Redesdale, and they were obliged to strike them out, because it was stated that Govern- ment would introduce a bill conferring those powers on all Corporations. At the time a Select Committee was sitting, and they reported that an Act should be passed for the benefit of Corporations generally. As time went on the Corporation got their Gas Bill, and the electric light kept progressing, and the companies com- menced t% promote their bills and take powers. The Cor- poration inquired from the Local Government Board when the bill they had promised would be introduced to Parlia- ment. They wrote in reply saying they had no intention of introducing a bill. The Corporation were then thrown on their beam ends, and thought, and did still, that if the light had to be introduced into the borough that they were the proper body to do it. Other corporations took the same view as themselves, and they had joined together in this opposition. The resolution was simply one of those formali- ties which ought to be abolished, but which they were obliged to conform to in presenting a petition against a bill, although it did not express their real feelings in the matter. Alderman DAVIES repeated the account given by Alderman Webster, and said the petitions against the bills had already been lodged. What bad been the result? The result had been of great good to Warrington and other corporations in- terested, for they were now told that it was the intention of the Government to introduce a bill, although in December last they stated they were not going to do so. The Corpora- tion would now be enabled to retain the power of adopting any electric light that should prove to be the ' best, and they might be well satisfied that in a case like this, the best companies now might only be small affairs in a few years hence. That was the reason why they had lodged the petitiens, and he should , be quite willing for the committee to go before the Council again if any action or further opposition was intended, but they must confirm what the Parliamentary Committee had done so far. Councillor BURGESS thought it desirable that the lighting of the town should be in the hands of the Corporation, and he thought no bill which would give a monopoly to these companies should be passed. If the resolution simply pro- posed that petitions should be presented to Parliament against the bills he should support it; but the resolution authorised the Council to charge the costs incurred in oppos- ing the bills upon the borough fund. Alderman DAVIES : Take my assurance that no heavy expenditure is intended in opposing the bills. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HARRISON thought it ought to be stated in., black and white what was intended to be done. Councillor PIERPOINT considered they ought to know what weight of coats was likely to be put on the shoulders of the ratepayers. They, as representatives of the ratepay- ers, had one object and one duty to perform towards them, and considering that they were now paving the enormous um of 7s in the £ for rates, he thought *the Council should be very: cautious indeed before they ran into any question that might probably entail upon them considerable more ex-' pense than any member of the Council at the present time could imagine. If the Council could be satisfied that the cost would be so trifling as they had been informed that night, he thought there would be no further opposition to the resolution, but he was of opinion that unless they could have a more definite figure fixed, an amendment should be moved, and he should have no objection to secending it, that the forwarding of a petitien against the five bills be all that the Corporation be empowered to do at the present time. They might depend upon it that the end of these costs were never known until the bill came in, and he, for one, should strongly oppose the resolution. Councillor SUTTON said he considered the words of the resolution as merely formal, and although it might not cost much to oppose these bills, that they were absolutely neces- sary. (Hear, hear.) •If the cost would only be £5 or any trifling sum, that form of words would be quite as necessary as if the cost were going to be £5,000, and he looked upon it that the question of the lighting of the town was of far greater importance to them than the question of £5OO or £l,OOO. If it were true that these companies would have the power to supply the town with light and overthiow any rights the Carpoaation enjoyed, and for which they had paid so much, he should support the resolution. The. T9-sys CLERIC was called upon to explain the matter. He said in doing so he did not propose to enter on any argumentative ground, but simply to state the facts con- nected with those hills, and the petitions that had been presented against them. Mr. Burgess had made some remarks taking exception to the form of the resolution, but pt it, teone l meeting required et wiqnuegri re et d b only ne there t ahAarict question e sOtf i night.o Pm or fl As Parliament, einnrt d., iwnzh Suttoni sc 1-51 hadnt he ac et aptlysfsoirtmat epdwuas it would have to be adopted as if an expenditure of £5,000

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY MARCH 18, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY MARCH 18, 1882.

was contemplated. With reference to the remarks of Mr. Pierpoint and Mr. Jeans, it must not be looked upon that the Council were opposing five single bills in the ordinary way, and therefore multiplying the costs five times, for they would be doing nothing of the kind. The town clerks and mayors of the different towns communicated with each other, and drew attention to the footing which the electric lighting companies were trying to gain in the towns. A united course of action was decided upon, and it was after- wards found that to put themselves in a right position it was necessary to file separate petitions against the bills. The meeting that night was to enable the expenses of lodg- ing those petitions' and any further expenditure, to be paid out of the rates. It *as out of the question to present five separate petitions before five separate bills, because the ex- penses would be something enormous, but as far as the matter had gone, it was intended immediately after the Easter recess to remit those bills to a committee of the House, and also all important bills containing electric light clauses. The fear of the time that might be wasted and the danger of the Bills not being passed, was causing a number of boroughs who had important Bills, to strike out their electric light clauses, sune as was done in 1879 by the Warrington Corporation. He was told by his agents that it was the intention of the Government after having the matter thoroughly sifted, to bring in a Bill enabling local authorities to contract them- selves, Assuming that the Corporation appeared separately and individually before the Parliamentary Committee, in order to bring evidence, the cost would not be anything like what was shadowed forth by Mr. Pierpoint. But he did not think it would be found necessary to do anything of the kind. He thought they had affected what they wanted by sending their petition. He did not think it would be necessary for them to spend any more money whatever. (Hear, hear.) Once grant consent to a company to intro- duce their system into a town, there was no power to with- draw that consent. They had obtained their monopoly. All these people were competing with each other. Some one started the matter, and all the others saw that, if the Act of Parliament was obtained, the first to get it would obtain the sanction of the different local authorities of thus obtaining the monopoly. What was contended by the committee was that they should not throw anything in the way of the in- troduction of the electric light, but that the town should have the power in their own hands. (Hear, hear.) They wished to take advantage of being their own masters and to contract with those with whom they could do best, If the different representatives appealed to that Corporation to contribute towards a general defence fund in bringing evi- dence before the committee, the contribution of a borough of the size of Warrington would not be much in comparison with Birmingham and other large places. No step would be taken by himself nor by the committee, before bringing the matter before the Council again. (Hear, hear.) Alderman KEAN suppqooted the resolution, and Councillor Mac= said he should certainly not vote against the resolution after the candid statement of the Town Clerk.

The 111.tvoR remarked that it had always been his opinion that what had been done was right under the circumstances. They had a monopoly in the gas works and if the electric light was to be introduced, let them introduce it them- selves.
The resolution was then put and carried without dissent. THE - THE ADJOURNED MONTHLY MEETING.
The adjourned monthly meeting was then held, His Wor- ship the Mayor again presiding.
THE ELECTION OF AUDITORS.

The TOWN CLERK read the report of the Deputy Mayor, stating that Mr. J. L. Tunstall and Mr. John Harrison had been elected auditors for the borough ; and be added that His Worship had appointed Councillor John Woolf all Mayor's auditor.
forward he made no secret of his intention to refuse to con-

eider any further development until they knew exactly the cost of the plant they had adopted. It, therefore, rested with Messrs. Manlove and Co. to send in their account; and he thought before they committed themselves to further expenditure of thousands of pounds they should know exactly how they stood in reference to the old account. (Hear, hear.) Since the machinery was started the manage- ment had been entirely in the hands of the contractor, and he did not hesitate to say, from the experience they had had during the past fortnight or three weeks, that they had lost very considerably by such management. Another thing he stated was that those who could make such a blunder as had been made were not exactly the guides he cared to follow, and that in judging of this matter he should be guided to a very large extent by the experience the committee had gained at Longford. Those were the reasons which led him to take the course he had adopted in this matter. There was no personal feeling in it. He did it because he felt it to be his duty, and he had always given a reason for any opposition he had offered on the committee. Whether his reasons and the reasons of his colleagues had received due consideration from the chairman of the committee was not a matter on which he cared to enter. He did not wish to raise any question that might be at all unseemly, but he held to the principle that a committee acted for the Coun- cil, and it was the duty of every member of that committee to express his own conviction, and to hold to his conviction. (Hear, hear.) It was not for the chairman, who was elected by the favour of that committee, to prevent discussion. (Hear, heao It was for him, with an impartial mind, to listen to what every member of that committee had to say, and in the event of a balance of opinion to guide the com- mittee. (Hear, hear.) He said nothing beyond that, but so far as he was concerned it was a matter of public duty for him to withstand Alderman Burgess in the Council when he took a position of tyranny in the matter. He would not submit to it. As long as the Council placed him on that committee, he was there to act in the interests of the borough and the Council—(hear, hear)—and he said it was the right of every member to be listened to with the same consideration as the chairman himself. (Hear, hear.) The whole matter spoke for itself. He did not know that the committee as it then stood had any recommendation to make beyond that. The Council would find that they referred to a machine which was likely to accomplish con- siderable results. A deputation went to look at it the pre- vious Tuesday, and it was almost completed. The engineer said he fully expected the machine to be at work at the end of this month, and they,would then be able to say whether the results obtained from it were anything like what he anticipated. If it turned out to be the best machine, who- ever had charge of this matter would, he presumed, come to the Council and make a statement for their consideration, and it would be for the Council to confirm, or otherwise, whatever proposition they might make. He moved the con- firmation of the minutes. Council] or BARBER seconded.

Councillor MACKIE asked that some representative of the minority of the committee would address them as early as possible that they might know the other side of the matter. Personally be knew very little about it, but so far his sym- pathies, if not his judgment,: went entirely with the minor- ity, and it did so in a very marked manner after the very strong language to which they had listened, in which the decision or conduct of one of the oldest, most useful, and most laborious members of the Council, or any other public body in Warrington, was spoken of as that of a tyrant. He thought that remark could not have reached the ears of the Mayor, and he strongly recommended that such phrases be entirely left out of that Council Chamber for use in other places. He had no doubt the decision of the minority was a decision based upon long experience. They were per- fectly willing, as he understood, to hand over the further development of the scheme to men who were prepared at any rate to pay the piper. That in itself was a great thing. They were pre- pared to carry out the scheme, which, according to the last report of the medical officer of health, certainly required to be carried out immediately. The death-rate of Warrington had risen to the enormous height of 28 per thousand. They could not expect Alderman Burgess to take the lead of a committee when he had been outvoted. He congratulated Alderman Burgess on the spirit he had shown, and said if he could not, with a good heart and clear conscience, carry on the duties of the committee, he was perfectly right in resign- ing. So were other members. He concluded by stating that so far as two members of the minority were concerned, he did not believe they had abler men in the Council to deal with such an unpleasant subject as that of sanitary legisla- tion.

Alderman DAVIES took it that if they listened to the dis- cussion on that subject until the following morning they would not be able to decide who was right. It was a larger matter than they could discuss in a single sitting. He was sorry Councillor Monks made use of the words he did, but they were not used exactly as Councillor Mackie had stated. Councillor Monks said that the chairman exercised some tyranny which he would not put up with.

The MAYOR: On the committee. Alderman Burgess: The words were—" to prevent dis- cuggio, and in a tyrannical manner," Al&rman DeviES suggested that the matter should be fairly discussed, but not in open debate. It would suffer in no way by being discussed with closed doors, because this was simply a question of figures. It was not at all a ques- tion of sentiment, and he therefore suggested that the General Purposes Committee of the Borough—imother words, the Council—should be called in to assist the deliberations of the Sanitary Committee. The MAYOR You might call it a special committee of the members of the Sanitary and creaeral Purposes Com- mittees,

Alderman DAVIES thought, with a view to maintaining their dignity, it would be better to discuss the matter as he had suggested. He should be very sorry to hear any re- crimination, and he therefore moved as an amendment that the minutes of the committee be confirmed except those of such and such a date referring to the Longford Depot.

The TOWN CLERK said he Could move t'lle confirmation of of the minutes, except certain portions which could be re- ferred to both committees. Alderman CHANDLEY seconded the amendment as he thought Alderman Davis' idea was a very happy one. He was sure they would all feel very keenly if any arguments were to be entered into which might lead to recrimination, and from one offensive word to another. (Cries of "Oh.") Well, he should especially regret if any acrimonious feelings were engendered by the discussion. He thought the members of the committee had rendered such services that the Council could not afford to do otherwise than consult their feelings and the interests of the Corporation in every way and shape. He therefore seconded the amendment and hoped the Council would see its way to adopt it.

Alderman HARRISON : I should like to understand ex- actly what we are going to do? Assuming Alderman Davies' motion is carried, what then ? The MAYOR: We all know what it means. Alderman HARRISON : Assuming this is relegated to the General Purposes Committee and the Sanitary Committee, and they are of opinion that the course taken by Councillor Monks and his colleagues is the correct one, will the mal- contents be satisfied ? The MAYOR: You cannot say. Alderman BURGESS: Malcontents? A VOICE: The minority. (Laughter). Alderman IliatitisoN said he did not use the word in an offensive sense. Would the gentlemen constituting the minority consent to accept the result of the majority ? Alderman BURGESS said he would answer that question a t once if permitted to do so. If this question was fairly gone into by the General Purposes Committee in its entirety, and the truth brought out, as it could be brought out, he should only, be too delighted, and he would accept fully and unreservedly the decision of that committee. (Hear, hear). Councillor FRANCOME could not see why there should be the slightest objection to the Council hearing both sides of the question discussed that evening. He thought it was a shame to smother the thing in the way which was being attempted. If Councillor Monks had made use of a strong expression he should withdraw it. (Hear, hear.) Councillor LITTON was astonished at the suggestion of Alderman Davies' and that it should be thought there was a committee of the Council which could not agree without indulging in recriminations. He was convinced that what- ever discussion was carried on that evening would be con- ducted with the gentlemanly feeling that they had always seen exercised. The MAYOR said it was not a question of recrimination. It was simply a question of the best method of settling the matter. Councillor MILNER said it would be most agreeable to him if the subject was referred to the General Purposes Com- mittee. It was a matter of figures and calculation. • They could not explain the processes which went on without ques- tions being asked and answered, and the ordinary rules of debate set aside. He hoped Alderman Davies' suggestion would be adopted. Councillor BURGESS thought the whole of the members of the Council should have a voice in the matter. (Hear, hear.) Councillor MONKS explained that when the committee were discussing, or attempting to discuss, this matter, he stated what they had seen at Birmingham and all the rest of it. He need not refer to the remarks then made. He said when they were threatened with the resignation of the chairman and other members, "Now, this is not fair; if you can convince me that I am in the wrong I don't say I will resign, but will stay and help you through the difficulty." The reply was, "We will resign if we are voted against." If the Council would free him from responsibility he was quite willing to let the matter drop there, but as long as he was in the position of representing the Council on the committee he was bound to hold his own convictions. If he had an assurance that the discussion would be fair and candid, then he should have no objection to the course suggested, but if the matter' was to be discussed in the temper in which it had been it would be far better that it should be discussed there. (Hear, hear.) Councillor SUTTON did not see why they should depart from the usual order of procedure in this case. The question simply was whether it wag desirable or not to spend some- thing like £7,000 or £B,OOO. Alderman BURGESS: 13 not Councillor Sutton discussing the general question ? Councillor SUTTON wanted the whole Council to under- stand what the facts were. Why should they depart from the usual proceedings? Alderman DAVIES altered his amendment so as to include the whole of the members of the Council. Councillor SUTTON stated that he was speaking against the amendment. He was present at the meeting when it was determined that a deputation should go to Birmingham, Manchester, and other places in order to ascertain what was
being done in those towns. There was an expression of opinion from one or two members of the Council to the __

effect that they were doubtful if the machinery proposed to be erected was of the best, and it was consequently decided to defer the consideration of the subject another week. There was very good reason indeed to defer the erection of addi- tional plant at Longford. He understood that it was cost- ina £B,OOO. Those gentlemen were of opinion that better machinery could be put up for £2,0b0. Under these circum- stances it would not be right to pass the resolution, as it would be putting the town to an expense of £B,OOO where £2,000 would do. It would be very foolish of any member of the committee, but especially for the chairman, to say because they could not have the resolution passed they would not come to the committee any more. _ _ _

The MAYOR remarked that the amendment was whether the whole of the members of the Council should form a com- mittee to vo into this matter or not. Councillor PLATT said it seemed to him that the course proposed by Alderman Davies was the very best that they could take. He did not see that there was anything to be lost by a few weeks' delay.

Alderman DAVIES said his amendment was as follows : "That the minutes of the Sanitary Committee be confirmed with the exception of the minutes referring to matters con- nected with the Longford Depot, and that the minutes so ex- cepted be referred to a committee of the whole Council, to be held on Tuesday, the 21st inst., at six o'clock."

Councillor FRANCOMB said that Councillor Platt had men- tioned the word "delay." The members of the committee had simply asked for a week's delay and the chairman would not give another hour. He simply said if they did not accept the resolution he would resign at once. It seemed to him (the speaker) a very unfair thing that those minutes could not be threshed out that night. (Hear.) Councillor WHITTLE: I object entirely to Alderman Davies' motion. It is a great mistake. It i 3 a gagging motion.

Councillor RIDGWAY said that after the remarks of the deputation dated the 22nd February, to the effect that "your deputation, therefore, are of opinion that it will be well to wait until the Birmingham Corporation machinery has been tried, which is expected to be at work in about foar or five weeks," he was quite at a loss to know why those gentlemen who opposed the amendment were in such a hurry to get it threshed out that night. He felt sure that the majority of the Corporation would agree that it was much wiser to have the matter referred to a committee of the whole Council. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BARKER said as Alderman Davies had altered his amendment to include the whole Council, he should sup- port it. Alderman HOLMES was willing to support the amendment, although he would rather have had it referred to the General Purposes Committee, because he thought a small committee was more manageable than a very large body. Alderman BußoEss said if the amendment was carried, he would take his place on the committee to discharge the duties. (Hear, hear.) But he added that he never said one word in that committee room about resigning until after the vote had been taken.
Councillor MONKS: Nonsense! Alderman BURGESS: I am in the presence of Councillor Milner.
Councillor MONKS: Mr. Mayor-

The MAYOR: I cannot allow you to speak again. Alderman THEWLIS thought there ought to be a due regard paid to the deputation which had reported to the Sanitary Committee that it was their opinion that it would be as well to wait until the Birmingham machine had been tried, which would be in about four or five weeks. Why could they not wait instead of increasing the expenses? Councillor MONKS make an explanation with reference to his position in the matter. It had become exceedingly un- pleasant to him. He was quite willing to accept the amend- ment if the matter was to be discussed pretty early, and there was no reason why they shduld not discuss it that week. The only difference was that it would be discussed in a com- mittee of the whole Council. Councillor Milner had said that
the public service would suffer, and he agreed with him. They had had to carry on the work at Longford in a tentative sort of manner, and the longer that went on the worse it would be for the town.
Councillor JEANS opposed the amendment, which, after a little further discussion, was carried unanimously.
TUE RESIGNATION OF INSPECTOR 2ROFFITT.-THE TEN-. DEMI FOR POLICE CLOTHING.

The Watch Committee's minutes contained resolutions that the tenders of the following persons be accepted :—Mr. John Massey for conveying prisoners in the prison van to the railway station; Messrs. J. Compton and Sons, of 2 and 3, Aldgate, London, for the supply of clothing for the police; Mr. G. Colman for the supply of constables' helmets; Mr. James Hinde, for the whitewashing, colouring and cleaning required at the Bridewell. It was resolved that a gratuity of £l4 be allowed to Inspector Proffitt in lieu of wages up to the 31st March next. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman HARRISON seconded tb.e adoption of the minutes. Alderman HOLMES asked for an explanation in reference to the last resolution that a gratuity of £l4 be allowed to Inspector Proffitt. Alderman KEAN said the committee were to be congratu- lated on having got free from Mr. Proffitt for the sum of £l4 instead of haying his further services until March. (Hear, hear.) He thought the committee had acted very wisely in considering the wants and necessities of Mr. Proffitt's wife and family. Councillor FRANCOMB thought Mr. Proffitt had really earned some of the money when he was asked to resign, and he had been paying to the superannuation fund, out, of which he deserved something. He did not look upon it altogether as a gratuity. Councillor BROADBENT said Inspector Proffitt's conduc did not call for any blame from the Chief Constable or the Watch Committee. It was largely on account of want of personal bodily activity that he resigned, and he thought they ought to let him retire without anything approaching to a kick.

Alderman HARRISON said there was nothing specifically against Proffitt. He believed that his inefficiency resulted from a cause over which he had not any control, and that was he was too fat. (Laughter.) He was too heavy a man. He had not that agility that the Mayor and he (Alderman Harrison) possessed. (Renewed laughter.) He thought Inspector Proffitt was not quite the kind of person they thought he was. Alderman THEWLIS : You mean a man of weight. Alderman CHANDLEY stated there was an error in the wording of the resolution. Alderman BURGESS thought the committee had acted fairly although the resolution should have been worded better. The MAYoR said the reason a gratuity was recommended to be given was that they requested Mr. Proffitt to resign. He could have stayed with them three months, but he com- plied with the committee's request, and they gave him something to help him on. Councillor PIERPOINT asked if it was not possible to get the police clothing made by some local tailor. He thought it waa too bad to go to London for the clething for the police officers, when they had tailors in town paying to- wards the heavy rates. But they were put aside by the Council, and not even asked to compete. His impression was that the competition should be confined to local trades- men. (Hear, hear.) Councillor MACKIE asked whether the contract was already settled and the clothing ordered. The MAYOR: Yes. Councillor MACKIE said they could not allow the Com- mittee to order police clothing until they had submitted the matter to the Town Council. He went on to state that he was told local tradesman had not had a proper opportunity of competing. The MAYOR assured Councillor Mackie that the notifi- cations were sent out at the same time to the London and Warrington tradesmen. Councillor BlAcioE said he was speaking by the brief he held. He granted what the Mayor said, but there was no doubt there was looseness connected with the contracts of the Council that ought to be put an end to. Alderman CHANDLEy thought young members should not charge the Council with doing business in a loose way. Councillor PIERPOINT rose to order. He was an older member of the Council than Alderman Chandley. Alderman CECANDLEY would not dispute the point, and went on to state that the most careful consideration was exercised when contracts were being entered into whether they should be given to local tradesmen, or those residing in other towns. He happened to be on the Committee at the time the tenders were accepted. Notices were sent out simultaneously to the tradesmen to the effect that the Corporation would be glad to receive tenders for certain goods, samples of which could he seen at the police office. Some men who sent in contracts, he understood, never took the trouble to see what they had to tender for, and surely the committee was not to be blamed for a man not looking after his business in a proper way. (Hear, hear.) Tenders came in from only one Warrington firm, and one or two distant firms. The committee carefully considered whether it was right for them to give the order out of town, but when the tenders were opened it was found the figures quoted were so much at variance that it would be an in- justice to the ratepayers to accept the tender of the local tradesman. For helmets last year they paid Os 8d to a local tradesman, whereas this year they had the offer of helmets equally goo.' or better for 7s 81-cl each. Alderman WEBSTER said their efforts were always to con- fine the expenditure of the borough as far as possible amongst the tradesmen of the borough. He thought it was a duty they ought to discharge, but in this case the Govern- ment, as would be the case by and by in everything they did (when centralisation got carried to its extreme), insisted on having the matter carried out in their own way. They did the best they could, and they had always up to now re- sisted their efforts, and he hoped they would be able to manage better in future. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH said the Inspector asked what did it matter to them whether the committee got better cloth or not. The clothes had only to last a certain time, and they ccst less in other towns and must cost less in Warrington. They were obliged to take notice to some extent of what he said, and the contract this veer had been entered into with another firm. Councillor PLATT remarked that whep they could fairly give the contracts to local tradesmen they would do so, and he thought the committee had done right in this case. It was the same in Manchester as in Warringtonos the firm that was making the clothing for the police of Warrington was also making the clothing for the Blanchester police. Alderman BURGESS had come to the conclusion that the committee had exercised a wise discretion. The MAYOR stated that as the Government granted one half of the police pay they had some right to say what the , clothing should be. The minutes were passed.

div.head: ROYAL COLLEGE OF MUSIC.
div.p: THE ROYAL COLLEGE OF MUSIC.

The MANOR. referring to the invitation he received from the Prince of Wales who had convened a meeting in London in reference to establishing a College of Music in London, said it might interest the Council to know that he attended that meeting which was attended by the most eminent men of the kingdom. A resolution was carried unanimously that a Royal College of Music was sadly wanted in England. (Hear, hear.) It appeared that on the continent, at Berlin, Paris; dr.c., they had colleges of music, and that was the reason why the standard of music was so much higher and so much more classical in the countries in which those cities were situated than in our own. Several mayors from various parts of the kingdom were present, and he met some of them afterwards when it was decided that subscription lists should be opened, and that lovers of music and those who thought a college of music was a good thing should be invited to subscribe. He had much pleasure in stating that Mr. Chorley, the borough treasurer, had kindly consented to act as treasurer of the fund, and if any lady or gentleman in the town were anxious to subscribe he would be glad to receive their subscriptions. His Worship concluded by quoting several extracts as to the objects of the college.

THE LOSGFORD DEPOT.—LITELY DISCUSSION. The minutes of the Sanitary Committee comprised a're- port of the Town Clerk, that he had received all erdu Of the Privy Council, declaring the provisions of the Sales in Districts (Foot and Mouth Disease) Order of 1882, and the Sales in Districts (Foot and Mouth Disease) Order of 1882 Amendment, had been applied to certain districts (including Warrington), which orders impose restrictions with regard to the sale of animals on and after the 14th inst.—,lt was recommended that the Town Clerk give public notice of such order by advertisements and in such other manner he may consider advisable, and that he take the necessary steps to put the orders in force within the borough.—[Note.—By an order received by the Town Clerk,' on the 2nd March, Warrington is declared free from the operation of the above orders.]—Minute, that Mr. Fryer again attended at the request of the committee. After discussing the terms of his proposals with regard to the eNtension,s at Longford, it was resolved to defer the consideration of the subject for a wek.—lt was recommended that a deputation of the committee (to consist of such members as could find it convenient to go) be ap- pointed to visit Birmingham, Manchester, and other towns, Ito inspect the systems in use in those towns for the treat- iment of refuse, and report in writing to this committee thereon at the next meeting; also that the tender of Messrs. Compton and Sons, of Aldgate, London, for clothing for the inspectors in this department be accepted. —Motion by Mr. Councillor Milner, seconded by Mr. Councillor Crosfield, that the proposition of Messrs. Manlove, Alliott, Fryer, and Co., as contained in their letters, to erect buildings and machinery at Longford sufficient to manufacture 144 tons of pail contents into concentrated manure (containing 20 per cent. of moisture) weekly on the same system as at present carried on, be accepted. The payment for this machinery to be made in manure calculated at the rate of £3 12s. per ton, the manure to be delivered on the rails in Warrington. The details of the agreement to be left to the Town Clerk to settle. For the motion 3, Mr. Alderman. Burgess, Mr. Coun- cillor Crosfield, Mr. Councillor Milner. Against 4, Mr. Councillor Barker, Mr. Councillor Francomb, Mr. Councillor Monks, Mr. Councillor Whittle. Majority against the motion I.—Recommendation, that the tender of Mr. W. S. Pierpoint to provide and fix an electric bell in each of the three wards at the hoepital, from the house, for £6 7s. Gd., be accepted. There was also a resolution that the reports of the deputations (which have alreaay appeared in The Examiner) be entered on the minutes. —lt was recommended that an offer be made to the Man- chester Corporation to sell them all the manure manufac- tured at Longford, to contain 20 per cent, of moisture, for 12 months, at per ton exclusive of bags, and delivered free on rails at Warrington; and resolved that the Medical Officer of Health, the Inspector of Nuisances, and Mr. Councillor Francomb, be authorised to visit Birmingham to inspect the machinery and works there for the treatment of the town's refuse. As no one rose to propose the confirmation of the minutes, the MAYOR called upon Alderman BURGESS, who said that inasmuch as there were two minutes that he could not approve of, and consequently that he could not ask the council to confirm, his Worship would be good enough to excuse him. Councillor MONKS then rose to propose the confirmation of the minutes. He remarked that he had not very much to say except that large extracts from the minutes had been published, for what purpose they would see by and by. The minute which had drawn that reference was the one in refer- ence to the adoption of Messrs. Manlove, Alliott, & Fryer's proposition. So far as he was aware the committee had acted in a manner which they undoubtedly had a right to do. (Hear, hear.) There was a majority in favour of the proposition being negatived, and he had yet to learn that the committee had done anything unconstitutional or for which they were at all to blame. (Hear, hear.) Speaking of himself, he said he was one of the members who voted with the majority, and he had his reasons for so doing. Seeing, however, that much had been made of the matter, he thought it would perhaps be well for him to state his reasons, and leave the Council to judge for themselves. He was one of those who were not satisfied with the proposed additions, because he did not believe they were sufficiently adequate, and because he was not quite satisfied that the •mode the Council had adopted was after all the best. (Hear, hear.) The other members of the committee had much stronger feelings on the subject than he had, and they succeeded in obtaining the appointment of a deputation to visit other towns. It was unnecessary for him to do more than to refer the Council to the reports which the deputation had made. He thought those reports stated the whole matter pretty clearly. He was rather anxious to be fully satisfied that he was acting with judgment, and he devoted two or three days in visiting Manchester and Birmingham. From what he saw at those places he was more than ever confirmed in the viewshe held. Then he had a very strong reason in addition to these, and that was in reference to the results obtained from the plant already at work at Longford. He was very grievously dis- appointed with the results attained there, which fell very far below what they expected. He did not mean to say that this was altogether due to the machinery, because he be- lieved on reference to the accounts it would be found there was a falling off in the value of what they called the crude manure. But he was not satisfied with the results of the machinery at work, and Mr. Fryer himself admitted that he had made an error. As to Mr. Fryer, he believed that gentleman had as much to learn as the committee, but so far as Mr. Fryer's treatment of any mernber of the commit- tee *went, he had nothing whatever to complain of. Mr. Fryer had treated him with considerable courtesy, and there was no personal antagonism. It was a matter of public duty with him, and nothing else. If it was necessary for him to go into the figures he was prepared to do so, but he did not think it was necessary at this stage of the proceedings. A further reason he had for not committing himself to the proposed expenditure was that he was not satisfied with the W3V in which the depot had been managed. He had complained again and again that the management was anything but creditable to them as a com- mittee, and when the supplementary estimate was brought

div.head: LIGHTING OF THE TOWN.
div.p: THE LIGHTING OF THE TOWN.

The minutes of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee recommended the following plans for approval: —Plan of alterations to the ladies' school in Smith-street ; plan of new tool works at Arpley, for Mr. Joseph Hughes ; plan of shed for Messrs. Cartwright Brothers, at Bank Quay; plan of addition to workshop in Museum-street, for Mr. T. Fletcher; and the Lighting Sub-Committee recommended various alterations and additions to the lighting of the streets of the borough.

Councillor BROADBENT moved the adoption of the minutes, and observed that they were somewhat important as they recommended the firing of a considerable number of aeditional lamps and the introduction of several improved Bray's burners.

Councillor PLATT, in seconding, said it had been felt for some time that there was an insufficiency of light in the principal streets of the borough, and it was sought to remove the cause for that complaint to some extent. Councillor MActuE asked if the changes, numbering 40 or 42, had already been made, or they were to be made subject to the approval of the Council. In asking that question he disavowed the slightest want of faith in the sub-committee. He had no doubt they had taken the gas manager into their counsel, and there was no abler man in Warrington to whom they could apply in such an arrangement; but with him it was a matter of principle whether they were to allow a committee of two to alter 42 lamps, at a cost, he should suppose, of at least £2 each. (Cries of "Oh, no.") Well, he just wanted to know. (Councillor Platt: 4s. each.) The gas lamp opposite his door was never put down for 45., nor anything approaching it. But he would not discuss that point. He thought it would be quite as well if the commit- tee would wait a week or two, until the Council had approved their suggestions, before they re-enlightened War- rington on such aa extensive scale.

Alderman HOLMES remarked that at the last meeting of the Council there was a strong expression of opinion with reference to the bad lighting of the town; and the commit- tee had taken it for granted that the Council would agree with their proceedings. Councillor SUTTON: It just shows how difficult it is to please everybody. A great clamour had arisen as to why the Lighting Committee did not provide sufficient gas in different parts of the town, and now when the lamps have been put up, there is the question arising why they were put up. (Cries of "No, no.") Councillor PIERPOINT : Why they were put -up before confirmed by the Council.

Councillor SUTTON: We were promised by the Lighting Committee that directly they were in a position to supply these lamps they would do so, and I consider they are justi- fied in doing as they have done. Councillor JEANS said it was not a question whether the lamps were required or not. He, himself, had intimated that light was wanted in various places, and he did not think one of these lamps unnecessary. But had the committee power to decide upon, and do that which they had, without the sanc- tion of the Council. With reference to Alderman Chand- ley's remark about young members of the Council, he, and several other gentlemen, had several times been snubbed by certain members who had been there many more years than himself, when they had ventured to express their opinions on the question before the Council: Now, he opined that some of the young members had quite as 'much common sense—(A voice: " More,")—and right to express their opinions in the Council, whether they had been there a year or two. If any member had any opinion to offer he was at perfect liberty to do so—(" Certainly,")—and he wanted it to be understood once for all that young members should be listened to if what they had to say was worth attention, or if it met with the approval of the Council. He did not _ _ _ _ _ _ _

think young members should be snubbed in that way. Councillor PLATT said when he found that the lamps had been fixed before the meeting of the Council, he was quite surprised, for the committee had most certainly not given any directions nor hint to that effect. He thought it had probably occurred in this way. At the present time there were lamps not put up which were ordered in December, and representation had been made to the gas manager that these should be put up before summer or no.?.benefit would be derived from them until next winter. He thought the manager had been anxious to carry out the orders and had overshot the mark. Councillor MACKIE : I am quite satisfied, and would simply say: Don't do it again. Councillor BROADBENT also gave an explanation :of the matter, and the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: IMPROVEMENTS IN THE MARKET.
div.p: IMPROVEMENTS IN THE MARKET.

The minutes of the Markets' Committee, which were moved by Alderman CHANDLEY and seconded by Councillor GREEN- ING, comprised the following recommendations :—That the tenders of Messrs. Brook and Son, of Huddersfield, for glazed bricks; of Mr. Jas. Craik for sycamore tops; and of Mr. Stephen Moss for the ironwork for.the fish-stalls, be accepted ; and also of Messrs. J. Compton and Sons of London to supply clothing for the market inspgtors. The income from all sources for the past four weeFs amounted to £232 15s. id.

The MAYOR, referring to the recommendation with referenceko sycamore tops, said it seemed rather strange to have wooden tops to place fish on. He should have thought slate or flag would have been better. _
Alderman CHANDLEY explained that the stall keepers gave several reasons why wood would be better than slate or stone, and as they had to use the stalls, the committee did as they desired.
The minutes were passed. THE STOPPING OF FOOTPATHS.

The MAYOR moved and Councillor Platt seconded the adoption of the minutes of the General Purposes Committee, which contained the report ot the Town Clerk, that the Court of Quarter Sessions, held at Liverpool on the 17th January last, had made the necessary order for the stopping up and diversion of the road and footpath in Howley. Alderman WEBSTER remarked that a footpath had been stopped up, for which the public got no corresponding ad- vantage. He did not think anyone had a right to stop foot- paths in this way. Alderman BURGESS inquired if the footpath was within the limits of the borough. Alderman WEBSTER : Yes, it is. Alderman KEAN said another footpath had been opened up in its place. The minutes were then adopted. MUSEUM, LIBRARY, ArND ARTS • COMMITTEE.

The minutes of the Museum, Library, and Arts Commit- tee contained the Curator's report for the month of January, which stated the visitors to the Museum were 2,970, an in- crease of 886, compared with January, 1881; vols. issued to subscribers, 2,670, an increase of 128 ; vols. issued to readers, 1,265, an increase of 362. There had been received the following gifts, for which the thanks of the Committee were ordered to be sent to the donors :—From the Incorporated Law Society, their Calen- dar; Local Books Fund, two local books; Mr. T. Fletcher, Wilson on Steam Boilers; Mr. J. P. Rylands, MacGowan's Dialogues of Devils, Nicholson's Life of Margaret Clithe- row, Lindley's Botany, Moliere's Works, Journal of Chester Archaeological Society (2 vols), 17 other books, a pair of Guinea scales, etc.; Mr. Wm. Fell, plaster cast (painted) of Hake. Mr. J. P. Rylands bad sent in his resignation as a member of the committee, which had been accepted; and it was resolved that Mr. T. G. Rylands be appointed one of the Hon. Curators of Antiquities; and that Mr. Robert Pier- point be requested to become a member of this Committee. The minutes were passed on the motion of Councillor GREENING seconded by Councillor BURGESS.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

On the motion of Alderman WEBSTER seconded by Coun- cillor Dixox, the minutes of this Committee were agreed to. The report of the Inspector stated that 54 cases had been enquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed for 97 children: that 41 cases had been summoned before the magistrates, when fines were inflicted in 33 cases, 3 ordered to attend school, one sent to the ship "Clio," two to industrial schools, and two warrants ordered. Forty- two cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The minutes of the Finance, Town Hall, Park and Baths, Paving and Sewerage, Cemetery, and Gas Committees con- tained nothing of public interest, and they were con- firmed. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

EARLESTOWN RATEPAYERS ASSOCIATION.—This associa- tion, which has been re-organised and seems to be going in for some good work, of which there is plenty before them, held a meeting in Mr. Clarke's Assembly-rooms, Bridge- street, on Wednesday evening last. Various items of busi- ness came up for discussion, amongst them being the elec- tion of Poor-Law Guardians. A number of persons were nominated, and from the number four were chosen, and are to be recommended to the ratepayers for support. 1.0.G-.T. HOPE OF EARLESTOWN LODGE.—On Monday evening, at the usual weekly session of the above lodge held in the Lodge-room, Bridge-street, one candidate was initiated and several proposed; and after other business the report of the annual meeting of the South-West Lancashire District Lodge was given by Bro. George Clarke, DL., representa- tive ; the report being adopted. The item on the programme being "A night with poets," a good number of pieces by various authors were well rendered by members of the lodge, several being very good and appropriate. The meeting was thoroughly enjoyed, and it was closed in the usual form by Bro. John Taylor, W.C.T., at 9-40 p.m. EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN JUVENILE MISSIONARY SOCIETY. —The annual meeting in connection with the above was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Earlestown, on Sunday afternoon last, Mr. John Roberts presiding. After singing and prayer, the secretary, Mr. R. Parr, read the report, which showed that the noble sum of £47 2s. 31-d. had been collected by 60 of the juveniles during the year, this being an advance of about £5 over' the previous year. For this advance Mr. Parr said he was very thankful. It showed good work done, and he hoped the progress would still con- tinue and that the present year's receipts would reach over £5O. They must ever remember they Were working for the Master, who would not fail to reward them for their labours. He was also very glad of the advance made for another reason, because his colleague (Mr. Thomas Hipwood) and himself were now retiring after three years' service, and he trusted the same sympathy and support they had uniformly received would be increased and extended to their successors in office, Mr. J. H. Profit and Mr. William Clare. Appro- priate hymns were sung, and a sacred piece, "Let the King of Glory in," was very sweetly rendered by Miss M. H. Parr, the chorus being sung by six of the juveniles. Ad- dressees were given by Mr. George Clarke and the Rev. J. M. Wamsley, of St. Helens, superintendent minister. At the close over 50 prizes of books were given to the various collectors of the association. There was a very good atten- dance.
