div.p: RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COM- MISSIONERS.

TUE WATERLOO ROUSE QUESTION. On Tuesday evening, an adjourned meeting of the Run- corn Board of Commissioners was held, for the purpose of considering a letter which had been received from the Local Government Board as to the hospital, and the course to be adopted in relation to Waterloo House. Dr. Steele presided, and there were also present :—Messrs. Taylor, Handley, Shaw, Meadowcroft, Hazlehurst, Briscoe, Timmins, J. :J. Speakman, Rhodes, Lake, McDougall, Williams, Norman, Linaker (law clerk), Brookes (secretary), and Barker (sur-

veyor). Ihe SECRETARY was first called upon to read the letter from the Local Government Board, which was dated the 25th ult. It enquired, first, whether the Commissioners desired a loan in respect to the proposed hospital. If so, they ought to pass a resolution applying for the Board's sanction to the borrowing, and should also forward a copy to the London Board, together with the estimates and par- ticulars as to the assessable value, and existing debt of the district. The writer further remarked he was to add that the Local Government Board would defer dealing with the proposal as to Waterloo House until the Commissioners were in a position to determine the purpose for which they desired to use it. Dr. McDoroAnt said that some time ago he proposed a resolution that the Commissioners should migrate from their offices in that building to Waterloo House, and an amend- ment was moved upon tlAt to the effect that they should simply write to the Local Government Board stating that they had not finally determined what to do in respect to the matter. After some farther conversation, Mr. HANDLEY agreed to move, as chairman of the Hospitil Committee, that an answer be sent to the effect that the Commissioners did not, at present, desire to take up a loan from the Local Govern- ment Board for hospital purposes. Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion, which was passed. Mr. HANDLEY then said that as the matter which had now to be considered by the meeting, was referred to the Hospital Committee, it became his duty, as chairman, to make some explanatory observations in relation to it. He would, first of all, submit for their consideration a resolution of a very definite nature, which would be easily unlerstood, to the effect that a reply be forwarded to the Local Government Board stating that the Commissioners intended occupying Waterloo House as public offices. He thought they would all agree with him that the present was not the best time for disposing of property, even if the Board were desirous of selling the building, as there was so much property in the market. This description of investment had of late been very much depreciated in value, and if they sold Waterloo House at the present time they could not expect to realise for it the sum they originally expended in its pur- chase, especially if they took into consideration the charges which had fallen upon the Commissioners whilst they had had had it in their possession. They all knew that land it- self seldom depreciated to any very great extent in value, and that in the neighbourhood of Waterloo House had for some considerable time been increasing in price. He remembered that some six or eight years ago, freehold land in the neighbourhood in question was sold for about 2s. 6d. a yard, but some very short time after, it was disposed of for considerably more than that price. Since that time land there had been sold for ten shillings a yard, and when the Board wanted some for the improvement of Waterloo-road, they wanted 20s. per yard. Under these circumstances, there was no need for hurry in disposing of the house and land, and they had also the satisfaction of knowing that if it came to a question of absolute sale, they would be able to recoup themselves for the outlay to which they had gone in regard to it. It must be pretty clear to all of them that as Water- loo House stood upon 3,000 yards of land, there was very little doubt that the Commissioners, if they wished to sell, Wald obtain a BUM which would quite cover the £2,000 ex- pended in the original purchase. The question for their consideration was whether the building referred to was adapted for public offices. He was of opinion that even if they had built Waterloo-house for that special purpose, it could not have been oetter planned. The speaker then pro- ceeded to dilate upon this point, and illustrated his remarks by a reference to plans prepared by the surveyor. One portion of the building might be at once separated from the main structure, and let as a private house having a private entrance,with about six bed-rooms. This would bring in a fair rent, and leave the sum to be provided by the Commis- sioners very small indeed. They had all no doubt observed how the inspector of nuisances had now no special office in which he could receive orders, or attend to the town's busi- ness; and in Waterloo House it would be quite possible to provide him an office, and a residence, as well as one for the caretaker. He believed that none of them would regret migrating from the present offices, which, though quite sufficient for the transaction of the town's business in the year 1848, were not sufficiently com- modious in the present year of grace. It had been said that Waterloo House was not in the centre of the town, but he was of opinion that if they took the Bridgewater docks as one extreme point, and the Old Quay docks as another, they would come to the decision that it was very nearly so. He found that there was a consensus of opinion amongst the ratepayers that the Commissionerewould do a wise thing if they took the step which he had the pleasure of proposing to them in the resolution. (Applause.) Mr. Heznzorunst seconded the motion. In reply to a question from Mr. Lake as to whether the Commissioners were possessed of any powers that would en- able them to let part of Waterloo House, The Law CLERK said he did not see how the Local Gov- ernment Board could object to their doing so if they decided to make the removal. Mr. LAKE pointed out that the money was borrowed for the purchase of the building, on the understanding that it was to be used for hospital purposes. Mr. LINAKER reminded the Board that when the Commis- sioners purchased the building they did so without asking the sanction of the Local Government Board to their pursu- ing such a course, but after becoming possessed of it they asked the question, Will this do for hospital purposes? They might send up a resolution to the Local Government Board stating they had adopted Waterloo House as offices. Mr. NORMAN asked whether the Board did not think it was possible to let Waterloo House and continue in the offices they at present occupied. He was of opinion that the Board-room they at present possessed was quite suffi- cient for all purposes. Even if they made the proposed change, they would probably soon have to move again owing to some one making them an offer for the house and

land. Mr. HAZLEHURST : But we need not accept the offer. Mr. Noremsar : But look at the interest on the money— £2,ooo! It appears to me a great place to be wholly occu- pied by the offices of this Board. I should be willing to move an amendment. Pr. McDotTGALL believed that if the town were polled they would find 90 per cent. of the population in favour of the proposed removal. He had a very distinct recollection that Mr. Norman was one of those gentlemen who actually voted the money for the purchase of Waterloo House, in order that it might be used as an hospital [Mr. NORMAN: Hear, hear], but when it came to spending 800 more upon the alterations, he, like every other sensible man, did not see the advisability of doing so. If they had expended the £BOO, it would have landed them in a total expenditure of about £3,000, for what would have been a perfect wilderness of a place for that particular pur- pose. He did not, however, think that Mr. Norman really meant to stunt the growth of the new institution which the Leval possessed—the Free Library. Mr. SHAW: You can only stunt something that is grow- ing. (Laughter). Dr. MCDOUGALL said there was not a doubt that the Free Library was growing. Since 1848, the population of the town had doubled, and they had a very greatly increased rateable value to fall back upon, which would quite justify them in going to Waterloo House, where the Free Library would find a home, and there would be an opportunity offered for its extension. Surely the Board did not take such a limited view of their duties as to merely consider the question from a monetary point of view. Surely there was something even higher and nobler than the mere keeping down of rates! The intellectual and moral growth of Run- corn was in their hands, to a very great extent. He was not desirous of ignoring the fact that they also held in trust the commercial interests of the town to a large degree, but he felt sure from the views they had taken of those interests in the past, they would come to th 3 conclusion that the present offices were not at all commensurate with the importance of the 'town. There was some talk of a prospective tenant for Waterloo House. If it were proposed to occupy it for the purpose of a public school, what would that really mean ? That one-half of the amount paid as rent would have to be expended in keeping the place in repair ! Mr. NORMAN: Who has made any reference to a public school? How do you know that some one from Widnes would not bid for it? Dr. MCDOUGALL hoped he would not be interrupted in the course of his observations. (Laughter.) He proceeded to ridicule the idea that any Widnes gentleman would be so wanting in judgment as to take a house situated like the one in Waterloo-road at a rental of £BO a year, when for a similar sum he could obtain a residence in a much more pleasant locality. He was not of opinion that much money would have to be spent in adapting the place for the pur- poses of the Board. He had greater confidence in the future of Runcorn than to think they would come to such a pass that they would have to sell Waterloo House to enable them to pay their debts. He had every reason to believe that they had more property in their hands than would actually pay for every shilling borrowed upon the rates. He hoped to see the day when Runcorn would not be looked upon as a place behind the age. Mr. SHAW said the argument of those who had spoken in favour of the proposal under consideration, appeared to be that they should leave their present premises in order that better provision might be made for the Free Library, con- cerning which he was sure ever member of the Board was anxious the town should have the full benefit. (Cries of hear, hear.) He considered that Waterloo House would be admirably adapted for public offices, but, to his mind, the real question appeared to be whether it was competent for the Board to saddle itself with an expense of £BO a year, merely for the purpose of carrying out the Free Libraries' Act. [Dr. McDougall: Query.] There was no query about that. If they moved to the building in question, it would be fixing a permanent charge of £BO a year upon the rate- payers, in addition to what there was at present, for the pur- pose of carrying out the Free Libraries' Act. Now, he had no hesitation in saying that for about DO a year he could provide them with a better room for a library than could be made out of any part of Waterloo House. [Dr. MCDOUGALL : Nonsense]. Anyone who bad seen the books which it was intended should form the Free Library for the town, would

admit that it was a library almost without an existence. The I moment the books became the property of the town, he con- I sidered it would be felt a disgrace to leave the library in so poor a condition. They would have to spend a considerable sum in the purchase of books. Dr. MCDOUGALL : But you have just said that we could not spend more than £l6O a year. Mr. SIIAW replied that he said so yet. If he was not labouring under a mistake, there had been an attempt made to get a considerable sum of money from outsiders, but he had not yet heard what had been the result of this effort. There were towns where the population had increased by leaps and bounds in the course of a few years, but Runcorn was not one of this class. It was not at all probable that in the course of a few years the population would have in- creased to 30,000. If such a thing was at all likely, he should vote for the proposed change, on the ground that it would be the bounden duty of the Board to do what they could for the rising generation. [Mr. NORMAN: Hear,

hear.] Mr. MEADOWCROFT was quite willing to admit that the present offices of the surveyor and collector were of a very shabby character and totally inadequate for the purpose. In fact they were a disgrace to the town; and there could be no doubt that Waterloo House would be admirably adapted for offices. Mr. Shaw contended that if they took such a course they would saddle themselves with an annual charge of:£80, but this was not a correct statement, because they must remember that the building was at present on the hands of the Board. It appeared to him that going to Waterloo House] would not cause them to be saddled with any additional rate. He should have been prepared to speak more strongly in favour of such a course if Mr. Handley and Dr. MeDougall had given the Board more information as to their intentions. Dr. McDouGam, replied that in the course of his remarks he mentioned, as one of his reasons for going to Waterloo house, that they ought not stunt the growth of the Free Library. Mr. Slaw: It was done by inference. Dr. MCDOUGALL : I hardly think that it is fair that third parties should interfere when lam addressing the chair. (Laughter and hear, hear.) Mr. MEADOWCROFT considered that it would be quite pos- sible to make use of the building in which they were then met, by letting it to a solicitor' or other gentleman. Mr. HAZLEIIVRST remarked that he considered it only right that he should tell the Board that the Library Com- mittee had under their consideration the desirability of having the library at Waterloo House, but they came to the conclusion that it would be much better that it should be in the present board-room. Mr. LAKE strongly objected to any decision being arrived at in regard to moving to Waterloo House until the Board had decided what they would do with their present offices. He should have thought that Waterloo House would have done very well for the library, as there were 13 rooms there. After some further discussion of a conversational charac- ter it was proposed by Mr. LaKE,and seconded by Mr. SHAW, that a reply be sent to the Local Government Board, to the effect that a committee were considering what should be done with the various properties of the Board (including Waterloo House), and the result should be communicated to them. Mr. HANDLEY, in reply, said the books of the Board would show that whilst Waterloo House had been on the hands of the Board it had cost them about £lOO a year. He con- tended that they had not, according to the 175th section of the Public Health Act, any power to let Waterloo House under the circumstances in which it was acquired. There voted for the amendment :—Messrs. Norman, Williams, Lake, J. J. Speakman, Shaw, Taylor, and the Chairman, 7. Against: Messrs. Handley, Briscoe, Hazle- hurst, Timmins, Meadowcroft, Rhodes, and McDougall, 7. The CHAIRMAN gave his casting vote in favour of the amendment, which was declared carried. The Secretary was instructed to write to the Local Government Board stating the result of the discussion. Dr. MCDOUGALL said he should call a public Meeting of the ratepayers to consider the subject, after which the pro- ceedings terminated.
WIDNES WESLEYAN QUARTERLY

div.head: CIRCUIT MEETING.
div.p: CIRCUIT MEETING.
PROPOSED NEW CHAPEL-GENEROUS OFFER OF MR. F. H. GOSSAGE.

The Widnes Wesleyan Methodist quarterly circuit meet- ing wits held in Victoria-road Chapel, on Monday. The Rev. J. H. Cummings (superintendent) presided, and there were also present the Rev. J. Tesseyman, Messrs. Benjamin Brown, R. Fogg, T. Sadler, W. Hartland, S. Robinson, T. Hadfield, C. Robinson, J. Hadfield, H. Stott, J. Williamson, W. Jackson, J. Duxbury' G. Proctor, T. Whitby, J. Hart- land, F. Lawrinson, D. Davies, G. Davies, T. S. Swale, P. G:over, Thomas Gill (secretary), Stott, Warham, Jones, Rickard, Frame, Littler Ormeroyde, Rogers, Hunt, Brime- low, Hewson, mime, and Houghton. Mr. T. SADLER, on behalf of the circuit stewards, read the statement of accounts which showed that the ordinary income had amounted to 4s. 7d., and, with the extra- ordinary, reached £l9O Cs. Bd. The total expenditure was £177 4s. 30., leaving a balance of £l3 2s. 4d.—On the motion of Mr. BENJAMIN BaowN, seconded by Mr. HOUGH- TON, the statement of accounts, as read, was adopted. The CHAIRMAN reported that there were 472 members in the society, of whom 41 were on trial, as compared with 417 members last years.—This statement was received with general satisfaction. ' It was decided that the two stewards (Messrs. T. Sadler and R. Fogg) should attend the forthcoming district meet- ing at Southport, in May, and they intimated their willing- ness to do so. The meeting gave its sanction to the erection of a new chapel in Oakland-street, at a cost of £2,500, to be called "The Hartland Chapel." The CHAIRMAN said that he had received a letter from Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., promising a dration of £l,OOO, and expressing a wish that the new building might be called by the above name. On the motion of Mr. BROWN, the following resolution was agreed to :—" That the thanks of the Widnes circuit, assembled at their quarterly meeting, are hereby tendered to F. H. Gossage, Esq., for his generous promised contribution; and the trustees of the proposed new Wesleyan Methodist chapel in Oakland-street, whereby the building of a suitable chapel is made practicable; and the meeting appreciates the suggestion that it be named 'The Hartland Wesleyan Chapel.'" The following proposition was passed, on the motion of Mr. SADLER, seconded by Mr. FoGG:—" That the thanks of this meeting be given to the Ladies' Sewing Meeting for their donations to the Circuit Committee,' thereby clearing off the circuit debt, and also granting a sum of money to be expended, especially on the ministers' houses." A vote of thanks was given to the Rev. J. H. Cummings for his services during the past year, on the motion of Mr. SADLER, seconded by Mr. R. FoGG. • A similar compliment was paid to the Rev. J. Tesseyman. The Rev. J. H. Cummings received a unanimous invita- tion to stay in the circuit as superintendent minister for another year; and said he would delay his answer for a few weeks. A similar invitation was given to the Rev. J. Tesseyman, and accepted. It was resolved that a convention of the class leaders in the circuit should be held at an early date; and Mr. Brown kindly offered to provide tea on that occasion.

div.head: WIDNES AND Tie AMALGAMATED
div.p: WIDNES AND Tie AMALGAMATED

• . _ SOCIETY OF RAILWAY SERVANTS. On Monday evening, the members of the Amalgamated , society of Railway Servants in Widnes, held a meeting at Anderson's Hotel. There was a good attendance, and al signalman from the London and North-Western Railway occupied the chair. Those present included the employes from the last-named company, and men belonging to the t Sheffield and Midland Committee. The principal feature of the meeting was an address of an interesting character from , Mr. Duffin, of London, (the travelling secretary) on the objects and operations of the amalgamated society. He re- marked that railway labour was entitled to be looked upon , as of a skilled character, in the main. They knew very well , that the engine driver must begin as a cleaner, and after , acquiring an acquaintance with the various parts of a loco- I motive, he must serve a long apprenticeship as a fireman in order to acquire a knovledge of the working of an engine in motion, and of the intricate system of signalling. The latter required great skill and constant watchfulness and I presence of mind. In like manner, the stationmaster, the inspector, the guard, the shunter, the checker, and the porter had to be trained to their work before they could become efficient servants, and they had further to master the geography of the system upon which they were employed. Railway employment, regarded from a numerical standpoint, was second only to one other industry in the United King- dom. The miners occupied the first position, and the rail- way service came next in order, with an army of net fewer than 300,000, of whom a'Jout 140,000 were engaged in manipulating the traffic and repairing the roads, whilst the rest occupied places in the offices, factories, and other branches of.the service. Napoleon the First once declared that every private soldier carried a marshal's baton in his knapsack, and they had often heard it declared that the ordinary railway porter or general clerk in the employ of a railway company had the opportunity, if he only had the ability, of becoming the general manager. The various efforts to form a permanent society of a similar kind to the Amalgamated were dwelt upon; and then a sketch was given of the constitution of the presentassociation on June 25, 1872, at a delegate meeting held at the Sussex Hotel, Bouverie-street, London, with Mr. Bass, M.P., as patron. The results of the agitation of 1871-2 and of the formation of the society were of the most gratifying description. Con- cession after concession in hours or wages followed. The hours of enginemen and firemen were on some lines reduced from twelve to ten per day; whilst on others their wages were increased, regular promotion ensued, and payment for overtime and Sunday work was satisfactorily amended. The greater independence of the men, and their improved posi- tion, accruing from the agitation and establishment of the society, were manifested in a variety of ways, and it would have been well for them had they had the prudence to retain all the great advantrges then gained by continued unwavering loyalty to the union. The society paid to its members when out of employment, 10s. per week for ten weeks, and ss. per week for a further ten weeks; ss. per week to members disabled by accident after 52 weeks' mem• bership ; and also the same allowance to those members over fifty who were incapacitated by reason of old age, after five years' membership, to those who joined in 1872, and ten years' membership to those who joined on and after January Ist, 1873. It was under-

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 18, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 18, 1882.

stood that strikes were not to be engaged in under any cir- ' cumstances. Amongst the other monetary advantages of the society were :—A grant of £2O when permanently in- capacitated by accident, or a grant of £2O when sixty years are attained after twenty years' membership. A member discharged for assisting in any movement, or holding office, was entitled to a protection grant of £35, or of 12s. per week , ' extra till re-employed. Orphan families of members killed on duty received from 3s. to 7s. per week (according to the number of children) until the youngest was 13 years of age. A. grant of XS was made to aid the destitute family of a member dying naturally. The entrance fee was one shilling, and the contribution fivepence per week. The speaker next alluded to the nine hours movement, which boon the artizan and unskilled tabourer had already obtained, whilst railway men worked from ten to twelve hours, or even as much as 84 hours per week. In conclusion, he pressed upon those present the absolute necessity of being true to one another. —Brief remarks were made by several of the MCA, and it was stated that in many cases a signalman worked froln 72 to 80 hours per week, and was paid at the rate of threepence per hour.—A petition was adopted in favour of the bill for the provision of continuous brakes, brought in by Lord de la Warr, after which the proceedings terminated.

AN "OPPRESSIVE ACTION BY A GR-OCER." - James Percival, grocer, Church-street, sued a I?:bourer named John Thomas, of Frodsham, for is. 64., the value of a can.—The plaintiff stated that he lent the car, to the defendant's wife in October last to enable her to take some blood to Frod- sham. He had many times p.sked her to return it, but she failed to do so until he tftok out the summons. When returned, the can was ricA in the condition it was when he lent it. It had another lid, and had been soldered, and in- dented.—Mrs. Thomas said she forgot to return the can which was soldered because it leaked when lent to her. The lid was the one lent with the can.—His Honour thought it was an oppressive action for a grocer to bring against a poor woman. She had forgotten evidently to bring the can back, and for the paltry sum of is. 6d. he thought the plaintiff ought not to have brought the action.—Plaintiff said defen- dant's wife had the can three months, and he borrowed it himself.—Mrs. Thomas: The can was only worth is. when it was new.—His Honour (to plaintiff) : You have got the can back. I don't think I can give you anything more. This court is not intended to encourage such litigation as this.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MoNneY.—Before the Rev. E. A. Pi Campbell (chairman),
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MoNneY.—Before the Rev. E. A. Pi Campbell (chairman),

and Mr. Wm. Bankes. LICENSING MATTERS.—Martha Griffiths was granted per- mission to sell at the George Inn, under the license held by her husband. A BUTCHER IN POSSESSION OF LIGHT SCALES.—Joseph Tickle, butcher, Bridge-street, was summoned for having in his possession a pair of scales which were two drachms against the purchaser. A boy named Thos. Wright appeared for defendant.—Superintendent Williamson said that on the Bth instant he visited defendant's shop, and found his scales two drachms against the purchaser. The shop was in charge of a female relative, and Mrs. Tickle was in attendance upon her husband, who had been ill some time. On Saturday, he again went to Tickle's and found that the scales had:been re- paired. On several previous occasions he had examined the scales, and always found them correct. Defendant's wife told him that owing to her husband's illness the scales had been neglected, and they had got out of order.—The Bench said that, under the circumstances, they had decided to only impose the lowest tine, viz., 6d. and us. 6d. Costs. PROSECUTIONS BY THE SCHOOL BOARD.—The following people were summoned by the Runcorn School Board for not sending their children to school :—Peter Crogan, Wilson's- row; John Whitfield, Bridgewater-street; Samuel Ashbrook, Canal-street ; John Cashin, Prescot-terrace ; John Davis, Salkeld-square. The cases were proved by Mr. Bowyer, attendance officer. Crogan, Whitfield, and Ashbrook were ordered to pay 55., including costs. The summons against Cashin was dismissed, and a warrant was ordered to be issued for Davis, who did not put in an appearance. CAUTION TO LURRY DRIVERS.—SamueI Hunt, driver of a miller's lurry, was summoned for havinw, on the 9th inst., at Aston, been at such a distance from his conveyance that he could not control his horse.—P.C. Egerton said that during the day time he saw defendant driving through Aston, sitting upon the shafts of his lurry, asleep.—Super- intendent Williamson said he did not wish to press the case, as to the defendant's brother had lately happened an accident at the Crewe works, and Hunt had been sitting up with him two nights, so that he was probably overpowered with slumber.—The Chairman said the offence was a very serious one, as it was only a comparatively short time ago that a child at Weston was killed through similar careless- ness. The justices had it in their power to impose a very heavy penalty, but in consideration of what the Superinten- dent had said, defendant would only be fined ss. and 9s. 6d. costs.

THURSDAY.—Before Mr. S. B. Chadwick.' ALLEGED lIIEFT OF A COW AT SUTTON. Edward Kil- kenny and James Backhouse, two young men, were charged with stealing a cow, the property of Mr. J. 0. Jackson, grocer, Bridge-street, Runcorn, and also with receiving it knowing it to have been stolen.—Mr. Moore, of Warrington, defended the prisoners.—The prosecutor said he lived at Sutton, in a house on the Warrington-road. Near the dwel- ling was an orchard, part grass land, and the rest dug ready for potatoes. In the orchard he occasionally kept a cow ; and on the side of the land nearest to Warrington there was a lane' about 150 yards in length. A fence divided the lane from the orchard, and the animal might easily jump over the fence.—Ann Ormson, post-mistress at Sutton, stated that she lived near the prosecutor's and the lane referred to divided their land. On Wednesday, she saw a number of cows and sheep being driven upon the -Warrington-road. The cows went up the lane adjoining the orchard, and she saw Kilkenny go tfter them. She told him that the cows might go through the gate of a person named Mr. Doodson. She did not see any of the animals go into the orchard, but she observed one jump out, and Kilkenny was behind Kilkenny then drove the caws down the lane into the road. and they were driven off in the direction of Warrington. There was another man in the road with the sheep.—ln cross-examination, witness said she could not say whose cow it was which jumped out of the orchard. She had no doubt that Kilkenny had no other intention than that of simply driving the cows dawn the lane. When the cow jumped over the fence it joined the others. She did not see Kil- kenny do anything to drive out the cow from the orchard. She had often seen the man driving cattle along the road.— George Ainsworth, a labourer employed by the prosecutor, said he saw the cow safe in the orchard about four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon. When he went to the orchard, about half-past five the cow had gone. In consequence of what Thomas Ormson told him, he went along the Warrington- road, and overtook the prisoners about half a mile from Mr. Jackson's house. Kilkenny was in charge of a number of cows and sheep, which were then standing. He shouted to Kilkenny to "turn that cow back again." He said "What cow ?" on which the witness replied "That cow standing ! still." Kilkenny asked him what he was making his row about. He referred to Mr. Jackson's cow, and he went to it, and turned it round towards home. 'The other prisoner came mut of a house near to, and stopped the cow. Witness , said "Heigh, let that cow go, it belongs to Mr. Jackson, of Sutton." Backhouse then shouted to Kilkenny that they had got the wrong cow, and must have lost one somewhere. He (witness) then took the cow back.—P.C. Egerton stated that be apprehended the prisoners at Warrington, on the previous day, and both of them said they were nut guilty.—Mr. Moore, for the defence, contended that a pinta facie case had not been made out against his clients. The cattle-ran away near the prosecutor's orchard,—he supposed because there was some attractive grass there. Several witnesses could be called to prove that Kilkenny did nothing to get the cow out of ' the orchard. In fact, it was not until they got to Taylor's farm that the prisoners knew the cow was with the other beasts, and he supposed it must have been attracted there by the fact that a bull was amongst them. The affair was I entirely a misadventure and mistake which any driver of ; cattle was open to.—Mr. John Taylor, farmer, Sutton; Mr. Harrop, auctioneer ; Mr. Joseph Davenport, War- rington ; Mr. Bate, Bridge - street, Warrington, and j Mr. Goodier, also of that town, were called, and gave the ; prisoners a very high character for steadiness and trust- worthiness. Mr. Davenport said they had been trusted by him with the charge of stock which was worth hundreds of thousands of pounds, during the last fourteen years.—Pri- soners were committed for trial at the Knutsford Quarter Sessions.

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes. SINGULAR ACTION BY A CHAPEL KEEPER.—WiIIiaM Clare, Wesleyan chapel keeper, Aston, sued the trustees of the Aston Wesleyan Chapel for 19s. Bd. for oil consumed and repairs to the chapel lamps. The trustees were • represented by the chapel steward, Mr. John Frodsham and the action was defended by Mr. T. H. Hitchin. The Rev. J. Nowell, superintendent of the Runcorn circuit, and Mr. Thomas Norman were also present during the hearing of the case.—His Honour: What have the trustees to do with the , oil? Who ordered it? The plaintiff said it was agreed that whatever he ordered for the chapel should be paid for to him when he paid his rent. His Honour: Who told you ? Plaintiff: The steward, Mr. John Frodsham.—His Honour: And how is it that you did not get the money back out of the rent? Plaintiff: I cannot say.—His Honour: Did you ever ask for it? Plaintiff: Yes, sir.—His Honour: What did he say? Plaintiff: He did not say anything.—His Honour: I can scarcely believe that he would not reply when j you spoke to him.—Plaintiff stated Mr. Frodsham said he I would not pay it until he had a bill. He sent Mr. Frodsham a bill but he had not received payment at present. He also j found four lamp glasses and found timber to repair the yard door.—His Honour: Who ordered the repairs? Plaintiff : I ordered them. It was agreed that when anything wanted doing I had to do it.—His Honour: But that was an agree- ment with Mr. Frodsham. Who are the trustees? Plaintiff : I cannot say.—Mr. Hitchen: It is a question whether the ' summons has been served rightly, though I have a defence on the merits.—His Honour: The plaintiff cannot say who the trustees are, and it is impossible that he can have served. _Plaintiff: Here is a letter from Mr. Frodsham.—Mr. Hitchen objected to the letter.—His Hor.our was afraid the summons must be amended by making Mr. Frodsham the defendant, and that it must be adjourned unless Mr. Frodsham would allow the case to go on at once.—Plaintiff: Mr. Frodsham is here.—His Honour (to Mr. Frodsham): Are you willing, to become the defendant —Mr. Hitchen: , No. sir.—His Honour: But stay, you do not represent any- one.—Mr. Hitchen : Yes, I do, sir. I represent the defend- ant. —His Honour: How can you? he is not on the cause. —Mr. Hitchen: Very well, sir.—His Honour said if Mr. Frodsham was willing, the summons could be , amended and regularly served upon him. He did not Isay who could be liable except the person who gave the order for the oil to be supplied, unless the plaintiff ould show him an Act of Parliament that enabled him to fue the trustees of the chapel. It was not likely that there might be one. He thought, however, that the plaintiff ought to take advice about the matter if he did not under- stand it himself. He only put himself to a greater expense by attempting that which he could not really do. It was quite irregular to bring the action against the trustees, and even if he brought it against Mr. Frodsham he could not say whether he would succeed.—His Honour ordered the sum- mons to be amended by making Mr. Frodsham co-defendant. A LENIENT LANDLORD. Thomas Middleton, owner of property in Granville-street, brought an action against Charles Lacey, labourer, to recover the sum of for rent. ' —Mr. Hitchen appeared for the plaintiff, and called Mr. • John Frodsbam, plaintiff's agent, who stated that the amount of arrears originally due was £27 Os. 6d., but the plaintiff had abandoned £2O Os. Gd. on account of the poor circum- stances in which the defendant was. The defendant ladmitted the debt, and a verdict was given for the amount claimed, payable at 3s. per month.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday afternoon, at the offices, Alforde Chambers. Major Cross presided, and there were also present Messrs. Kershaw, Matthews, O'Keeffe, Shuttleworth, Sadler, Booth, Carey, Brown Pankhurst, Heyes,Handley, Forster,Gaskell,juu., Allen,(cferk),Roberts, (engineer), Higginson (surveyor), and Dick- son (nuisance inspector).

THE NEW BYE-LAWS. The minutes of a special Board were read and confirmed. They stated that the new bye-laws were considered, and Mr. KIIRSHAW proposed some alterations and amendments which were carefully considered, and most of them were adopted. The bye-laws, as altered, were unanimously approved, with the exception of Mr. KERSHAW, who did not vote. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. The minutes of this Committee stated that the duplicate pumping gear on the ground at Netherley had been taken over by Mr. Timmins, as arranged, he having accepted the amount offered by the Board, viz., £4OO. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 1676 candles. The Engineer had been instructed to press for the completion of the work by Messrs. R. Daglish and Co. The Engineer submitted a statement as to a proposed change in the ,system of working, which, witb a slight modification, was approved, and the Engineer was instructed to adopt the

same. Mr. BROWN, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the uew arrangements as to the making of gas would pro- bably effect a saving of between £2OO and £3OO. It had previously been the practice to do the work in shifts of eight hours each, and some of the Committee were in favour of making an alteration to twelve. There had in the past been an overlooker over each shift, and it had been decided to abolish this official, and to keep the shifts eight hours each, as before.

HIGHWAY 1110MMITTEE. Mr. KERSHAW proposed the adoption of the minutes o this Committee, which motion was agreed to. At the meet- ing on the 20th ult., Mr. Oppenheim attended and reported result of the proceedings brought "by the executors of Smith" as to Moss Brook-road. The injunction to stop the building of the breast wall was refused. At the meeting on the 7th inst., letters dated the 22nd and 27th ult. were read from the Rev. Thomas Peters asking for the flagging to be completed at Simm's Cross in accordance with agreement. Recommended that the Surveyor be instructed to proceed with the work at once. The Surveyor had called Messrs. R. Davies St Co.'s attention to the dangerous state of the pit opposite Miss Rimmer's farmhouse. The Engineer to the Cheshire Lines Committee had agreed to see to the pav- ing and cleaning of Moorfield-lane and Peelhouse-lane bridges. Recommended that hereafter the following streets and roads should be declared public highways, and repaired by the Board out of the rates :—Church-street, Cholmond- ley-street, Bank-street (from Mersey-road to Viaduct-street), Oakland-street (from Irwell-street to Parsonage-road), Ter- race-road (from Mersey-road to Bank and Beaumont-streets), Earle-street, Ann-street East (commencing at the S. & M. railway bridge and going in a westerly direction for a distance of about 120 yards), Caroline-street, Catherine- street, Sutton's-lane (from Croft and Appleton-streets to Catherine-street), Moorfield-lane (commencing at or near to Crow Wood, and terminating at the Moorfield- lane bridge, over the Liverpool Extension of the Cheshire Lines Committee), Kent-street (from Albert-road to Thorpe- street), Oilier-street (from Sutton's-lane to Guest-street). THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.—THE FAIR QUESTION. Dr. O'KEEFFE moved, and Mr. PANICHURST seconded, a resolution for the adoption of the minutes of the Health Committee. These contained the report of the Medical Officer, which showed that during the last month the births had been 58, or 27.84 per 1,000, and the deaths 32, or 15'3 per 1,000. The latter included eight of children under one year, and six of children between one and five years. Com- plaints had again been made as to the lead works in Hutchinson-street, and the Medical Officer and Mr. Dickson had seen Mr. Glover, who had not carried out the alterations agreed to some time ago, but stated that the chimney was too weak to bear any increase in height. It was agreed that notice of proceedings be served upon Mr. Glover. It was recommended that the tender of Mr. G. Proffitt (£42153. fid.) for cleaning unadopted streets be accepted, subject to the property owners agreeing to pay their proportions. A notice of action had been received from Messrs. Teebay and Smith respecting the Farnworth drainage. The market receipts for February amounted to £l7 Bs. 3d., being a decrease over the corresponding month of last year of £1 Bs. ld. In reply to a question from Mr. Brown, Mr. CAREY (who had now entered the room) stated that he nelieved the steps which had been taken in regard to the fair were precisely the same as those in previous years. Mr. BROWN : But what are the steps? Mr. CAREY replied that applications for ground had been made by those persons who were accustomed to attend. The usual handbills about it were being sent out by the com• mittee, but no newspaper advertising was being resorted to. The handbill was similar to the one a dopted some years since. The resolution was then passed. A DANGEROUS PLACE.

Mr. CAREY drew the attention of the Surveyor and High- way Committee to the dangerous condition of the quarries at UptAn. The walls were only about 21t. 6in. high in some places, and they were dangerous to people driving in carriages.

FINANCE.—PROPOSED LOAN. The minutes of the Finance Committee were passed, on the proposition of Mr. HEYEs, seconded by Mr. GASKELL. They recommended that a sewerage loan be obtained from the Public Works Loan Board, to the extent of £20,000, by instalments, as required. at the rate of 31 per cent. per annum, the principal to 'be repaid by 60 half-yearly instal- ments. Letters were laid before the Committee from the Local Government Board as to the surcharge upon the treasurer; and it was recommended that the Clerk's reply be approved. Recommended that the general district rate be debited, the United Methodist trustees credited with £7l 7s. 31, the amount of apportionment for Oakland-street. That legal expenses account be debited, and Mr. 11. S. Oppenheim's aecount be credited with £394 13s. 10d., the amount paid on account of costs. That Newton Building Society be credited, and the following accounts debited : Amount allowed on appeal to the Local Government Board, Oakland-street £9 ss. 3d., and Bank-street £6 18s. Bd. The interest and establishment charges as to Cholmondeley-street were £234 Bs. 10d., Terrace-road £77 12s. 11d., Oakland- street £37 Gs. 100., and Bank-street £59 19s. Bd. The amount allowed on apportionment in the case of West Bank- street was £214 85.,100. The other minutes contained nothing of interest, and this I concluded the public business.

The movement is under the patron' many of the local gentry. At the I,v•a WO „ ril ikes, ACTION By A STATHAM PUBLICAN.— County Court, on Thursday, before Mr Wynne Ff°ll ear i judge, John Southern, publican, Star na, Stathanl,. oele, Lymm, brought an action against Henry' Di° for 35. labourer, Statham, to recover the sum of £2 goods sold and delivered, and money lent. Mr. Addeebro 00 appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J .. :Moore kMessrs. m. and Son) for the defendant. During the summer info the defendant carries on the occupation of a mower July and August, 1880, he went to plaintiff's hellus:oid ordered quantities of beer to be sent out to him to in which he was working. div.head: CENTENARY OF THE PHCENIX FIRE
div.p: CENTENARY OF THE PHCENIX FIRE
OFFICE.

At the Centenary dinner of the directors of the Pbconix Fire Office, held at the Albion on the Ist instant, at which many gentlemen of distinction were present, the chairman' 0. E. Coope, Esq., for Middlesex, in proposing the toast of the evening—" The Phenix Fire Office "—said : "I believe the general impression is that the PhLonix ' is but a bird of fable, hut I am able, on this occasion, to intro- duce to your notice a living Phcenix,' full of health and vigour, and maintaing a useful and beneficial existence. On the 17th Janu cry, 1782, the first policy of the Phoenix Fire Office was issued, written on an ordinary sheet of paper and full of corrections and inaccuracies! The amonnt of capital which was deemed sufficient for the commencement of the undertaking was sixteen thousand pounds! At the time of its formation our Company supplied a great want, and met with extraordinary support and success. We had however reverses, and in 1794 there were such severe losses, culmi- nating in a very extensive fire in Ratcliffe Highway, as pretty well exhausted our resources. But the Directors were men of courage and determination, and resolved to raise new capital among themselves, and they were well rewarded by a complete success. Twelve years later there was a loss of £200,000 at St. Thomas, West Indies, which the Company were well prepared to meet; more recently fires at Ham- burg, Newfoundland, Tooley-street, and North Amer; whose extensive dimensions are fresh in recollection. has paid in losses over thirteen millions and has accumu- lated reserves exceeding one million sterling, and has paid good dividends to its proprietors! During the whole of the period of its operation the business has been carried on on the same spot, and though the Phcenix ' has found it needful to build a larger nest, still this building is on the old site. Our firm of bankers remain the same as at the commencement, as does also that of our solicitors, whose services and advice we value very highly; while our secretaries and actuaries, if not absolutely born hi the office, have been brought up under the 'Phoenix' wings. It is to be observed, as not without its interest and useful- ness, how trifling causes operate to produce extensive con- flagrations. Old Homer has remarked— What great events from trivial causes rise; '

and, surely, with truth, this applies to fire; for example, the fire at Chicago was caused by the upsetting of a lamp in a stable; lucifer matches are believed to have been the cause of the Tooley-street tire, and a mouse nibbling lucifers in his nest is found guilty on another less important occasion. Now, in view of this centenary of experience that we have had, he would be a bold man who would venture to foretell the career of the Phoenix ' in this our second century. Changes, the result of discoveries of science, have been so extraordinary of late, that, perhaps, the advance of civilisa- tion has been more rapid in the last 50 years than in the 300 preceding. There is the Channel Tunnel bringing us into closer union with the Continent, where already our relations are so intimate and important. We have also carefully to observe those pioneers of that wonderful and undeveloped power of electricity by which doubtless before long our houses and streets will be lighted, and when our danger from fires and explosion is to be removed; though it is true that, perhaps, even from this, new danger may arise to some of Captain Shaw's firemen, whose wet clothes may come in contact with wires highly charged with the subtle fluid. Also the increase of popula- tion must produce great changes ; that of the United States will possibly by the end of the second century quadruple that of the old country, and our Phoenix ' Agents there, now about twelve hundred, and will then be numbered by thousands. Australia, an island nearly the size of Europe, may in this time have a population of many millions of British origin, having property to insure, and offering a good fielal for our operations ; and even the interior of Africa may, by British enterprise, be found to yield sugar, rice, coffee, cotton, and other tropical produce, and the Phoenix find itself, on its Eery nest, firmly established in a well- doing agency in the thriving commercial centre of Tim- buctoo ! In a quaint old book of the Company, full of wise saws and modern instances,' written we know not by whom, in the early years of its existence, we find it recorded

div.head: FARNWORTIT BANKRUPTCY CASE.
div.p: A FARNWORTIT BANKRUPTCY CASE.

An application has been made to the Liverpool Court by the trustees (Mr. Lewis Voisey and and Mr. Thomas Hayes Sheen) in the bankruptcy of John Knight, of Farnworth, to have declared null and void a mortgage by the bankrupt to the West Derby and Everton Building Society, in so far as it gave to the society a right to distrain upon the bankrupt's chattels and effects for monthly subscriptions in arrear. The society are first mortgagees on an advance of £7,500 made in August, 1875, on which was due to them, at the date of the bankruptcy in December last, a balance of about £7,470. The bankrupt had at times been much in arrear with his monthly payments, and had thereby become subject to fines at the rate of 5 per cent. per month, or 60 per cent. per year, and at one time the arrears were as much as £2,000. The society had also included in the arrears fines upon fines. Their first mortgage, taken in August, 1875, was not re- gistered as a bill of sale, neither was a second mortgage taken• in October, 1881, under an arrangement whereby the large arrears of subscriptions then owing were capitalized. The society distrained at the date of the bankruptcy (after capitalizing £1,600 thereof) for a balance of arrears of £664, and have gone on distraining since that date for the succeed- ing monthly subscriptions in respect of both mortgages as ttrey have accrued due, so that at the date of the application the society claimed in respect of these distresses a sum of about £l,OOO against assets, which but for their claim would be distributable amongst the unsecured creditors. Mr. Voisey was the trustee in attendance, and with him, as wit- nesses in support of the application, were Mr. Wm. Owen and Mr. Beesley, architects and valuers, and both of War- rington. For the trustees it was contended that the attorn- ment clause was an evasion of the bankruptcy law, that the society could not impose fines upon fines, that the clause was bad for the excessive rent it entitled them to distrain for and for uncertainty as to what that rent was to be (see- ing that the arrears was a constantly varying amount), and for non-registration of one or both their securities as bills of sale. It was further contended that at one date or in one month the society had the right to distrain for no less a sum than £2,000, or at the rate of £24,000 a year,. and that often the monthly subscriptions and monthly fines were together more than £l5O, or £l,BOO a year. Mr. Voisey's evidence was to the effect that the property in the society's mortgage was not worth more than a rental of £5OO a year. and in this he was supported by the t et° professional valuers named above. Proof was also given that the gross assess- ment to the poor rate was £2BB per year, and the rateable value of £216. The evidence for HA building society put the annual value at a much higher figure. In this particular case it was shown that the bankrupt had paid to the society since he got his advance in August, 1875, of £7,500 (less a premium of £3OO they charged for the loan, reducing his advance to £7,200), sums amounting in the aggregate to about £5,000- and that notwithstanding this large payment the society still .claimed from him at the date of his bank- ruptcy a sum of £7,470, or a sum within £3O of the original advance. Figures were also submitted showing that in one year of the period the society had imposed fines amounting to nearly £Boo.—The Judge, Mr. P. Thompson, deferred his judgment.—For the trustees appeared Mr. Mulholland, in- structed by Messrs. Brook and Morris; and for the society Mr. James, instructed by Messrs. Harris and Gorst.

div.head: FRODSHAM,
div.p: FRODSHAM,

VOLUNTEER PROMOTIONS.—Mr. Thomas Davies and Mr. Thomas Earlam have each qualified for and been promoted to the rank of sergeant in the Frodsham Volunteer Corps. VOLUNTEER CHURCH PARADE.—On Sunday morning the Frodsham Volunteer Corps attended divine service at the Iron Church, Frodsham, the officers present being Lieuten- ant Colonel Ashton, Captain and Adjutant Kerr, Captain Robert Ashton, Lieutenants R. G. Henry and H. Harrison; also two sergeants, and 38 rank and file. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, FRODSHA M.—A tea meeting in connection with the choir at the above place of worship was held on Wednesday, and in the evening a pub- lic meeting was held in the chapel, when Mr. Thos. Hough, of Frodsham, presided. Addresses were delivered by the Chairman, Rev. D. Schofield, Messrs. William Booth, Peter Riley, and William Locket; and a number of sacred -songs were very nicely rendered by the choir, which deserves every encouragement, as it contains some good voices, and evidenced careful preparation of the musical part of the pro- gramme. The Rev. D. Schofield, in his address, referred to the success of mission work in several places in the neigh- bourhood, and in forcible language expressed the hope that a similar revival might take place in Frodsham. Mr. James Hough presided at the organ with his usual ability, and in good taste. A collection was made at the close of the meet- ing in aid of the choir fund. MR. STANLEY WARDE'S DRAMATIC COMPANY.—This company has again been the attraction at the Town Hall during the week, and has been well supported. We need hardly state that the dramatic representation each evening has been of high merit, indeed, were it not for the all round excellence of the company we should not have to record the successful termination of the second week. On Monday evening the drama called "The sailor of France" was placid on the boards and showed that any role could be assumed and sustained by the company, so as to secure the interest of the audience throughout, the principal parts being taken by Miss Kate Read, and Messrs. Frank Seymour, J. M. Ward, and George Herbert. On Tuesday, the domestic drama entitled " Smoke " was produced, in which Miss Kate Read played the suspected artizan's wife with much pathetic power. Miss Hamilton, as the spitfire "Abigail," appeared thoroughly in her element. Mr. J. M. Ward, as the husband, acted with power. Mr Kruger, as bluff Richard Burton, was excellent ; while the part of James Brown, the car- penter, who was forced to smoke " Hayeany," was taken by the comedian of the company, Mr. Frank Seymour, Nillao provoked much laughter by his original acting and natural wit. The remainder of the week has been occupied with "Napoleon's Old Guard" and "Leah." Last evening Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., and Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P., patronised the entertainment, on the occasion of Miss Kate Read's benefit, when Mr. Buckstone's comedietta "Good for nothing" was given, concluding with the comedy" Check- mate." Mr. Frank Seymour's topical hits have been much enjoyed. AM,

div.head: • ASSESSMENT FOR WATER RATES.
div.p: • ASSESSMENT FOR WATER RATES.
WARRINGTON WATERWORKS COMPANY v. LONG-
SHAW.

In the Queen's Bench Division the case of Warrington Waterworks Company v. Longshaw was on Saturday before Justices Field and Bowen, sitting at Westminster. The case came on appeal from the County Court of Wigan. The learnel Judge having given judgment for the defendant,and stated a case for the opinion of their Lordships. The ques- tion had been the subject of considerable discussion in the neighbourhood and in different parts of the country, and was, whether water rates should be payable upon the rateable I value of the premises charged or upon the gross estimated value. The present action was brought in respect of the premises 6, Priestley-street, Warrington, and at a gross value of £lO, upon which the plaintiffs claimed Gs., being at the rate of 6 per cent., as authorised by the Act. The defendant paid 4s. 10d. into Court, and the learned County Court , Judge, after having heard arguments upon the several statutes, commencing with the Act of 1846, gave judgment for the defendant. Mr. Webster, Q.C., (with whom was Mr. J. Taylor) appeared for the plaintiffs, and drew attention to the several provisions of the Acts of Parliament, the most important of which were sections 63 and 65 of the Act of 1855. Section 63, was: "The company shall, at the request of the owner orpccupier, furnish to every occupier of a private dwelling-house, or a part of a private dwelling-house within certain limits, a sufficient supply of water at a rate not ex- ceeding £6 per cent. per annum upon the net annual rack rent or annual value of the premises, so supplied with water." Section 65 said such water rates shall be paid by the owner or occupier, and shall be paid at the annual value at which the premises shall from time to time be assessed to the poor rate if the same be so assessed, or if not so assessed, according to the net annual value of the premises. He con- tended that by the construction of these sections the de- fendant should pay upon the gross estimated rental.—Justice Field: The Act says in section 63 that it is to be a rate upon the annual rack rent or value, and if the matter stoppcd there there would be no need for discussion; but section 65 says that the rack rent or annual value of section 63 is the annual value at which the premises are assessed. —Mr. Webster: If it could be contended that the ratable value is the same as the annual value lam wrong, but I wish to contend that they are not the same.—Justice Field: But supposing the Legislature said that they should be con- sidered the same ?—Mr. Webster: Certainly. Under those circumstances I should be precluded hem arguing the case at all. I say it is the same between landlord and tenant, but not for the purposes of the water rate. The learned counsel then submitted several provisions of Acts of Parlia- ment and authorities in support of his contention.—Sir H. Giffard and Mr. Aspinall appeared for the defendant, but were not called upon by their Lordships.—The judgment of the Court was reserved until _after some cases raising the same point had been argued.

WIDNES POLICE COURT.

WEDNESD_kY.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. (chair- man), Holbrook Gaskell, sen., and John Brock. THE SCHOOL BOARD AT WORIL—The following were summoned by the Widnes School Board for not sending their children regularly to school :—Michael Monaghan, Wm. Thompson, Thomas Cookson, Pat Coogan, Philip Riley, Joseph Pennington, Henry Fountain, James Varley, and Michael McDermott. Each defendant was ordered to pay ss. including costs. Mr. G. H. Danby appeared on behalf of the School Board, and the cases were proved by attendance officers, Davies, Wood, and Joynson. REFUSING TO LEAVE A PUBLIC-HOUSE.---Wm. Stanley,

who did not appear, was charged with refusing to quit the Bridge Hotel, Church-street.—An officer gave evidence, that about ten o'clock on the night of the 4th instant, he was called into the public-house, and found the defen- dant there making a disturbance, and refusing to quit.— Stanley had to be forced out, and he was now ordered to pay a fine of 10s. and costs. _

OBSTRUCTING THE FI7BLIO FOOTPATH.—CbarIes Clifton was summoned for obstructing the footpath in Waterloo- road, on the 3ra instant.—P.C. Skinner gave evidence, which was supported by the Inspector of Police, to the effect that defendant blocked the footpath with two hampers and a box of greengrocery, and would not remove the things when re- quested.—He was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.—Matthew Boyle and Michael Roy were summoned on a similar charge.— P.C. Snowden said he saw the two defendants obstructing
the footpath in Lugsdale-road, at a quarter to eleven on the night of the 4th instant.—Each defendant had 2s. 6d. and

co-its to pay. DEVOTEES OF " PEGGY."—John Thompson, Samue Woods, —. Glasheen, Thomas Turner, Michael Croaloy, Elijah Brown, and Richard 13attersby had each is. sne and 7s. 6d. costs to pay for playing at " peggy" in Parsonage- road, Lacey-street, Albert-road, and other places. A similar charge against a youth named John Davis was dis- missed. DEAR AMITSEMENT.—Two youths named Thomas Quinn and John Delaney were each fined is. and 7s. costs for throwing stones near Widnes-road, on the sth instant. QUARRELSOME WOMEN.—Ann Halton, in custody, was charged with assaulting Mary Kruse, on August 7th, 1881. It appears that the prisoner asked complainant for 6d., and as she would not give it her, became very abusive and struck her. Halton was told that she must enter into sureties to keep the peace for six months, in one surety of £lO.-- Lydia Harrison was summoned for assaulting a respectably dressed young married woman, named Mary Ann Neilson, on the 6th inst. Complainant said defendant came up to her whilst she was standing at Dr. Brown's door and charged her with having been guilty of "making a jangle." She told her that she had no ground for making such an accusation, and requested her "not to make a black- guard of herself," as she had no desire to be the hero of a street row. Mr. Swift, jun., appeared for the defence, and submitted that it had not been proved his client had com- mitted any assault. The action had merely been brought by Neilson to give vent to her overcharged feelings. Defendant was ordered to find sureties in £lO to keep the peace for six months, or, in default, be sent to gaol 14 days.—Mary Noon was convicted of raising a disturbance in Waterloo-road, on the 4th inst., and was bound over to keep the peace for three mouths in £lO. A RAID ON UNLICENSED DOG KEEPERS.—Isaac ,Gandy, John Poole, John Tenon, Owen Tansey, Henry Hartley, William 'Welding, and John Stead were each fined 5s and costs (total 17s) for keeping dogs without licenses. Ann Rimmer, who was convicted of keepin a couple of canine favourites, for which she had no licence, had 34s to pay. GROSS ASSAULT ON A WIDNES METAL CO.'S WORKMAN. —Henry Richards was charged with assaulting William Hunt.—Complainant said he was a bricklayer, and in con- sequence of the defendant being exceedingly busy in the arduous pursuit of "fuddling,;' he was taken on to do some work at the Metal Company's place. On the afternoon of the 11th inst., Richards and two others entered the works, having just returned from a neighbouring public-house, and commenced to quarrel with him. Richards, after asking him for a chisel which he was using, struck him, ran him amongst some hot metal, tore his shirt off, hit him on the arm, and scratched his cheek. Several witnesses were called in the case, and ft was shown that the chisel which the com- plainant was using belonged to Richards, who was fined 20s and 19s Gd costs, or, in default, one month's imprisonment. —The Chairman said defendant might consider he had escaped with a very lenient sentence, as he might have been sent to gaol without the option of a fine for such an unjusti- fiable assault. ASSAULT. Hannah Conlan was summoned by Kate Loughlin for assaulting her, on the 10th int.—The evidence was to the effect that defendant met complainant in the street, and after a few sentences had passed between them, bit her across the face, alleging that she had been making fun of her.—Conlan was fined ss. and Bs. Od. costs, or, in default, seven days' imprisonment. MR. GASKELL, SENR., ON MATRIMONIAL MATTERS.— Robert Caldwell, a young man, who is a clogger, and lives in Church-street, was charged with assaulting his wife, a rather prepossessing-looking woman.—Mr. Husband ap- peared for the wife, and said she was married to defendant about 17 months ago, at which time she was a widow. He was instructed that Mrs. Caldwell had suffered very keenly from the effects of the peculiar temper and disposition of her partner in life. He left her after they had only been married five weeks, and she was forced to apply to the re- lieving officer for assistance. They were constrained to live together again, but their second experience of one another did not appear to have been a very happy one. On the 26th ult. the wife happened to make some observation which defendant did not like, on which he seized her by the throat, and picked up a large knife, with which he said he would take her life. She tried to live with him for three days afterwards, but foand it impossible to do so with any iegree of comfort.—Mr. Swift, jun., appeared for the de- fence, and said it was clear from what happened after the assault, that complainant could not be very much afraid of her husband, or she would have at once left the house. He maintained that the assault was not an aggravated one, as in order to constitute such a case, it must be shown that the wife's future safety was imperilled. It was simply an action brought with the object of obtaining a judicial separation, so as to secure a separate maintenance. He thought the utmost penalty the justices could impose, was to order de- fendant to enter into sureties to keep the peace.—The Chair- man said the magistrates had decided to treat the case as one of common assault. Defendant would be bound over, to keep the peace six months, himself in £lO and two sureties of a each, or, in default, be sent to prison one month.—Mr. Gaskell, senr., remarked that it was a very distressing thing to see two young people, such as the two who appeared in this case, who had not been married more than 12 months, living so unhappily together. The Bench had decided to give them another chance of seeing if they could not settle their mutual differences. The wife ought to be careful not to aggravate her husband, and both should try to control their tempers, and make one another happy, in- stead of making themselves miserable.—Complainant said she had been a good wife to her husband.—Mr. Gaskell, senr. : I speak as I feel. I am old, and you are young, and you may find what I say well worth listening to. You should try to contribute to each other's happiness, instead of making each other miserable. DAMAGING PROPERTY.—John Howard was charged with doing damage to a brick wall connected with some property for which Mr. Owens is agent.—Defendant was fined is., and 12s. costs, and 20s. damage. ca, It

SHOCKING CASE OF PARENTAL NEGLECT AT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, before Cap- tain Litton and Alderman Webster, John 'Gandy, a big, strong-made fellow, was charged with neglecting to main- tain his wife and five children, who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union.—Mr. Garnett, relieving officer, said he received an application for relief from the wife of the prisoner, and on the previous day be visited the prisoner's house in Wellington-street. It had a most desolate appearance. The only article of furniture in the first room was a small table, and crouching round the fire werefour children, whose ages Varied from four years to twelve. The youngest child was voraciously eating a little raw turnip. There was no one in charge of the children, but he afterwards discovered that the mother was a sempstress for Mr. Worralls, in Church-street, but she said she had no food for the children. Mr. Garnett at once relieved the family. He afterwards went upstairs. On the floor in one room was an old bolster and bag filled with chaff and flocks, and not a thing to cover the children. In . the back room was a pallet without any clothing, and this was all the sleeping accommodation in the house. The prisoner was an able-bodied man, and able to maintain his family, but their whole support for some time had been the earnings of his wife and one daughter, the former earning 6s. and the latter 3s. 6d. per week. With this small sum the rent had to be paid and five children sustained.—Prisoner: Did my" missus" tell you that she had £24 a few months back, and that she made it away in about three weeks? No, she did not.— Prisoner: Well, she had.—ln reply to Captain Litton, Mr. Garnett said the fire was composed of cinders, which the boy had collected from the ash-heaps.—P.C. Neill gave evidence of the destitute condition of the prisoner's family. He ap- prehended the prisoner in a beer-house in Buttermarket- street, on the previous evening.—The prisoner alleged that he and his wife had " words " three weeks ago, and the house looked desolate because she then sold the furniture. The children had never been short of anything.—Alderman Webster: You cannot say that. They are in the lowest depth of starvation.—Mr. Garnett said the family were in the greatest destitutior on the 21st Fetruary, when the wife applied to him for relief. She was, however, very reluctant to prosecute her husband, and on his promis- ing to work and attend to it, she withdrew her application. The prisoner had not kept his promise, and the family were in a more destitute condition than ever.—Captain Litton: Do you press this case?—Witness: Yes; I think it a very bad case, and calls for severe treatment.—ln answer to the Bench, the prisoner said if the case was adjourned for a

Mallen 15TH, 1882. THE FOLLOWING REPORT 11AS JUST BEEN RECEIVED BY EL C ATTERALL FROM A LEADING PROFESSIONAL AND PRACTICAL BOTANIST. REPORT" upon CLOVERS and GRASS SEEDS received from Mr. ROBERT CA.TTERALL, Seed Merchant, Ormskirk and Kirkham, March Ist, 1882. , "I have carefully examined the Seeds sent to me, and have tested their purity, genuineness, comparative weight, and vitality, and I can confidently say that they are, one and all, of a very superior quality. They are perfectly true to kind, and as clean as seeds can possibly be, The following is a detailed description of the several samples : "No. 2. RED CLOVER.—An extremely well-ripened and well-harvested Seed; heavy, and the individual seeds of large size, and, therefore, certain to make strong plants. Almost absolutely clean, only containing here and there an accidental seed or two of Rib-grass and Trefoil. These, however, amount to 0 per cent. It is almost entirely free from shrivelled or broken grains. Germinates quickly, evenly, and strongly, up to 91 per cent. No. 4. COW GRASS.—A heavy and large Seed, of an excel- lent colour, being well ripened and well harvested. Thoroughly free from weeds. Germinates quickly and evenly. Weeds 0 per cent. Germinates up to 83 per cent. (one more since last night, making 84.) "No. 1. WHITE CLOVER.—A very superior sample. Heavy Seed. Very well ripened, and perfectly Clean. I only , found in the whole sample one or two seeds of Trefoil, which had probably fallen la accidentally; and it appears to be quite free from sorrel, which is almost always found, more or less, in White Clover. Weeds 0 per cent. Germi- nates quickly and evenly up to 91 per cent. "No. 3. ALSYKE.—A good coloured well-ripened, and heavy seed, almost free from weeds, and very free from broken grains. What few weeds there are (and it is unite impos- sible to avoid a few) are the common Daisy, a very few seeds of Sorrel, and here and there one of Timothy Grass. The weeds, however, amount to 0 per cent.; ge minates up to 85 per cent. "These samples of Clovers, therefore, are most satisfac- tory, as regards cleanliness and general quality, and they likewise show a high percentage of vitality. "No. 7. CRESTED DOGSTAIL GRASS.—This is a very fine well-ripened sample, heavy, quite true to kind and almost absolutely clean. I only found a seed or two of rye-grass in the sample. Weeds 0 per cent. "No. 5. COCKSFOOT.—A heavy sample'of light colour, quite true to kind, and quite clean. Weeds 0 per cent. "PERENNIAL RYE-GRASS.—A fine coloured, bright, and very heavy seed. True to kind, and quite free from weeds. Weeds 0 percent. "MEADOW FESCUE (American).—A rem irkable seed, totally different In quality, and infinitely superior to the ordinary seed of this species ; ills as heavy as a moderately heavy Rye-grass, and of a fine bright colour. It is quite ttue to kind, and free from any admixture with other seeds. It contains a very few, accidental seeds of Rye- grass, amounting, however, to 0 per cent. This is the first time I have seen American Fescue; but it is impossible not to recognise its superiorityiat once. " March 13th, 1882." The written report from the Botanist can be seen, and the Seeds from which samples were taken for testing, can be obtained at R. CATTERALLB WAREHOUSE, Moor-street, Ormskirk.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. 5.* To insure insertion it is necessary that all items of news intended for publication should reach this office as early in the week as possible. ANSWERS TO CORRESPONDENTS. RADICAL, Warrington.—Mr. Brad'augh's majority in April last was 132. FINANCIER, Lymm —ln settling accounts of £2 and upwards. it is the debtor who is legally bound to provide the stamp if he requires an acknowledgment in writing. TRAVELLER, Nantwich.—The distance from England to New Zealand by the Brindisi route is about 12,000 miles, and by the Ban Francisco route 13,850 miles. From New York to West Virginia is about 750 miles. F. T., Widnes.—We do not know, nor does anybody else, "the proportion per ten thousand of the population of Great Britain," either of "infidels," or of 'persons who do not attend any place of worship on the Lord's Day." A. S. M., Runcorn.—As "county "and "shire "mean the same thing, it is incorrect to use them together. You may say "Lancashire," or the "county of Lancaster," but it would not be right to say the "county of Lancashire." J. Green, Frodsham.—The ports of England (including Wales) are 81 in number. Whether these are all "seaports" must depend upon the definition given to that somewhat elastic term. Legal and maritime authorities extend it to any port where sea-borne ships enter and clear—in which case inland ports like Gloucester would be included. Among the lexico- graphers, some confine it to ports on or " near " the sea—in which case London and Glasgow would be shut out. Others again more strictly limtt it to ports actually on the sea or on an " arm thereof"—in which case Liverpool itself would not be a seaport.
